cropfarming-soybeans

What it is: A growers' advice page on cropfarming.org, an unsigned farming trade site, headed "What do soybeans look like growing in the field?" It describes the soybean plant as a field crop looks: an erect, bushy plant on a central stem, two to four feet tall, with broad, pointed, medium green leaflets.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it only for the shape and the color of the plant, so that a bean plot on a map is drawn as something a reader could tell from rice, and a plant's habit and leaf color are not much changed by the century. Its limits are that it is a commercial how-to page rather than a botanical or historical study, and the heights it gives are for modern varieties in the American Great Plains and Corn Belt, bred shorter and more even than the landraces an East Asian farmer would have sown, so we treat the height band as an approximation rather than a measurement of our setting's crop.

cssn-jiangnan-weitian

What it is: An article on 中国社会科学网 (the Chinese Social Sciences Net, the public articles portal published under the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences), "古代江南圩田开发及其社会效应" (The development of polder fields in premodern Jiangnan and its social effects), from February 2025. It traces how the Lake Tai plain of the lower Yangtze was turned into diked polder fields from the Five Dynasties and Song onward, and quotes the Song officials who described the system.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the kind of source we want for how a wet-rice polder actually worked - channels inside the dike, gates and sluices on the outside, opened in drought and shut in flood - and for the spacing of the embankment channels that gives a polder landscape its grid, and it carries the Song-era wording rather than a modern paraphrase. Its limits are that it is a scholarly outreach article rather than the primary texts themselves, so we are reading Song descriptions at one remove; that the spacings come from a memorial recommending an ideal layout, not from a survey of what was built; and that this is Chinese Jiangnan standing in for our setting's rice country, which leans as much on Japan.

cssn-sangji-yutang

What it is: An article on 中国社会科学网 (the Chinese Social Sciences Net), "从生态美学视角研究桑基鱼塘" (Studying the mulberry-dike fish pond from the perspective of ecological aesthetics), from September 2022. It describes the dike-and-pond farming of the Pearl River delta, in which low ground is dug out into fish ponds and the spoil raised into planted dikes, and gives the proportions and the crops the dikes carried.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the proportion of dike to water and for what grew on the dikes, which is what decides how a dike-and-pond block is drawn and tinted, and it is written by a scholar for an academic institute's public site rather than by a promoter of the landscape. Its limits are that the "six dike, four pond" figure is a remembered classic proportion rather than a measured average, that the piece is an essay on aesthetics and heritage rather than a field survey, and that the practice is specific to Lingnan in southern China, so we treat it as one attested way of farming wet ground and not as a norm for the whole setting.

cssn-sangyuanwei

What it is: An article on 中国社会科学网 (the Chinese Social Sciences Net), "水乡农谚见证桑园围发展" (Farming proverbs of the water country witness the development of Sangyuanwei), from September 2022, on the Sangyuanwei polder in Guangdong. It gathers local sayings about the polder's silk and fish economy and about the sluice that let water through its dike.

Why it applies, and its limits: Proverbs are good evidence for the ordinary shape of a working day - who traded the fish fry, who fed the silkworms, that pond mud went onto the mulberry - which is the sort of thing that tells us what buildings and yards a polder settlement needs, and the sluice named in a place-name saying confirms the feature we draw. Its limits are that folk sayings are evocative rather than quantitative, that they were collected in a heritage article celebrating one polder in the Pearl River delta, and that nothing in them can be turned into a distance or a count.

daozuofang

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article 倒座房 (daozuofang, the "reversed" row), on the southernmost range of rooms in a Beijing courtyard house, whose doors and windows face north into the court so that its back is the blank wall along the street. The article sets out what those poorly lit rooms were used for: guest rooms, the servants' quarters, a family school at the east end and the privy at the west.

Why it applies, and its limits: It answers directly the question we ask of it - who lives in the row a walled compound turns toward the street, and why that face is blank - which governs how we draw the street frontage of a courtyard compound and where the servants go. Its limits are that an encyclopedia is a tertiary summary whose statements we take only where its own references support them, and that it describes the Beijing siheyuan in particular, a northern Chinese townhouse form, which we apply to our compounds as a family resemblance rather than as a plan to copy.

daxiangguo-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the Daxiangguo Temple, the great imperially patronized Buddhist monastery in Kaifeng, the Northern Song capital. It gives the temple's history and its size at its height, when it is said to have managed sixty-four departments with several thousand monks.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it as an upper anchor for how large a capital monastery could get, which is what keeps our own biggest temple from being drawn too small. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, that its numbers come from later temple histories rather than from a count anyone made at the time, and that this was one exceptional court-supported monastery, so it bounds the top of the range and says nothing about an ordinary temple.

desire-path-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article "Desire path", a general account of the informal tracks worn by people walking the route they prefer rather than the one laid out for them. It states that as few as fifteen passages over a site can be enough to make a distinct trail, and that such a path usually takes the shortest or most easily walked line, citing Hampton and Cole's 1988 handbook Soft Paths.

Why it applies, and its limits: Our maps draw the worn tracks between a farmhouse, its yard and its fields, and this tells us how little traffic it takes to make one visible and what line it follows around a slope or an obstacle, which is exactly the rule we needed. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary, and that the fifteen-passage figure comes from a modern wilderness-recreation handbook about soft ground in American backcountry rather than from any study of a premodern farmyard, so we use it as an order of magnitude and not as a threshold.

dili360-2005-sangji

What it is: A 2005 magazine feature by 邓芬 (Deng Fen) in 中国国家地理 (Chinese National Geography), "桑基鱼塘 最常见的美景风光不再" (Mulberry-dike fish ponds: the commonest of beautiful landscapes is no more), on the disappearance of the dike-and-pond country of the Pearl River delta. It describes what the landscape looked like: fish raised in the ponds, mulberry and fruit trees on the dikes, banana groves and seas of sugarcane, and the net of creeks running through it all.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the look of the thing - which plants stood where, and how the water threaded between them - which is what a map has to show, and a photojournalistic feature is unusually good at that. Its limits are that it is popular magazine writing rather than research, that it gives no dimensions at all, and that the scene it describes is the twentieth-century remnant the writer remembers rather than a Ming or Qing landscape, so we take the arrangement from it and any measurement from elsewhere.

dongjing-menghualu-rujia

What it is: An article by 吴钩 (Wu Gou), "大宋消防队" (The fire brigade of the Great Song), on 儒家网 (Rujiazg, a Chinese website on Confucian culture and history), which quotes the twelfth-century memoir 東京夢華錄 (Dongjing meng hua lu, Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital) on Kaifeng's fire watch: a military patrol post every three hundred paces in each ward, and on high ground a fire-watch tower with lookouts above and a hundred soldiers quartered below with buckets, brooms, hooks, saws, axes, ladders and ropes.

Why it applies, and its limits: The quoted passage is a firsthand description of the institution we draw - a watch tower that is its own building, staffed and equipped, standing apart from the ward gate - and that is precisely what we take from it. Its limits are that we are reading the primary text through a popular history article rather than in a scholarly edition; that the memoir is a nostalgic recollection of the capital written after it had fallen, so its regularity may be tidier than the city was; and that it describes one great Chinese capital and gives no count of towers for a city, let alone for a provincial town.

economy-song-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article "Economy of the Song dynasty", a survey of Chinese agriculture, industry, trade and money in the tenth to thirteenth centuries. We use its account of the iron trade: Robert Hartwell's estimate that per capita iron output rose sixfold between 806 and 1078, and the description of iron-smelting households working with government support such as charcoal supplies and skilled craftsmen.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives us the scale and the organization of premodern heavy industry - how a smelting operation was staffed and supplied, and how much iron a large premodern state could make - which is what sizes and sites an ironworking quarter on a town map. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, and the article itself reports that Donald Wagner questions Hartwell's method, so we treat the tonnage as a contested estimate; and a dynasty-wide output figure has to be scaled down hard before it says anything about one town's forges.

edago-ja

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 枝郷 (edago, "branch village"), on the Edo-period relationship between an original village, the hongo, and the new settlement that split off from it. It explains that the branch's assessed yield was in most cases apportioned through the parent village's headman, and that there were nonetheless branch villages with their own headman and group elders, treated on a par with the parent.

Why it applies, and its limits: Our maps have to decide whether a small outlying hamlet has any officer of its own or is administered from the village down the road, and this is the attested form for exactly that, including the exceptions - which is what lets us mark our setting's flat rule as a deliberate departure rather than pass it off as history. Its limits are that an encyclopedia is a tertiary summary, that this one is short and lightly referenced, and that it describes a particular Japanese tax and registration system, so we use it for the shape of the arrangement and never for a rate or a proportion.

edo-36-mitsuke-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 江戸城三十六見附 (the thirty-six mitsuke of Edo castle), listing the guarded gate posts around the castle, many of them built as a single unit with a bridge thrown across the moat. The article notes that the figure of thirty-six is a popular saying and that other counts, such as sixty-six or ninety, are argued.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for how a great castle's approaches were watched - a guardhouse paired with a bridge at each crossing of the moat - and for the conventional round number a place of that size was said to have. Its limits are that an encyclopedia is a tertiary summary, and that the article's own hedge is the point: thirty-six is a traditional figure rather than a count of gates, so we treat it as a convention and not as a total to reproduce.

edo-josui

What it is: A group of public pages on the Tamagawa Josui, the aqueduct that carried drinking water into Edo from 1653: the Tokyo Waterworks Historical Museum and the Tokyo Metropolitan Waterworks pages on the channel, the Wikipedia article, and an unsigned article, "Tamagawa Josui: Edo's Precious Waterworks", on IHCSA Cafe, the English culture site of the International Hospitality and Conference Service Association, which is the page our quotations come from. Between them they describe roughly forty-three kilometers of open cut from the Hamura intake to the Yotsuya gate, falling only about twenty-one centimeters in every hundred meters, and then buried stone and wooden pipe inside the city feeding thousands of draw-wells.

Why it applies, and its limits: This is the best-documented premodern water supply in Japan and it answers the questions a city map asks - where an aqueduct is an open channel and where it goes underground, what gradient it needs, what the pipes were made of, who built them, and how the water reached an ordinary tenement's well. Its limits are that these are museum, utility and cultural-outreach pages written for a general reader rather than engineering history, mostly unsigned, so the lengths and gradients are round public figures; and Edo was the largest city in the country, so its waterworks is an upper bound that a provincial town would never match.

edo-machi-kido

What it is: A page from "Edo - the EDOPEDIA", an encyclopedia blog on the historical city written by Gabi Greve as a project of the Daruma Museum, posted in 2013 and titled "machi - towns and villages". It sets out how the city was divided into districts and how each block was closed by a wooden gate, the kido, open from about four in the morning until about ten at night, with finer gates on the tenement lanes inside.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the gate that shuts a block at night, its hours and who held the keys, which is what tells us that these gates belong on a town map at all and roughly where. Its limits are that it is an enthusiast's compilation rather than a peer-reviewed or closely referenced work, so we use it for the shape of the practice rather than as an authority on any figure, and that it describes Edo, by far the largest city in Japan, which we apply to smaller towns with care.

edo-sanza-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 江戸三座 (the three theaters of Edo), on the playhouses licensed to stage kabuki by the Edo town magistrate's office from the middle of the period onward. It records that the city once had a great many playhouses, which were consolidated to four and finally to three.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives us the institution we need for a town map - that a theater is a licensed establishment, that the magistracy decided how many there were, and that the number ended up very small - which is why a settlement gets one playhouse or none rather than a row of them. Its limits are that an encyclopedia is a tertiary summary, and that the licensing was an Edo city policy under one government, so we take the arrangement rather than the number itself.

edo-three-dojos-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 幕末江戸三大道場 (the three great dojos of bakumatsu Edo), on the best-known swordsmanship halls of the city in the last decades of the Tokugawa period, with the year each was founded and the district it stood in: Nihonbashi Minami-Kayabacho, Nihonbashi Shinagawacho and the foot of Kudanzaka.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for where a martial hall stood in a large city - on central commercial ground among the townspeople rather than out among the samurai residences - which is a placement rule a map has to get right. Its limits are that an encyclopedia is a tertiary summary, that a "three great" list is a later convention rather than any census of the city's halls, so it cannot tell us how many a town had, and that these are all late Edo, the very end of the era our setting draws on.

kozukappara-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on 小塚原刑場 (Kozukappara), the execution ground that stood at the northern edge of Edo on the road out of the city, in what is now Arakawa ward in Tokyo. It covers the ground's history, its size, what was done with the bodies left there, and the temple hall founded next to it in 1667 to bury and pray for them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a compact account of a kind of place a city map has to put somewhere and rarely describes, and we use it for how many such grounds a capital kept, where they sat relative to the city, and roughly how much land one took. It is a tertiary encyclopedia summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, and it describes one particular city in one particular period, so it tells us the pattern for a shogunal capital rather than a rule for every town.

kubota-transplanting

What it is: A page from the public-education series on the history of Japanese rice growing published by Kubota, the farm machinery manufacturer, covering transplanting: how seedlings were set out by hand, and how the older scattered pattern the page calls 乱雑植え ("disorderly planting") gave way to marked straight rows laid out with ropes and rolled frames.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the date at which straight-row transplanting spread and for the simple tools that marked the lines, which is what tells us our premodern paddies should still show the older irregular clumps rather than a ruled grid. It is a company's outreach page rather than scholarship, and it is written looking back from modern Japanese farming, so we take its sequence and its rough date and not any figure of yield or spacing.

kuniezu-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the kuniezu (国絵図), the series of provincial land maps that the Tokugawa shogunate ordered every province to produce during the Edo period.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it only for the plain fact that a central government of this kind commissioned province-wide maps with boundaries drawn on them, which is what justifies a domain in our setting knowing and marking its own edges. It is a tertiary summary and a short one, so it carries no measurement for us and nothing beyond that single point.

kuramae-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on 蔵前 (Kuramae), the Edo district named for the Asakusa Okura, the shogunate's great rice storehouse ground on the Sumida River, in what is now Taito ward in Tokyo. It describes the eight numbered channels cut into the right bank of the river and the rows of rice storehouses that faced them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives us the form of a large official granary quarter: boat channels driven in from the water, numbered in order along the bank, with the storehouses ranged along each one, which is exactly how bulk grain moved before carts. It is a tertiary summary, and it describes the biggest such installation in the country, so we borrow its arrangement rather than its scale when a provincial city gets a storehouse quarter.

kuwa-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on クワ, the mulberry (genus Morus): its botany, its species, and its cultivation for silkworm rearing, including the note that although a mulberry can grow into a tree of ten meters or more, most are bushes and cultivated ones are usually trained low.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for that one habit, because it decides how a mulberry plot is drawn on a map: a field of waist-high bushes rather than an orchard of trees. It is a tertiary summary, and it is the only readable support we have here, so the plant heights and planting densities we needed alongside it are labeled as guesses rather than findings.

kweon-youn-2021

What it is: A peer-reviewed article by Kweon Deogkyu and Youn Yeo-Chang, "Factors influencing sustainability of traditional village groves (Maeulsoop) in Korea", published open access in Forest Policy and Economics in 2021. It surveys twenty-four red pine village groves around Mt. Jiri in Namwon, South Korea, reporting each grove's area and how many trees it holds along with the social conditions that keep such groves alive.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the closest thing to a measured answer we could read on a public page to the question of how big a village's planted grove actually is and how many trees stand in it, so it sets the size band our groves are drawn to. Two honest limits: it is Korean, standing in for Japan and China because no comparable open survey of Japanese or Chinese village groves could be read, though village grove planting is a shared regional practice; and it measures groves as they survive today, which records what has lasted rather than what was originally planted.

kyomachiya-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on 京町家, the Kyoto townhouse: the narrow-fronted, deep-lot merchant house, its plan and its history. It also takes up the popular story that the shape was a dodge against a tax on frontage width, and rebuts it, explaining that Edo-period Kyoto assessed a total on the block community, which the house-owning townsmen then divided per house.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the shape of an urban lot in a dense premodern city and for the correction to the frontage-tax story that a more popular source repeats. It is a tertiary summary, and it describes one city's building tradition, so our towns take the proportions of the form rather than Kyoto's specific detail.

kyototuu-unagi

What it is: A page from 京都通百科事典, a Japanese web encyclopedia about Kyoto, on the saying 鰻の寝床 ("an eel's bed") for the long narrow townhouse, giving typical dimensions of about two ken of frontage (roughly 3.6 m) and ten to twelve ken of depth (roughly 18 to 22 m).

Why it applies, and its limits: Those two numbers are what we use it for; they give a town lot a believable width and depth on the map. It is a regional reference site rather than scholarship, and it also repeats the frontage-tax explanation of the shape, which the page itself hedges as something "it is said" and which the Japanese Wikipedia article on the machiya disputes, so we take its measurements and not its causal story.

l7r-median-domain

What it is: The setting's own notes, written by the game master, in the sections "The Median Domain" and "Place Names". They set out how many hamlets and villages a typical domain holds, how many inhabitants live at each tier, the size of a household, where a hamlet's headman lives, and how a village and its district come to share a name.

Why it applies, and its limits: This is canon rather than evidence: where the historical record is silent, contradictory or simply messier than a map can show, the setting's own notes decide, and every settlement count and tier on these maps follows from them. There is no historical limitation to state, because the notes are not making a historical claim.

lacey-regime

What it is: Lacey's regime theory, the standard canal engineering account of the stable size of an unlined channel cut in loose alluvial soil, named for the irrigation engineer Gerald Lacey. It gives a wetted perimeter that goes as the square root of the discharge, and power law exponents relating a channel's width, depth and velocity to the flow it carries. We read it in a review article in the Journal of Hydrology (2003), "The width of a bankfull channel; Lacey's formula explained", alongside standard canal design references.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supplies the law behind the way our channels taper, which is that width grows as the square root of flow rather than in proportion to it, and it gives an absolute check on drawn channel widths that caught a network drawn five or six times its true hydraulic size. The honest limits are that this is a modern engineering formula, calibrated largely on big colonial-era irrigation canals in sandy soil, applied here to small village ditches, so we use it for the relation between flow and width and not to pronounce the exact width of any one ditch.

loess-plateau-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the Loess Plateau of northern China, covering the region's wind-blown soils, its erosion, its agricultural history and its climate, including the concentration of the year's rain into June, July and August.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for that one climatic fact, because a summer-concentrated rainfall is what makes storage ponds, bunds and flood channels worth drawing in a dry-looking landscape. It is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, and it covers one region of northern China, not the whole of the country our setting draws on.

louzeyuan-zhwiki

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on 漏澤園 (louzeyuan), the state-funded paupers' burial grounds of imperial China, from Cai Jing's proposal of 1104 through their continuation under the Yuan and Ming. It describes how they were sited on high, open, barren ground behind a fence on all four sides, and how each plot was numbered by the Thousand Character Classic and registered with the dead person's name, origin and dates.

Why it applies, and its limits: It answers, for a city map, where the poor were buried and what that ground looked like: bad land, deliberately walled off, laid out in numbered rows rather than left as an open field. It is a tertiary summary in Chinese, and it describes a Chinese institution, which suits the imperial-Chinese half of our setting more directly than the Japanese half; we take from it the siting and the layout, which its own sources support, rather than any count.

ma-2017-fengshui-carbon

What it is: A peer-reviewed article by Ma Lei, Shen Chunyu, Lou Duo, Fu Shenglei and Guan Dongsheng, "Patterns of ecosystem carbon density in edge-affected fengshui forests", published in Ecological Engineering in 2017. It measures forty-five plots of 40 by 40 m across five surviving fengshui forest fragments around Guangzhou in southern China, reporting among other things how much tree trunk area each hectare of grove carries.

Why it applies, and its limits: The basal area it reports is our best readable measure of how densely a village's protective grove actually stands, which is what decides whether a grove is drawn as scattered trees or as a solid canopy. Its limits are real: the full text is behind a paywall, so we use only the abstract and the publicly visible passages; it measures subtropical Guangdong fragments as they survive today, so it is a modern measurement of the remains of an old practice, and a southern Chinese figure applied to a setting that leans Japanese.

maff-drain-shape

What it is: A chapter of the Japanese Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries' land improvement technical standard, issued as a PDF, on the shape and structure of farm drainage channels and the conditions under which each is used. It gives the gradients such channels run at and how the interceptor, collector and outfall channels are laid out relative to the slope of the ground.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for drain gradients and channel cross sections, and the layout it describes - an interceptor run nearly along the contour at a gentle grade, with collectors dropping away from it at right angles a few hundred meters apart - follows from the fall of the land rather than from any machinery, so it still describes a hand-dug system. Two limits worth stating: it is modern government engineering guidance, and this particular chapter is the standard for upland fields rather than for wet paddy, so it is used for drainage geometry and not for anything about a flooded field.

maff-suitou-mizu

What it is: An extension leaflet from the Japanese Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, 水稲栽培のポイント ("points for paddy rice cultivation"), setting out how deep the water is held in a paddy at each stage of the season: somewhat deep until the transplanted seedlings root, shallower afterward to warm the water and encourage tillering, then the mid-season drain until the mud cracks and shows a footprint, with deep water held only as a guard against a cold snap.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for that sequence, which is dictated by the rice plant rather than by any machine and so held as well in a premodern paddy as in a modern one; it is what tells us a paddy is not simply a pond kept full all summer, and that a drained, cracked field in midsummer is normal rather than a failure. It is modern extension advice for modern varieties, and it is labeled as such wherever it is cited, so the centimeter depths are read as the shape of the practice rather than as a historical measurement.

maff-tameike-shizen

What it is: A document prepared for an advisory committee of the Japanese Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries on the part irrigation reservoir ponds play in the natural environment. Its figure shows the bands of plants that succeed one another on a gently sloping shore, from waterside woodland through wet meadow, emergent plants such as reed, cattail and wild rice, then floating-leaved plants and finally submerged ones.

Why it applies, and its limits: That banding is what we use to draw the edge of a village pond, and it is ecology rather than history, so it changes little between a modern pond and a premodern one of the same shape. Two limits: the paper is a modern government document about present-day ponds, and the zonation figure is credited to a book we were not able to read, so we cite the banding from this document at one step from its original.

nagaya-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the nagaya (長屋), the row tenement of Japanese towns - one long building divided across its width by party walls into separate rented dwellings. It covers the form in general and the Edo-period back-alley version in particular: the small unit of nine shaku by two ken, the shared privy in the alley, the shared well, and the townsmen and craftsmen who rented there while the better merchants kept shops on the main street.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the plain definition of the building type we draw along a town's back lanes, and of who lived in one, which is exactly what we take from it. It is a tertiary summary rather than a study, so we use its figures only where its own references support them, and what it describes best is Edo, the largest city in the country, so a provincial town's tenements on our maps are that pattern scaled down.

nagoya-castle

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on Nagoya Castle, the great Tokugawa castle of Owari domain, describing its enclosures and buildings - the keep in the inner bailey, the Ninomaru palace that served as both the lord's residence and the domain's supreme government office, and the third bailey holding the auxiliary mansions of the lords and the houses of senior retainers.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for two structural points about a lord's seat - that the palace, not the keep, is the working center of government, and that senior retainers are housed in the outer bailey - and both are stated on the page itself. It is a tertiary summary, so its numbers are taken only where its own references carry them; the citation line also names an AI-written encyclopedia page of the same title, which this project does not treat as a source; and Nagoya was one of the largest castles in Japan, so we take the arrangement from it and not the scale.

nakasendoway-dosojin

What it is: "Dosojin", a page on Nakasendo Way, an English-language guide to the history and culture of the Nakasendo highway published by Walk Japan Ltd., a walking-tour company. It describes dosojin - the small carved stone guardians of roads, travelers and local boundaries, often a paired couple - and where they are found, most often on the lonelier stretches of the highway and near the mountain passes, along with the related Jizo and horse-head Kannon.

Why it applies, and its limits: It settles the one thing we need, which is where such a stone stands: on the road and at a boundary rather than inside a farmyard. It is a tour operator's cultural guide written for walkers, not a scholarly work, and it describes one highway in particular, so we use it for placement and for what the stones are, never for a count or a measurement.

nanbu-date-mounds-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the Nanbu-Date border mounds, the earth mounds raised in the early Edo period to mark the boundary between Morioka domain and Sendai domain - a line of about 130 km running from the Ou mountains east to the Pacific - which the shogunate re-confirmed along with the two clans' holdings in 1642.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the fact that a domain boundary in this period was a made thing, marked on the ground by heaped earth, which is why such mounds can appear at the edge of a map. It is a tertiary summary whose details we take only where its own references support them, and it records one boundary in the far northeast standing for the general practice, so we draw the type of marker from it rather than any particular spacing.

nanjing-wall-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the City Wall of Nanjing, the Ming circuit built around the first Ming capital, describing how it was laid out in a winding, free form that followed the city's broken topography, used the river as its natural moat, and so departed from the square or rectangular walls of Beijing and Xi'an.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is our evidence that a great walled city need not be the textbook rectangle - that a wall may be pulled around hills and a river - which is the point we take for our own walled towns. It is a tertiary summary; the total circuit length so often quoted for this wall is not carried by any page we were able to read, so we do not use that number; and an imperial capital is far larger than anything we draw, so the principle transfers and the dimensions do not.

nanushi-en

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the nanushi (名主), the Edo-period village headman who administered a village under a district magistrate, with a number of group heads (kumigashira) and one or more peasant representatives (hyakushodai) beneath him - one nanushi to a village.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for that ratio, one headman to one village, which is the general rule our settlements follow. It is a tertiary summary, and it has a specific gap that matters here: it never says whether its "village" is the natural cluster of houses or the larger administrative unit that could contain several, which is the very question at issue, so it fixes the ratio and leaves the unit open.

ndl-hongo-edago

What it is: An entry in the National Diet Library's Collaborative Reference Database, where Japanese librarians publish researched answers to reference questions with the works they consulted. This one explains the parent village (hongo or oyamura) and its branch settlement (edago or komura): the cadastral register and the tax notice stood in the parent's name, the branch could pay its land tax only through the parent, and even a petition to the lord needed the parent's consent.

Why it applies, and its limits: That fiscal dependence is the reason a branch hamlet on our maps has no headman of its own standing, and it is the clearest statement of the mechanism we could read. It is a librarian's compiled answer drawing on Japanese reference works rather than original research, and it describes administrative practice under the Tokugawa - the era our settlements are modeled on - so it is close in both place and period.

ndl-kokumori

What it is: Another entry in the National Diet Library's Collaborative Reference Database, on kokumori (石盛), the assessed yield per tan of land fixed at the cadastral survey. It gives the grades that had largely settled into use: 1.5 koku for upper paddy, 1.3 for middle, 1.1 for lower and 0.9 for the poorest, while noting that this varied by region.

Why it applies, and its limits: The middle-paddy figure is the first input to the yard area we derive from a household's crop, so we need a period number for what a tan of ordinary paddy was reckoned to yield, and this is one. Two honest limits: it is a tax assessment rather than a measured harvest, and the entry itself says the numbers differed from region to region, so we use the middle grade as a plausible ordinary case and not as a precise yield.

neixiang-yamen

What it is: A feature article by the Henan Daily reporter Zhang Dongyun, republished on China Daily's Chinese-language site in March 2021, on the Neixiang county yamen in Henan - a county government compound first built in 1304 and rebuilt by a late Qing magistrate, now a museum. It describes the plan in detail: more than 47,000 square meters, eighteen courtyards in succession and over 280 rooms, laid out by Ming and Qing regulation with the offices in front and the residence behind, and it names what stands on each side of the first two courtyards.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the fullest readable description of a county seat's plan, which is what our magistracies are built on - the three lines of the compound, the clerks' quarters on the west, the runners' duty courtyard, the sheds thrown up against the wall. It is a newspaper feature rather than an archaeological report, and it describes one unusually well preserved Chinese compound, so it stands for the imperial Chinese county yamen our setting borrows from rather than for Japanese practice.

neixiang-yamen-zhwiki

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the same Neixiang county yamen (内乡县衙), covering its history, its layout and its individual buildings, including the jail in the southwestern part of the compound and the shrine to Gao Yao, the god of prisons, kept inside it.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the "offices in front, residence behind" arrangement as an instance of the older palace rule, and for where the jail and its shrine sit, all of which the page itself states. It is a tertiary summary, so we lean on it only where the page carries the words; one further detail sometimes attributed to it, the pair of small shrines on the eastern line, could not be found on the article as it can be read, so that point rests on the newspaper feature instead.

nies-tameike

What it is: A page from Japan's National Institute for Environmental Studies, "The life of farm ponds and their environment" (ため池の生物とその環境), comparing the wildlife of irrigation ponds in different condition - about six dragonfly species in a pond swallowed by the town, walled in concrete and choked with nutrients, against twenty-nine or thirty over the year in a pond ringed by worked woodland and full of water plants.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the check on an easy mistake, that a pond a village works must be the barren one: the impoverished pond in this comparison is the urban concrete one, while the farmed pond in its living landscape is the rich one. It is a modern ecological account of present-day ponds, so we take the direction of the contrast - managed is not the same as bare - and none of its counts appear on any map.

ninety-nine-pi-desire

What it is: An article from 99% Invisible, the American design magazine and podcast, on desire paths - the informal tracks that people wear across open ground where the built route does not go, which the article says can form after as few as fifteen crossings.

Why it applies, and its limits: It corroborates the reading behind the worn shortcuts on our maps: where the shortest walk is not the made one, feet make a line of their own. This is ordinary human behavior rather than a historical finding, and the article draws its examples from modern parks and campuses, so it supports the principle and supplies none of our distances.

nishikori-tsunaba

What it is: A Kotobank entry - Kotobank reprints articles from published Japanese dictionaries and encyclopedias - on the site of the Nishikori tsunaba, the rope boom strung across the Kiso river northeast of Nishikori, at the point where the river leaves the Sosui gorge and turns west, to catch the timber floated down from the mountains. It is read together with local history pages published by the town of Yaotsu, which give the working detail: the autumn to spring season, roughly 300,000 logs a year, the timber magistracy of 138 officials, and an origin in the 1340s.

Why it applies, and its limits: Between them they describe how a river timber catch actually worked and where it was placed, which is what our riverside timber yards are drawn from. The dictionary reprint is solid for the site and its position; the numbers and the staffing come from a town's own local history rather than from a scholarly count, so we treat them as a local account, and one boom on one river is standing in for the practice at large.

nisshinkan-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Nisshinkan (日新館), the domain school of Aizu, which stood immediately west of Aizu-Wakamatsu castle on a ground of about 120 ken by 60 ken and was among the foremost such schools in the country, with a recitation hall for boys up to fifteen, a swimming ground and an observatory. The article also covers the modern reconstruction, which serves as museum and as archery and martial-arts hall.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the size of a domain school's ground and for the fact that archery and martial-arts halls belong on it beside the lecture rooms. It is a tertiary summary, and a good deal of what it describes in physical terms is the modern reconstruction rather than the school that burned, so we take the ground's dimensions and the presence of the halls; the article does not present any pairing of lecture hall and drill hall as a rule, and we do not treat it as one.

nogyo-zensho-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Nogyo Zensho (農業全書), the farming manual published in 1697, the tenth year of Genroku - the standard general treatise on Japanese agriculture of its day.

Why it applies, and its limits: It identifies and dates the manual named in our note on why night soil was aged before it went on a field, and a period farming manual is the right kind of authority for what a farmer was told to do. The limit is exact: this encyclopedia page describes the book and gives its year but says nothing about night soil or manuring, so it supports the manual's identity and date and not the practice - the passages about letting dung rot to ripeness before use are quoted on the encyclopedia's separate page for night soil.

nougyoudoboku-keihan

What it is: "On bunds in paddy fields" (水田圃場における畦畔について), an article published in December 2022 and revised since on のうぎょうとぼく ("Agriculture and Me"), a Japanese site about agricultural civil engineering written under the name Oimoya by a former prefectural officer in that field. It explains what a bund is and what it does - holding the water in, dividing the plots, giving a footway for weeding and spraying, growing fodder grass - and tabulates the standard cross-section: a trapezoid with a 1:1 batter, 30 cm high and 30 cm across the top, with heavier sections where the drop between plots is large and in cold regions.

Why it applies, and its limits: Those dimensions set the width of every bund we draw and the grassy strip on top of it, and they come from a trained agricultural engineer rather than a general-interest writer. The honest limit is era and method: this is a present-day design standard for consolidated, machine-worked paddy, published on a specialist's own site rather than in a reviewed journal, so we use it as the shape a soil bund naturally takes for the job, which a hand-built one also had to do, and not as a measurement of a premodern field.

kakegawa-castle-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Kakegawa Castle (掛川城), a castle in what is now Shizuoka prefecture that headed a domain of roughly 51,000 to 59,000 koku. It describes the castle's history and the buildings of its enclosures, including the ninomaru goten, the palace in the second enclosure.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one plain point about how a lord's territory was administered - that the everyday business of government was transacted in the ninomaru goten rather than in the keep - and the article states exactly that, with the article on Kawagoe Castle putting the lord's residence and an armory office in the same enclosure at a far larger domain. Its limits are the kind and the sample: an encyclopedia article is a tertiary summary whose statements we take only where its own references support them, and two castles are a thin base from which to generalize to every castle town our maps draw.

kameyama-yashikigami

What it is: A page from the folklore volume of the 亀山市史 (the official city history of Kameyama, Mie prefecture), published online by the city's historical museum, collecting recorded examples of yashikigami - the small household deity shrines kept within a farmstead's grounds - and where on the grounds each stood.

Why it applies, and its limits: A city history's folklore volume is exactly the sort of local fieldwork that records where a homestead shrine actually sat, which is what we wanted for the corner our maps favor. The limit is decisive and we state it rather than hide it: the page would not render for us, so the counts we would have taken from it cannot be read by anyone following the link, and the record therefore treats the corner weights as unsupported rather than citing this work for them. The entry survives as the record of where we looked.

kamikanai-1771-houses

What it is: A scholarly article in the Transactions of the Architectural Institute of Japan (日本建築学会論文報告集, issue 418), analyzing the main houses of Kamikanai village against a 1771 (Meiwa 8) village tax ledger that records each peasant household's assessed holding in koku, and setting the resulting house sizes beside those of a neighboring village.

Why it applies, and its limits: This is the best kind of source for what we take from it - the SHAPE of a village's houses, meaning how sizes are spread across a village and how much bigger a house gets as a household's land grows - because it works from a surviving eighteenth-century document rather than from surviving buildings, so the small and the poor are counted rather than lost. Its limits are place and sample: one village in one province in one year, thirty-odd houses, and it is the pattern we carry into our maps rather than the exact tsubo figures, since a different province with different timber and different tenure would not reproduce the same numbers.

kanazawa-teramachi

What it is: A visitor listing on VISIT KANAZAWA, the official travel guide of the city of Kanazawa, describing the Teramachi temple district - a quarter of the old castle town where the ruling Maeda family gathered temples together when the town was laid out.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for what the place IS - that a castle town could hold something like seventy temples pressed into one district - which is a fact about the town's plan that a city's own guide states plainly. Everything else about it argues for caution: a tourist page is written to attract visitors, not to be counted from, so we treat the round seventy as an order of magnitude rather than a census, and the page itself notes that Kanazawa's temples were gathered into three such areas, not one, which is a detail our maps must not flatten.

kanda-kakehi

What it is: A digitized Edo-period view with the Tokyo Metropolitan Library's own commentary, showing the Kanda Josui - Edo's water supply - crossing above the Kanda River in a kakehi (懸樋), an open wooden flume carried on a bridge at Ochanomizu, read alongside a Nippon.com piece on Suidobashi and the Tokyo Waterworks Historical Museum's material on the aqueduct's stone pipes.

Why it applies, and its limits: For the question we ask of it - whether a city's water main crossed a river in the open, visibly, where a map would have to draw it - this is about as direct as evidence gets: a contemporary picture, a surviving place name meaning "aqueduct bridge", and a public library's description of both. The limits are scale and singularity: this is the shogunal capital, the largest city in the country, and one celebrated crossing there does not establish that a provincial city of ours would have built the same thing, only that the form existed and was ordinary enough to be a famous sight.

kannushi-wiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the kannushi, the priest who tends a Shinto shrine, covering the office, its duties, and the way it has been passed down within families.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one structural fact that shapes who lives beside a shrine on our maps - that the office was hereditary, held by a married priest whose children succeeded him, so a shrine implies a resident priestly household rather than a celibate community. It is a tertiary summary and we take its figures only where its own references support them; note too that its most concrete statements are about the modern era, including the abolition of hereditary appointment in 1871, which is well after the period our setting is modeled on and which we use only as evidence of how deeply rooted the practice was before it.

karamete-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia articles on the karamete (搦手) and the ote-mon (大手門), the terms for a Japanese castle's rear approach and its main front gate.

Why it applies, and its limits: A castle in our maps needs a back way out as well as a ceremonial front, and these articles establish the plain vocabulary and the plain geometry - the karamete-mon stands opposite the ote-mon. That is all they establish: they are tertiary summaries of a generic form, they name no particular castle, and they say nothing about the divination or orientation reasoning that might have decided which side was which, so any such reasoning on our maps is ours and not theirs.

karo-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the karo (家老), the senior retainers who formed the standing council of a daimyo's house and ran its administration.

Why it applies, and its limits: Our castle towns have to place the great retainer mansions and to decide where government was actually done, and this article supplies both in general terms: the karo decided matters in joint council at a hall such as the hyojosho, and their mansions stood near the castle. Its limits are precision and kind - it is a tertiary summary, "near the castle" is not a distance, and it names no ring or block of the town, so the concentric arrangement our maps draw is our reading of a general statement rather than something this article says.

kashi-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia articles on the kashi (河岸), the river landing and port of a Japanese town, and on gangi (雁木) in the harbor sense, the stepped stone stairs built down a quay so cargo can be worked at any water level.

Why it applies, and its limits: A river town on our maps needs to know what grows around a landing, and these articles give the pattern we draw - that a kashi was not merely a mooring but the seed of a warehouse and merchant quarter, with stepped landings where goods were carried up and down. They are tertiary summaries of a form that persisted over centuries, so we take the arrangement and not any date or dimension from them, and the stepped landing is drawn as a type rather than as any particular surviving quay.

kashima-kainyo-1987

What it is: A 1987 survey of the homestead groves (yashikirin, locally kainyo) of Kashima in Tonami city, Toyama prefecture, counting the trees in the grounds of 46 households - 1,542 trees of at least 10 centimeters trunk diameter, of which 735 were sugi, an average of 16 sugi and about 33 trees per homestead - as reported by Tonami city's own digital archive 砺波正倉 in its account of the city's homestead groves.

Why it applies, and its limits: Nothing else we could read gives the real scale of the tree stand that surrounds a farmhouse - how many trunks, of what species, in what layers - and this is a household-by-household count on the Tonami plain, where the scattered-farmstead settlement pattern and its wind-breaking groves are the classic Japanese case. The honest limits are era and reporting: it is a twentieth-century count of a much older practice, so the trees standing in 1987 had been planted, cut and replanted under modern conditions, and the primary report itself is not online, so what a reader can open is the city's summary of it rather than the survey. A later city count and two published ecological studies of Tonami groves agree with it in order of magnitude, which is why we trust the scale rather than the exact number.

kasoba-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the kasoba (火葬場), the crematory, covering the history of cremation grounds in Japan and their relations with the neighborhoods around them, including the Edo-period record for Asakusa and Shitaya.

Why it applies, and its limits: Where a city burned its dead is a placement question our maps must answer, and this article carries the useful pattern - cremation done inside temple precincts across a whole quarter by the mid seventeenth century, then a group of temple crematories moved out to the edge in 1667 after the smoke gave offense - which is the drift toward the city's margin our maps draw. It is a tertiary summary and the sources behind those episodes are what we would trust rather than the article itself; its later material, including a nineteenth-century proposal to ban cremation outright, belongs to a modernizing state and is outside the period our setting is modeled on.

kawara-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on kawara (瓦), fired roof tile, covering its manufacture, its types and the course of its spread through Japanese building from the temples of antiquity to ordinary houses.

Why it applies, and its limits: This settles a decision every map makes hundreds of times - what an ordinary townsman's roof looked like - by stating that commoners' houses were board-roofed as a general rule throughout the Edo period and that tile only became widespread at its very end, which is why our roofs are boards and thatch and our tile is reserved for temples, gates and the wealthy. It is a tertiary summary, so we take the direction of the trend rather than any proportion from it, and "the end of the Edo period" is later than the eras our setting draws on, which makes this a reason to draw less tile rather than a licence to draw some.

kayabuki-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on kayabuki (茅葺), thatched roofing, describing the materials used, how a thatch roof is built and maintained, and the constraints the material puts on the roof's form.

Why it applies, and its limits: Our farmhouses are thatched, and this article gives the physical reason their roofs are drawn steep: thatch is pitched steeply to shed rain, and the coarser and thicker the stems the wider the gaps and so the steeper the pitch required. The limit is that it gives no number - no angle, no degrees - so the specific pitch on our roofs is our own choice within a requirement the article states only in words, and as a tertiary summary its claims are ones we take where its own references support them.

kiba-koto

What it is: A 2023 post on the tokyo files, an independently written site about Tokyo's history and neighborhoods, on the kiba (木場) of Koto ward - Edo's timber quarter, where logs rafted down from upstream were held in a maze of canals and storage ponds and worked by the sawmills around them - read together with museum notes on Hiroshige's prints of the same district.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the shape of a thing rather than for a measurement: that a city's timber trade occupied its own water-laced district away from the main river, that logs were stored floating rather than stacked, and that rafts were poled through the canals to reach the yards. It is a personal history site, not a scholarly work, so it counts as a well-informed secondary account whose value here is that the arrangement it describes is confirmed by the period prints it discusses; no figure of ours comes from it.

kichijoji-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on Kichijoji, now a district of Tokyo, which was founded as a farming village when households burned out of central Edo in the 1657 fire were resettled onto new land and given long strips running back from the road.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a clean and legible example of one settlement form our maps use - a planned village of deep strip lots laid out from a single road, each household's house at the road end and its fields behind - and the article says so directly, including that the strips ran more than a thousand meters back and that the poor soil made them dry fields rather than paddy. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary with little of substance behind it here: it gives no founding year and no survey, and it says nothing about the woodlots at the far end of such strips, so where our maps draw those the reason comes from elsewhere.

kichinyado-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the kichin-yado (木賃宿), the cheapest class of Japanese inn, whose name means "firewood-fee lodging" - guests brought their own rice and paid only for the fuel to cook it.

Why it applies, and its limits: Our towns need somewhere the poorest travelers stayed, and this describes it exactly: one large shared room, bedding often at the guest's own expense, and the fuel charge that gave the inn its name, with such houses spreading off the highways into the poor quarters of cities. It is a tertiary summary, so what we take is the character of the establishment rather than a price or a floor area, and its account runs on into the modern era where the same word came to mean a flophouse, which is a later sense we do not draw.

326woods-stack

What it is: A 2021 how-to post, 薪の保管方法 ("how to store firewood"), on the site of 326-woods, a Japanese firewood supplier. It tells a customer where to put a woodpile and how high to build it, and says that even heavy split wood can be stacked to about 1.5 m and is best kept under an eave.

Why it applies, and its limits: A woodpile is one of the few farmyard features whose height is set by what a person can lift and stack rather than by fashion, so a working supplier's own advice is a reasonable guide to how tall the stack beside a farmhouse should be drawn. It is nonetheless a modern trade page and not a survey of anything old: the 1.5 m figure describes present-day practice with present-day tools and sheeting, and we use it as an upper bound rather than as a measurement of a premodern woodpile.

aburana-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article アブラナ and the Chinese Wikipedia article 油菜, both on rape (oilseed rape, the yellow-flowered brassica grown for oil and as a green vegetable). Between them they give the crop's calendar - sown in autumn, carried through the winter, cut in March and April - and describe rice farmers in Taiwan scattering rape seed on the paddy after the second rice crop and plowing the flowering stand in as green manure before the next transplanting.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use these pages only for when rape stands in a field and for the habit of using it as a winter cover on harvested paddy, which is what decides whether a map drawn in one season shows yellow flowers between the rice. Both are encyclopedia articles, that is, tertiary summaries whose figures we take only where their own references support them, and the green-manure passage describes a modern Taiwanese double-cropping practice rather than an attested premodern Japanese one, so we treat it as evidence that the habit is natural to a rice landscape and not as proof that our villages did it.

adachi-kosatsu

What it is: A collection page from the museum of Adachi City, one of Tokyo's wards, about 高札 (kosatsu), the public notice boards on which the Edo-period government posted its edicts. It lists the standing boards of the early Edo period and says where boards were put up: at bridge ends and on the ground before the gates of village officials' houses.

Why it applies, and its limits: For a map, the useful question is where a notice board stood and who read it out, and a municipal museum writing about the boards held in its own collection, from its own district, answers exactly that. It is a short public-facing museum page rather than a study, so we take from it the placement and the practice and not any statistic; and it describes the Edo region specifically, which we treat as representative of Japanese practice generally.

adashino-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 化野 (Adashino), on a district at the western edge of Kyoto. It records that the place was formerly used for exposure burial, that it later became known as a cremation ground alongside Toribeyama, and that Adashino in the west, Toribeno in the east and Rendaino in the north were called the city's three great burial grounds.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one thing only: where a city put its dead, which turns out to be at the edge, in named districts on the outward side of the settlement, and that is a placement rule a map can follow. It is a tertiary summary of one city's arrangement, so it tells us the shape of the custom rather than any measured distance, and Kyoto is a capital, so the pattern is applied to smaller places by analogy rather than by evidence.

afcd-hkbio-8

What it is: An article by Yip, Ngar, Yip, Liu and Lai reporting the Hong Kong government's survey of local fung shui woods, published in the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department's newsletter Hong Kong Biodiversity, issue 8 (March 2005). It describes what these village woods are, notes that they typically form a crescent behind a village, and explains how the surveyors drew each wood's boundary.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a government field survey of the actual feature we draw - the planted or protected belt of trees standing behind a village - by the people who measured it, which is why we take the crescent form and the boundary convention from it. The woods surveyed are in Hong Kong, in subtropical southern China rather than Japan, and they are the twenty-first-century remnants of a much older practice, so the form is better attested by this source than any historical extent is; the surveyors themselves note that boundaries were drawn when there were significantly fewer large trees than the wood once held.

afcd-ncsc-9-06

What it is: A December 2006 paper, "Fung Shui Woods in Hong Kong", put before the Nature Conservation Subcommittee of Hong Kong's Advisory Council on the Environment by the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department. Its annex lists all 115 surveyed village woods with their species richness and their areas as measured on survey maps with a geographic information system.

Why it applies, and its limits: This is the one large table of measured areas we could find for the village grove, so it is what sets how big a grove is drawn behind a settlement: the annex's 115 rows run from about 600 square meters to a little over 5 hectares, with most under 2 hectares. The caveats are that these are modern measurements of surviving woods, which may have been cut back or grown out since a village first planted them, and that Hong Kong stands in here for the wider East Asian practice because no comparable published measurements for Japanese or mainland Chinese village groves could be read on a public page.

artic-pigsty-latrine

What it is: The Art Institute of Chicago's catalog entry for a ceramic tomb model of a pigsty and latrines from Eastern Han China (object 37716). Its catalog text explains the arrangement the model represents: latrines customarily built above a pigsty and connected by pipes to a cesspool.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one placement rule, that the privy and the muck belong together in the same corner of a farmyard rather than apart, and a museum's description of a model made by the people who used such a yard is good evidence that the combination was ordinary rather than exceptional. It is a catalog note rather than an excavation report; the object is a tomb model, that is, an idealized miniature and not a measured building; and Han China is far earlier than the Japan-leaning period our settlements are drawn from, so we take the habit and not the dimensions. The museum's own object page can be slow to open, though its catalog text is public.

asakusa-kuramae

What it is: The English Wikipedia article "Rice broker", read together with general histories of the Asakusa and Kuramae districts of Edo. It explains that the shogunate's rice storehouses stood on the Sumida riverside, that the brokers known as fudasashi worked in the Kuramae ("before the storehouses") quarter of Asakusa, and that they both warehoused and lent against stipend rice.

Why it applies, and its limits: A capital map has to decide where the government's granaries go and what grows up next to them, and this describes exactly that chain: water access for bulk rice, the storehouses on the bank, the brokers' district in their shadow, and the money spilling into the entertainment quarter beyond. It is an encyclopedia article, a tertiary summary whose statements we take only where its own references support them, and it describes one city in one period, so we use it for the arrangement of quarters and not for numbers.

aze-standard

What it is: Japanese public-works standard drawings for 畦畔 (keihan, the earth bunds that hold water on a paddy): Aomori Prefecture's standard drawing set for farmland consolidation (ほ場整備), together with a Yamato river-basin technical standard for paddies used as water storage. The Aomori sheet specifies a bund 30 cm above the higher field surface with a 30 cm crest and 1:1 side slopes, and notes that the outer slope is a standard value to be eased where the soil requires it.

Why it applies, and its limits: The bund is the single most repeated line on any paddy map, so its real cross-section decides how wide those lines are drawn, and an engineering standard states that cross-section in numbers rather than impressions. The honest limits are era and region: this is a present-day standard for machine-built consolidated fields, so a hand-piled premodern bund would have been less regular, and Aomori is a cold northern region whose standards allow for frost heave and deeper water, which is why the enlarged cold-region figure is kept separate from the ordinary one.

azolla-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on Azolla, a genus of small floating water ferns. Its ecology section describes the fern's use on flooded rice paddies, where its symbiotic cyanobacterium fixes nitrogen from the air and the rotting mat releases that nitrogen into the water for the rice.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it to explain why a flooded paddy might be drawn carrying a green film rather than clear water, which is a visible surface feature with a reason behind it. It is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, and the productivity numbers it quotes come from modern agronomy, so we cite the practice and the mechanism rather than any yield.

bamboo-growers-hardiness

What it is: Species pages from commercial bamboo growers, chiefly completebamboo.com and two others, for madake (Phyllostachys bambusoides, Japanese timber bamboo). They state the plant's cold limits, which the pages give variously as about -15 C and hardiness zone 7, and elsewhere as -18 to -23 C.

Why it applies, and its limits: Whether a bamboo grove can stand beside a given settlement is a climate question, and growers who sell and replace plants have a practical interest in stating the temperature at which one dies. These are nursery pages rather than a study, they describe cultivated plants in gardens rather than managed stands, and they disagree with one another, so the record keeps the disagreement and uses a spread rather than pretending to a single number.

bambubatu-madake

What it is: The plant profile for Phyllostachys bambusoides (Japanese timber bamboo) on Bambu Batu, a bamboo-focused enthusiast and retail site. It gives the species a cold hardiness of roughly -20 to -23 C and warns that colder weather will damage leaves and canes.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is one of the grower pages behind our madake cold limit, and it is quoted separately because it sits at the tolerant end of the range the others give. Like the rest it is a commercial plant description rather than a survey, so it fixes the outer edge of a spread rather than settling where madake grows.

beijing-imperial-city

What it is: The English Wikipedia article "Imperial City, Beijing", on the walled precinct that enclosed the Forbidden City and the imperial services around it. The passage we take describes the Corridor of a Thousand Steps south of Chengtianmen, with the offices of the government ministries lining either side of it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It answers a layout question for a capital map: the bureaucracy sits on the ceremonial avenue outside the palace wall rather than inside it, which decides where the ministry compounds are drawn. Two limits are worth stating plainly - it is a tertiary summary, and that particular sentence is flagged in the article as lacking a citation, so we treat the arrangement as a plausible shape to draw rather than as a documented fact; and Ming and Qing Beijing is a Chinese imperial capital standing in for our setting's own, which is modeled on both China and Japan.

beitang-studies

What it is: A peer-reviewed article in Nature Communications (June 2023) on reactivating small water bodies for irrigation and drainage in Chinese rice farming. It describes the beitang (陂塘) pond systems of the Jiang-Huai region as a pond-based irrigation paradigm with more than 2,500 years of history, and records that in the 1950s some 8.3 million such decentralized systems served 39 percent of China's irrigated area.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the source for our assumption that a village in rice country waters itself from ponds it holds locally, rather than only from a canal running past it, which changes what a settlement map has to show. It is a modern paper whose real subject is present-day sustainability, and its one big number is a 1950s count rather than a premodern one, so we take the system's antiquity and its village scale from it and treat the share as an indication that the pond mode was ordinary rather than marginal.

bench-terrace-riser

What it is: A technology profile of traditional irrigated rice terraces on the Food and Agriculture Organization's Science, Technology and Innovation portal, compiled from WOCAT survey data and describing hand-built level bench terraces on steep slopes in Nepal, read alongside pages from ICIMOD and general references on bench terracing. It gives the dimensions of the structural face: risers 0.8 to 1.5 m high at slopes of 80 to 160 percent, stone-faced where stone is available, with a small lip of 20 to 25 cm holding 10 to 15 cm of water on the platform.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supplies the physical distinction our terraced maps depend on, that the tall riser is a retaining wall holding up the soil while a separate low lip holds in the water, which is why micro-basins belong on a hillside and not on a valley floor. The clear limitation is place: these are Himalayan terraces in Nepal standing in for East Asian ones because no comparable published measurements of Japanese or Chinese terrace risers could be read on a public page; the profile also describes a working present-day system that has taken up some modern methods, and parts of its text are automatically compiled, so we use it for the geometry of the structure and not for the details of how it is farmed.

bernstein-fire-and-earth

What it is: Andrew Bernstein's article "Fire and Earth: The Forging of Modern Cremation in Meiji Japan", published in the Japanese Journal of Religious Studies 27/3-4 (2000), a scholarly account of the Meiji government's short-lived national ban on cremation and its repeal. Only the abstract is on a public page; the specific episode we cite - an 1873 proposal to move the crematoria, notably those at the Senju temples, outside the city's "red line", on the argument that the stench from burning bodies injured health - is quoted from a later account of the article rather than from Bernstein's own text.

Why it applies, and its limits: It bears directly on where a city puts the burning of its dead and why, which is the rule a capital map needs when it places a crematory ground relative to the built-up area. Two limits: Meiji Japan is later than the period our settlements are drawn from, so it shows an older arrangement coming under pressure rather than the arrangement itself; and because the passage comes from a secondary retelling and not from a page carrying Bernstein's own words, we treat the 1873 proposal as reported rather than as read in the article.
