pitt-zhengzhou-coop

What it is: A news item from the University of Pittsburgh's Department of History of Art and Architecture announcing that graduate student Yuqing Tao and colleagues had published, in the Chinese journal Popular Archaeology (大众考古), a report on a chicken coop of about the early seventeenth century found during a 2023 salvage excavation at Zhengzhou. The coop was a square structure with six niche-like openings in its west wall, some of them holding eggshell fragments.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is excavated evidence, from late Ming China, of how an ordinary urban household actually housed its chickens, which is the form our farmyard coops are drawn from. Its limits are that it is a short departmental announcement rather than the excavation report itself, that it rests on a single structure at a single town site, and that the page carries no measurements at all, so it can settle what a coop looked like and never how big one was.

plos-2016-pine

What it is: A 2016 research article in PLOS ONE by Lou and colleagues, "Response of Plant Height, Species Richness and Aboveground Biomass to Flooding Gradient along Vegetation Zones in Floodplain Wetlands, Northeast China". It measured three herbaceous marsh communities on the Sanjiang Plain and sorted them by how much of the year their ground stands under water: sedge marsh at the streamside, meadow marsh on the middle terraces, and wet meadow grass on the terraces that flood only occasionally.

Why it applies, and its limits: The ladder it measures - which plants hold the ground that floods every spring, which the ground that floods for part of the season, which the ground that floods rarely - is a physical response to water depth rather than a modern agricultural fact, so it is good evidence for what greens the wet margins of a floodplain on our maps. Two honest limits: it is a present-day ecological survey of one plain in northeastern China, not of Japan, and it is entirely about sedges and grasses, so it says nothing whatever about pine or any other tree and cannot be read as evidence about a tree's tolerance of soggy ground.

pmc5723622-bamboo-range

What it is: A 2017 peer-reviewed paper in Ecology and Evolution by Kohei Takenaka Takano and seven co-authors, "Detecting latitudinal and altitudinal expansion of invasive bamboo Phyllostachys edulis and Phyllostachys bambusoides (Poaceae) in Japan to project potential habitats under 1.5C-4.0C global warming". The team surveyed bamboo stands near 145 weather stations across northern and eastern Japan, compared aerial photographs spanning three to four decades, and modeled where the two species could grow under warmer climates.

Why it applies, and its limits: Moso and madake are the two bamboos a Japanese village actually grew, and this is a measured field survey of where in Japan they can and cannot stand, with a stated cold limit, so it tells us whether a bamboo grove belongs beside a given settlement. The limits are that it is a modern survey of a modern and still-spreading distribution, and that its central subject is future warming, so the ranges it projects are not historical ranges and only its present-day survey figures and cold thresholds are safe to use.

pmc7538448-levee

What it is: A research paper available through PubMed Central, "Earthworm species and density in semi-natural grasslands on rice paddy levees in Japanese satoyama", which counts earthworms in the grassy banks between paddy fields and, in describing its study ground, sets out what those levees are and how farmers keep them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is fieldwork on Japanese paddies, and it states plainly what a levee is for - holding the water in and carrying the farmer and their tools between fields - and that the banks are kept as mown grass, which is exactly the paddy edge our maps draw. Its limits are that it is a modern study whose real subject is soil ecology rather than farming history, and that its account of upkeep includes present-day herbicide use, so we take from it the levee's purpose and its cut grassy surface and not the details of modern management.

pmc7898781-fukugi

What it is: A research paper available through PubMed Central, "Distribution and utilization of homestead windbreak Fukugi trees", a survey of the fukugi trees planted in strips around houses in the villages of Okinawa, which the authors trace to the Ryukyu Kingdom of roughly three hundred years ago and to the feng shui planning of its rural landscapes.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a survey of a surviving, dated example of the thing we plant on our maps - a maintained belt of trees set around a homestead to break the wind - so the form is attested rather than assumed. The limits are of place and of time: Okinawa is subtropical, and neither its tree species nor its Ryukyuan siting rules are those of the main Japanese islands or of imperial China, so we take the form and not the species or the spacing; and the trees measured today are the survivors of a much older planting, which makes the modern distribution an incomplete record of the old one.

qimin-yaoshu-yangji

What it is: The chapter on raising chickens (卷六 養雞第五十九) of the Qimin Yaoshu (齊民要術, "Essential Techniques for the Common People"), the sixth-century Chinese agricultural treatise compiled by Jia Sixie, read in the Siku Quanshu edition hosted on Chinese Wikisource. Its instruction on housing is direct: set a cage on the ground with a perch inside it rather than letting the birds roost in the trees, where wind and cold thin the big ones and kill the small.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a farming manual from the very tradition our setting is modeled on, telling us how a poultry shelter was meant to be built and why, which is what fixes the ground-level coop in a farmyard rather than a roost in a tree. Three limits worth stating: a manual prescribes good practice and does not record what an average household did; it is sixth-century northern China, far in both time and place from the Edo Japan our maps also draw on; and the text is a much later imperial edition of it, given here in this project's own English rendering of the classical Chinese.

qing-zhalan

What it is: "Dashilan Street: The Fence Culture of Ancient Beijing", a conference paper by Fei Liang, Shaoshuai Liu and Xiaoxi Liu in the proceedings of the 2023 International Conference on Social Sciences and Humanities and Arts, published by Atlantis Press. Drawing on court paintings, old maps and archival photographs, it traces the ornamental street gates and palings (zhalan, 栅栏) that gave the Dashilan commercial district its name, and their role in the curfew and block policing of Ming and Qing Beijing. Reporting on the curfew hours and penalties themselves is gathered under the same key.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is directly about the feature we draw - a fence closing a street at night - and it supplies the reason such a fence existed, which is the curfew that a city's night watch enforced. Its limits are that it is a short conference paper rather than a full study, and that Beijing is an imperial capital and so the strictest case of urban policing in the empire: a provincial town would have had a looser version of the same arrangement, and the specific curfew hours and lash counts come from separate reporting rather than from this paper.

qingming-shanghe-tu

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on Along the River During the Qingming Festival (清明上河圖), the early twelfth-century handscroll attributed to Zhang Zeduan, which describes the painting scene by scene - the wheeled wagons and the donkeys and mules moving goods, and the handful of guards at the city gate.

Why it applies, and its limits: The scroll is contemporary pictorial evidence of what the ground just inside a Chinese city gate actually looked like in use - carts and pack animals standing in a crowd, tethered, on open trodden ground with no fence and no lawn - which is the arrangement our gate yards copy. The limits: we read the painting through a tertiary encyclopedia summary rather than the scroll itself or the scholarship on it, and the painting is an idealized composition of city life rather than a record of one place, so it is good for the convention of a gate yard and not for measuring one. It is also Song China rather than Japan.

qiushen-zhwiki

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the qiushen (秋审), the Qing dynasty's autumn assize, in which the court decided each autumn which death sentences would be carried out. It describes the route a case took: the Three Judicial Offices - the Board of Punishments, the Court of Judicial Review and the Censorate - heard the provincial cases jointly, and the prisoners waiting in provincial jails were held over until the review returned.

Why it applies, and its limits: A magistracy on our maps has a jail and an office, and this gives the shape of what happens in them: a capital case climbs from a provincial cell to the capital and the confirmed sentence comes back down, which is why the jail holds prisoners for months rather than days. Its limits are that an encyclopedia article is a tertiary summary, so we take its procedure only where its own references support it, and that this is Qing Chinese law standing for the setting's justice generally, our setting drawing its officialdom from the Chinese pattern as well as the Japanese one.

religion-song-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article "Religion in the Song dynasty", a survey of Buddhism, Daoism and folk religion in China between 960 and 1279. The one figure we take from it is a dated count: records for the year 1221 gave 400,000 monks and 61,000 nuns in the dynasty, against a population the same article puts at around 100 million.

Why it applies, and its limits: Deciding how many monks a settlement of a given size can hold needs an order of magnitude for the share of a population living in religious orders, and this supplies one attributed to a dynastic record - under half a percent. The limits are real: an encyclopedia is a tertiary summary, so this figure is used precisely because it is stated as coming from a record and no further; a Song Chinese count is standing in for the whole setting; and an imperial count is a count of registered clergy, which is not the same as everyone living in a temple.

rice-rape-calendar-summary

What it is: A paper in the Chinese Journal of Eco-Agriculture (中国生态农业学报) by Liu Dan, Tian Jun and Duan Licheng on how a warming climate has shifted rice planting within the rice and rapeseed rotation of Jiangxi Province, built on weather records from 85 stations and concentrating on the years 2011 to 2022. It prints the district-by-district calendar: rapeseed harvested in early April in the south of the province and early May at Jiujiang, with rice transplanted from mid-April to early May.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is one of the few readable sources that gives actual dates for both halves of a single plot's year, which is what decides whether a field on a map is under water, under a yellow crop, or bare in a given month. Its limits are era and place: this is a recent calendar for a southern Chinese province, and the paper's own subject is that warming has moved these dates, so the windows it gives sit somewhat earlier in the year than an older calendar would, and the rapeseed sowing window we pair with it does not come from this passage.

ridgelineimages-gsi

What it is: "Reading GSI Topographic Maps", a guide on Ridgeline Images, a website about hiking and mapping in Japan, which walks through the legend of the topographic map series published by the Geospatial Information Authority of Japan. It shows the bamboo grove carrying its own symbol, listed separately from broad-leaved forest, from coniferous forest, and from the dwarf bamboo (sasa) zone of the high ridges.

Why it applies, and its limits: What we take from it is a map-drawing convention rather than a fact about plants: Japan's own national mapping agency treats a bamboo stand as a distinct class of ground, which is why our maps draw it as neither woodland nor scrub. The limits are that this is an enthusiast's explanation rather than the agency's own legend document, and that it describes the present-day map series, so it is evidence for how Japanese maps show bamboo today and not for any older cartographic practice.

sado-bugyosho-fires

What it is: A listing for the Sado magistracy (佐渡奉行所) on asoview, a Japanese leisure and sightseeing booking site, carrying a short history of the building: put up in 1603 at the start of the Edo period, burned down and rebuilt five times thereafter, remodeled into offices and a school after the Meiji Restoration, named a national historic site in 1929, and destroyed entirely by fire in 1942.

Why it applies, and its limits: One plain point is taken from it - that a magistracy's halls were ordinary timber buildings that burned and were rebuilt again and again, which is why our administrative compounds are drawn as wooden and replaceable rather than monumental. It stands in because nothing closer could be read on a public page: the encyclopedia, museum and tourism pages about the same building describe only its modern reconstruction, so the count of five fires rests on this page alone, and the page is a commercial listing written for visitors, with no sources of its own and its Japanese rendered into English by this project.

saijo-mizu-rekishikan

What it is: A page from the Water History Museum run by the city of Saijo in Ehime Prefecture, part of a series on local groundwater, explaining how a well is dug by hand: a vertical shaft about a meter across, wide enough for a digger to get down inside it, sunk by human labor until it reaches the aquifer.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the true diameter of the thing our oversized wellhead glyph stands for, from a municipal museum describing the well-digging of its own famously watery district, and the figure is not really local - a shaft has to be about that wide for a digger to work at the bottom of it. The limits are that a museum's public-education page is a summary written for visitors rather than a survey, and that it describes the technique in the present tense, so it is the dimensions of hand-digging we take from it and not a dated historical measurement; the English here is this project's translation of the Japanese.

saitama-minuma-tsusenbori

What it is: A page from the city of Saitama titled 見沼通船堀のしくみ ("how the Minuma boat canal works"), explaining the layout of the Minumadai irrigation system and the lock canal built to join its two arms. It states the arrangement in one line: the east-edge and west-edge canals run along the rim of the plateau, while the Shiba River runs down the center of the lowland.

Why it applies, and its limits: That is an eighteenth-century Japanese irrigation scheme described in exactly the terms our water layouts use - supply carried high along both margins so the fields can be fed from either side, with the drain running low down the middle - which makes the pattern attested rather than invented. Its limits are that it is a municipal heritage page written for residents rather than a technical study, that it covers one system on the Kanto plain, and that it describes the works as they survive today; its dates for the canal differ slightly from other accounts of the same construction.

sando-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the sando (参道), the approach road to a shrine or temple. It gives the term both narrowly, as the path inside the sacred bounds within the torii or the temple gate, and broadly, as the whole road running to the shrine from somewhere busy such as the line of a highway; it also notes the torii-front and gate-front towns that grew up along such approaches, and highways whose course was bent to bring them nearer a shrine.

Why it applies, and its limits: Placing a temple on a map is mostly a question of how its approach meets the road network and where the shops along that approach go, and this is the definition that ties the two together. Its limits are that an encyclopedia article is a tertiary summary whose statements we take only where its own references support them, and that it describes the general Japanese case across many centuries rather than any dated practice; the English is this project's translation of the Japanese.

## APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS, write-up MISSING a limit

### `fao-ac180e-rice-fish`

- **kind / authors / date**: FAO field/technical manual, *Fish Culture in Rice Fields*, ch. 7
  "Culture Operations". No author or date on the page; it cites Coche (1960, 1967) and IRRI
  high-yielding varieties, so it is a modern (post-1960s) extension document. FAO hosts it under
  `docrep/field/003`, i.e. a field-project document rather than a numbered technical paper.
- **place and era described**: present-day rice-fish practice across several regions - the chapter's
  worked examples are Zaire, Madagascar, Liberia, Ivory Coast and Indonesia as well as Asia.
- **scale**: one rice plot. **method**: extension prescription ("should be", "is recommended"), not
  measurement of any historical field.
- **what we use it for**: the permanent dry bund and its height, quoted at `homesteads.html` fn 42
  against a competing 20-30 cm figure - explicitly as the number "pulling the other way".
- **verdict**: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS. (1) A modern extension manual prescribing a bund, not a
  record of one; the same chapter assumes inorganic fertilizer, Lindane/Dieldrin and IRRI varieties,
  which locates the document firmly in the modern era even though the bund figure itself does not
  depend on them. (2) The bund is specified for a rice-FISH field, which must hold deeper water and
  retain fish, so 60 cm is an upper bound on a plain paddy bund. (3) It is a pan-tropical manual,
  not an East Asian one.
- **What it is:** ACCURATE. Kind, publisher, chapter, subject and both figures match the page. It
  gives no date or author, but none is stated on the page either.
- **limits: MISSING** - the region. The write-up names the modern-manual limit and the fish-bund
  limit (both correct, and the fish-bund one is the load-bearing discount), but says nothing about
  the manual being written for tropical aquaculture projects in Africa and Southeast Asia rather
  than for a Chinese or Japanese paddy. Under the record's own "a different region standing in"
  rule that limit belongs in the entry.

### `fao-ac241e`

- **kind / authors / date**: NACA working paper NACA/WP/84/13, December 1984, by Hu Bao-tong and
  Yang Hua-zhu, published by the Network of Aquaculture Centres in Asia and hosted on fao.org.
- **place and era described**: 1980s China - BOTH the Pearl River delta AND the Taihu basin (Dongshan
  commune, Wuxian, Suzhou; Jinwan production brigade). Collective-era units.
- **scale**: pond blocks and commune examples. **method**: descriptive report of then-current
  practice plus farmers' rules of thumb.
- **what we use it for**: `archetypes.html` fn 32-35 - the dike:water ratio (1:1 where the worms
  alone feed the fish, 6:4 or 7:3 with other feed), pond depth 3.5 m falling to 2.5 m in summer,
  the 1.5 m slope to the dike top.
- **verdict**: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS. (1) A 1984 development report on collective-era practice,
  not a historical record, even though the dike-pond system it describes is centuries old.
  (2) China standing in for a Japan-modeled setting. (3) The POND DEPTH is the number in the set
  least defensible as premodern: 3.5 m of excavation with a summer drawdown reflects modern
  stocking and modern earth-moving, unlike the area ratio, which does follow from the feed loop.
  (4) The paper's own caution: "in actual practice, the ratio of water area to dike surface area is
  more complicated and generally, governed by traditional practice".
- **What it is: INACCURATE**, in two ways. It says the document describes "the dike-and-pond farming
  of the Pearl River delta", but the report covers the Taihu basin too - and fn 32, the footnote
  that carries the 6:4 ratio, quotes the Taihu (Dongshan, Wuxian) worked example, not a Pearl-delta
  one. And it calls it "a report published by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization with the
  Network of Aquaculture Centres in Asia-Pacific": it is a NACA working paper (NACA/WP/84/13, Dec
  1984) by two named authors, hosted by FAO, and NACA was the Network of Aquaculture Centres in
  ASIA at the time.
- **limits: MISSING** - the pond depth. "The proportions it reports ... follow from the feed cycle
  itself rather than from any modern input" sweeps the 3.5 m depth in with the area ratio, and only
  the area ratio is a consequence of the feed loop. Also, calling the numbers "regional averages"
  is not what they are (two worked examples and a farmers'-experience rule), and the paper's own
  "governed by traditional practice" caveat is the honest frame.

### `fao-ac264e`

- **kind / authors / date**: FAO/NACA technical manual, *Integrated Fish Farming in China*, ch. 7
  "Introduction of Chinese integrated fish farming and some major models". No author or date on the
  page; the practice described is 1970s-80s, with historical references back to 1934.
- **place and era described**: China, 1980s, from household ponds up to brigade and state fish farms
  (Zhangzhuan Aquaculture Brigade, Helei and Dong Hu fish farms).
- **scale**: a single pond and its dike. **method**: description of observed models.
- **what we use it for**: `archetypes.html` fn 61-62 - the pig shed "constructed on the pond dyke or
  over the water surface", 1-5 pigs per mu, and the fenced dry run on the dike with a wet run in a
  corner of the water. The entry says explicitly: cited as the FORM, not as premodern prevalence.
- **verdict**: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS. (1) 1980s practice under collective and state management,
  used only for physical arrangement. (2) China standing in - here that is close to no discount at
  all, since the map that uses it (the silk-and-fish hamlet) is deliberately the Chinese archetype.
  (3) The stocking rate is a modern intensity figure.
- **What it is:** ACCURATE. Kind, publisher, chapter subject, and both structures match the page.
- **limits: MISSING** - the stocking number. The write-up's discount is "form, never prevalence",
  which covers the shed and the duck run but not the "1-5 pigs per mu" the entry's own `Used for:`

### `fao-x6708e`

- **kind / authors / date**: FAO Training Series, *Simple methods for aquaculture: Pond
  construction*, ch. 10 "Pond outlet structures". No date on the page; the series is 1980s-90s.
- **place and era described**: present-day small-scale aquaculture in developing countries,

- **scale**: one pond dike. **method**: extension prescription.
- **what we use it for**: `archetypes.html` fn 40 - the sluice gate as "a protected opening in the

### `fei-1939`

- **kind / authors / date**: village ethnography, Fei Hsiao-tung, *Peasant Life in China: A Field
  Study of Country Life in the Yangtze Valley*, Routledge 1939 (his LSE doctoral study; Malinowski's
  preface dated 1938). Fieldwork July-August 1936.
- **place and era described**: Kaihsienkung (Kaixiangong), "on the south-east bank of Lake Tai ...
  about eighty miles west of Shanghai", 1936.
- **scale**: one village, household by household. **method**: participant observation plus household
  economic data over two months.
- **what we use it for**: `archetypes.html` fn 5, 20, 47-59, 66 - silkworms on tray stands inside the
  dwelling, the front room as workroom, home reeling, nearly every household owning a boat and the
  village laid out along its streams, the agent boat, half-buried earthenware manure pits behind the
  house and along the road, mulberry on the 10-30 m raised yu margin that is also the dyke with
  houses on it and vegetables beneath, sheep huts as a recent innovation, threshing in the open
  space before the house or in the front room.
- **verdict**: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS, and it is the strongest source in the batch for what it is
  used for - a first-hand account of the exact settlement form the maps draw. Limits: (1) 1936, not
  premodern: the same chapters record railways, motor roads, motor-boat and bus services, and the
  collapse of domestic silk reeling under city filatures. (2) Fei chose THIS village because "in
  this village an experiment at industrial reform has been made during the past ten years" - it is
  a reform site, which is a selection bias for exactly the silk arrangements we take from it.
  (3) Two months of one summer: Fei writes "I was naturally not able to follow the complete annual
  cycle of social activities". (4) One village of one delta, China, standing beside the Japanese
  material. (5) The readable copy is an OCR scan; the footnotes carry its garbles ("ifigher", "yw").
- **What it is:** ACCURATE. Title, author, publisher, year, the village, its position by Lake Tai
  and the subject all check out against the text.
- **limits: MISSING** - two. The write-up names the era and the filature disruption, which is the
  main one, but not (a) that the fieldwork was two months of a single season by Fei's own statement,
  which matters because seasonal claims (the silkworm peak occupying the rooms, threshing at
  harvest) are taken from him, and (b) that the village was selected as the site of an industrial
  reform experiment. Worth adding too: the source we can read is an OCR text, not a clean edition.

### `fires-in-edo-enwiki`

- **kind / authors / date**: English Wikipedia article, open-edit tertiary; extensively sourced to
  Japanese scholarship (Nishiyama Matsunosuke, Kuroki Kyo, Yamamoto Junmi, Yoshihara Kenichiro).
- **place and era described**: Edo, 1601-1867.
- **scale**: a capital of roughly a million inhabitants. **method**: summary of others' counts.
- **what we use it for**: `urban-features.html` fn 55 - the seasonal clustering of serious fires; and
  fn 82 - dozo storehouses "with thick plastered earthen walls and ... tiled roofs in most cases".
- **verdict**: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS. (1) Tertiary summary, so it is a pointer to the Japanese
  works it cites. (2) Edo is the largest city in Japan; the season transfers, the frequency and
  scale of its conflagrations do not. (3) The "great fire" count is Edo-specific in its own
  definition and in its calendar.
- **What it is:** ACCURATE as far as it goes, but it describes only the fire-season material and
  omits the storehouse construction, which is the second thing we take from the same article.
- **limits: MISSING**, and one wording correction. The write-up covers only one of the article's
  two uses - nothing about dozo walls, which fn 82 cites it for. And "the serious fires clustered
  in the dry, windy winter" is tighter than the article's own count, which ranks March first, then
  February, April and January - i.e. late winter INTO spring, with the article attributing it to
  dry weather under prevailing northwest and north winds. The claim on the research page is used to
  explain charcoal braziers in winter; the source supports a winter-and-spring dry season.

### `forests-2020`

- **kind / authors / date**: peer-reviewed open-access article, *Forests* 11(12):1286, received 28
  Sep 2020, published 30 Nov 2020. Jianling Chen, Weiming Lin, Yaoqi Zhang, Yongwu Dai and Bixia
  Chen (Fujian Agriculture and Forestry University; Auburn; University of the Ryukyus).
- **place and era described**: seven villages, one in each town of Youxi County, Fujian, southern
  China, surveyed July-August 2019. The villages themselves are 350-951 years old.
- **scale**: seven villages in one county, with province-level statements quoted from others.
- **method**: field survey plus semi-structured interviews (county forestry staff n=4, fengshui
  masters n=7, village cadres n=7, clan chiefs), and a list of famous and ancient trees. No stem,
  canopy or area measurement of its own.
- **what we use it for**: `vegetation.html` fn 1 - roughly two fengshui forests per village; fn 77 -
  the "over three hectares" / "over six hectares" / Lingtou's over 20 ha entries in Table 1; fn 78 -
  the water-tail forest type and where the three types sit.
- **verdict**: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS. (1) A 2019-2020 study of the groves that SURVIVED
  collectivization and modern forestry - a remnant landscape, not the ordinary one of several
  centuries ago. (2) The two-per-village figure is not this paper's measurement: it appears in its
  Fujian Province paragraph, attributed to reference [40], Xu, F.; Qiu, E.F.; Wang, C., "Tree
  species structure of Fengshui forest in Fujian Province", *J. Jiangxi Agric. Univ.* 2012 - which
  the record has not read, so the number reaches us at second hand. (3) Seven villages of one
  county, interview-based. (4) China standing in.
- **What it is: INACCURATE** in one place: "reported there from an earlier county survey in Fujian".

  in section 3.1's paragraph about Fujian Province ("most villages feature two fengshui forests on
  average and ... 80.4% of the fengshui forests have not been damaged [40]"), not about Youxi County.

  (The same "Youxi County" slip is in the registry entry's `Used for:` line; fn 1 has it right.)
- **limits: MISSING** - that the two-per-village figure is second-hand from a source we have not
  read, and the survey's actual scale and method. The write-up is honest and correct on the two
  limits it does state (no grove areas in it; a remnant landscape in one province).

### `fao-charcoal-safety`

- **kind / authors / date**: FAO forestry handbook, *Simple technologies for charcoal making*, ch. 5
  "Safety precautions". No author or date on the page; it covers both "the traditional way" and
  industrial methods (batch retorts, continuous converters, earth cooling bins).
- **place and era described**: modern small-scale and industrial charcoal production, no region.
- **scale**: a kiln and its stockpile. **method**: safety guidance drawn from handling experience.
- **what we use it for**: `urban-features.html` fn 56-58 - fresh charcoal absorbing oxygen and
  self-heating, fines as the worst case, the 24-hour open-air rule, and that water-spraying does
  not reliably prevent self-ignition - all to explain why a charcoal yard has an open cooling apron
  away from thatch.
- **verdict**: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS. The self-heating is a property of the material and carries
  back without discount; the handling RULES (24 hours in the open, the 25-hour no-heat test) are
  modern guidance for bagged and bulk-stored stock, and part of the chapter's context (retorts,
  converters) has no premodern counterpart.
- **What it is:** ACCURATE. Everything it attributes to the page is on the page.
- **limits: HONEST.** It says plainly that the specific waiting times are today's handling guidance
  and an anchor rather than a rule anyone stated in hours.
- **Note for the session (not a write-up defect):** the registry's `Used for:` line claims "the
  8-day threshold". There is no 8-day statement on this page - its own figure is "If there is no
  evidence of heat or active fire after 25 hours, the charcoal can be considered safe for storing".
  The research page already labels the eight-day claim unsourced; the registry line should be
  brought into line with it.

### `fao-paddy-duty`

- **kind / authors / date**: two FAO irrigation training manuals. The registered URL is the table of
  contents of *Irrigation Water Management: Training Manual No. 6 - Scheme Irrigation Water Needs

- **What it is:** ACCURATE in substance. It names neither manual's date, authors nor series number

### `fao-pond-water`

- **kind / authors / date**: FAO manual *Water for animals*, based on the work of Ph. Pallas, Land
  and Water Development Division, Rome 1986. The cited file (r7488e06.htm) is chapter 5, "Surface
  water resources development for rangeland".
- **place and era described**: semi-arid and arid rangelands in developing countries, present day.
- **scale**: a dug pond or small dam. **method**: engineering guidance.

  losses of a standing reservoir, and the need for a spillway to pass storm runoff - which carry the
  water-balance argument that a fed moat must have an outlet.
- **verdict**: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS. Evaporation and seepage are physics; the MAGNITUDE is an

  correct use.

bitchu-takamatsu-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia articles on Bitchu Takamatsu Castle and on the 1582 battle fought there. They describe a Sengoku-period fortress in what is now Okayama that stood on a belt of low, wet ground, and Hashiba Hideyoshi's siege of it, in which an earth dam thrown around the castle drowned it in an artificial lake.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a plain, well referenced account of a castle whose defense was its marsh rather than its stonework, which is exactly the question our wet defensive belt asks: whether low wetland was treated as a work of fortification and not merely as bad ground. It is a tertiary encyclopedia summary, so we take its figures only where its own references support them, and the flooding is a single spectacular siege rather than routine practice; it tells us that a wet belt was defensively real, not how wide an ordinary one was.

bodaiji-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the bodaiji (菩提寺), the temple whose sect a household follows generation after generation and at which it holds the memorial rites for its ancestors. It also covers the related danna-dera and the Edo-period danka system that bound each household to a temple.

Why it applies, and its limits: Our small urban temples are drawn as places with named patron households rather than as public monuments, and this is the article that defines that relationship and names real examples of it. It is a tertiary summary of a religious institution, definitional rather than quantitative: it fixes what a small temple is for and who pays for it, and carries nothing about how large such a temple is, where it sits on a street, or how many a town holds.

boso-no-mura-kigoya

What it is: A page from the Chiba Prefectural Museum's open-air museum Boso-no-Mura, describing one outbuilding of its reconstructed farmstead: the kigoya (木小屋), the shed that held the charcoal and firewood a household burned.

Why it applies, and its limits: A museum describing its own reconstruction is good evidence for what a farmyard outbuilding was and what went in it, which is what puts a fuel shed on our farmsteads at all. It is a reconstruction of one region's farmhouse presented for visitors rather than an excavation report or a survey, and the page says nothing about where in the yard the shed stood, so the placement on our maps rests on other reasoning.

buke-hokonin-wiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on buke-hokonin (武家奉公人), the servants of a samurai household: the chugen, komono, genan and kobito who did the household's odd jobs and attended their master out of doors. It covers their live-in status, their annual contracts and how they were hired.

Why it applies, and its limits: Whether servants show up on a city map as their own little houses or as nothing at all turns on whether they lived in their master's compound or in their own, and this article answers that directly: they were live-in staff on yearly terms, taken on through brokers in the merchant quarter. It is a tertiary summary about people and their conditions of employment, not about buildings, and it describes a specifically Edo-period arrangement, so the drawn form of the quarters they occupied comes from other sources.

bukeyashiki-wiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the buke-yashiki (武家屋敷), the samurai residence of an early modern castle town. It sets out the zoning of such a town: upper samurai in hedged and walled plots inside the middle moat near the castle, and the row houses and small plots of ashigaru and other low-ranking retainers arranged outside them, often massed at the town's entrances for defense.

Why it applies, and its limits: This is the source for the rule our samurai wards follow, that rank sets distance from the castle and that ranks of small uniform housing belong on the outer fringe rather than inside a great house's fence. It is a tertiary summary and gives no plot dimensions, setbacks or counts, so it decides the pattern while the measurements come from elsewhere, and it describes the Edo-period castle town specifically rather than samurai housing in every era.

caishikou-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the Caishikou execution grounds in Beijing, the Qing dynasty's public execution site, whose name means "vegetable market". It records that the ground lay at the crossroads of Xuanwumen Outer Street and Luomashi Street, in a busy commercial district.

Why it applies, and its limits: Our maps have to decide whether an execution ground is hidden away or is a named public place, and the Chinese answer is visible here: a working market crossroads, chosen so that a crowd would see it. It is a tertiary summary of one site in the imperial capital, so it anchors the Chinese habit rather than sizing anything, and it is only half of the question our record has to settle, since Japanese practice pushed such grounds out of the settlement entirely.

cambridge-animals-china

What it is: Francesca Bray's chapter "Where Did the Animals Go? Presence and Absence of Livestock in Chinese Agricultural Treatises", in Animals through Chinese History, edited by Roel Sterckx, Martina Siebert and Dagmar Schafer (Cambridge University Press, 2018). It is a peer-reviewed scholarly chapter reading four centuries-spanning Chinese farming manuals to ask whether livestock really vanished from Chinese farms, and argues that they remained ordinary even where the manuals stopped writing about them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supports the modest claim our farmyards need, that an ordinary smallholding kept a pig and some poultry in the yard, and it does so from an authority that has weighed the counter-argument rather than assumed it. Two honest limits: the picture of the ordinary household leans on twentieth-century survey data, so a 1930s count is standing in for the older practice the treatises describe, and it is about China, while the farmstead our maps draw is Japanese in its surface detail.

cdlib-local-elites

What it is: The editors' introduction to Chinese Local Elites and Patterns of Dominance, edited by Joseph W. Esherick and Mary Backus Rankin (University of California Press, 1990), a collection of eleven scholarly essays on how local elites held power in late imperial and Republican China. The introduction summarizes the volume's finding that by Qing times much of the gentry had moved into administrative centers and canal towns and drew their income from land they no longer lived on.

Why it applies, and its limits: It answers the question our hinterland has to settle, whether rich houses cluster along the road outside a city gate, and it answers it against the clustering: an urbanized, absentee landlord class collecting through agents leaves the countryside without a ring of grand suburban compounds. It is a synthesis across widely varying Chinese regions and centuries, it is about China rather than Japan, and it describes where elites lived and how they drew rent rather than what their houses looked like.

chang-jiang-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Chang Jiang, the Yangtze. Among much else it lists the separate names the river carries along its course, from the headwater Tuotuo He through the Jinsha and the Chuan, Jing and Yangzi reaches, the last of them taken from a ferry crossing.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is straightforward evidence for something our maps get wrong by default, that a real river is not one name from source to sea but a chain of local names, each belonging to the stretch the people beside it know. It is a tertiary encyclopedia summary, and it describes one enormous continental river in modern usage, so we take the naming habit from it as a principle and not the names or the reach lengths as anything to scale from.

chang-morphology-walled-capitals

What it is: Sen-dou Chang's scholarly chapter "The Morphology of Walled Capitals", in the geographer G. William Skinner's edited collection The City in Late Imperial China. It is a comparative study of the physical form of Chinese walled administrative cities: the models their street nets follow between the gates, the drum tower at the crossing, and the cultivation, ponds and lakes that occupied surprisingly large parts of the ground inside the walls. The copy available online is a page-image scan.

Why it applies, and its limits: This is the strongest source behind the way our county seats are laid out, a thin skeleton of trunk streets with lanes elsewhere, walls sized to a city's administrative rank rather than its population, and a real share of the enclosed ground left unbuilt as siege insurance. Its limits are stated in our own text: the only proportion Chang gives is the lake at Jinan taking about a fifth of the walled area, so the share of unbuilt ground our maps use is this record's synthesis rather than his measurement, and his generalization is drawn over late imperial administrative cities, which is a larger and grander class of place than most of the settlements we draw.

changan-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on Chang'an, the Han and Tang capital at modern Xi'an. It describes the city's walled residential wards, its two controlled markets opened and closed by drum and gong, the deliberately irregular rectangle of its outline, and the fact that Japan's ancient capitals at Nara and Kyoto were laid out in imitation of it at a smaller scale.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives us both the walled ward as a real urban form and the historical bridge that lets a Chinese plan sit under a Japanese-flavored setting, since the Japanese capitals were consciously copied from this one. It is a tertiary summary, and it describes a planned imperial capital of extraordinary size, so it anchors form and not scale; the number of wards in particular is a figure the readable pages do not agree on, and our text says so rather than quoting the popular round number.

changmen-zhwiki

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on Changmen (阊门), the northwest gate of Suzhou. It describes the district that grew up outside the gate, which in Ming and Qing times was, by the article's account, the busiest commercial quarter in China, with streets radiating outward from the gate and shops in the thousands.

Why it applies, and its limits: Our city maps have to decide how much of a place lives outside its wall, and this is a concrete, named case of a suburb that outgrew the walled town beside it, with the street pattern that goes with it. It is a tertiary summary making an unattributed superlative claim, and Suzhou at its height was one of the wealthiest commercial cities of the empire, so it shows the extreme end of extramural growth rather than what an ordinary county seat would have outside its gates.

chaoguan-zhwiki

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the chaoguan (鈔關), the Ming and Qing tax barriers that levied transit duty on goods, carts and boats. It records where they were placed, at points where goods gathered and at strategic junctions of the water and land routes, and that by the Wanli era only eight major stations remained, seven of them strung along the Grand Canal.

Why it applies, and its limits: We cite it for a negative that matters to the drawing: Chinese customs practice put the barrier on the trade route, not at an ordinary town's gates, so our gate-throat inspection post cannot claim Chinese precedent and rests instead on the Japanese sekisho. It is a tertiary summary of a fiscal institution rather than a study of gate architecture, and it is used to rule a layout out rather than to justify one.

chinese-city-wall-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia survey article on Chinese city walls: their construction from a rammed-earth core faced in brick or stone, their surviving examples at Nanjing, Xi'an and Kaifeng, and their plan, rectangular for capitals and important northern cities but irregular in broken country, where the line followed the terrain.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supports the shape rule our town walls obey, that a wall is a costly thing pulled tight around what must actually be defended and bent by the ground, rather than a tidy circle drawn around empty space. It is a tertiary summary covering the whole country over two thousand years, it gives no costs and no dimensions tied to a settlement's rank, and the economic argument our text makes from the shape is our own reasoning rather than the article's.

chuo-royashiki

What it is: A local history page from Chuo City, one of Tokyo's wards, on the site of the Denmacho jail compound (伝馬町牢屋敷跡), the shogunate's central jail in Edo. It gives the compound's area as 2,600 tsubo, about 8,595 square meters, or more, notes the moat and embankment enclosing it on three sides, and describes the numbers held and the execution ground within the walls.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the hard numbers our jail block needs, an area, an enclosure and a population, from the municipality that now owns the ground and maintains the marker. It is a local government heritage page written for residents and visitors rather than a scholarly study, and it describes the largest jail in the shogunal capital, so for a provincial town it is an upper bound to work down from rather than a figure to copy.

coggins-minor-2018

What it is: Chris Coggins and Jesse Minor, "Fengshui Forests as A Socio-Natural Reservoir in the Face of Climate Change and Environmental Transformation", a peer-reviewed article in Asia Pacific Perspectives 15:2 (2018). It is a field study of the village woodlands of southeastern China, mapping where each grove sits in relation to its village and arguing that these small protected forests carry an outsized ecological and social weight.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the source that corrected our first idea of what a village grove is: not a belt around the settlement but a set of separate patches at particular positions, behind the village on its hill, at the water head and the water mouth and in the mountain gaps, with the paddies lying open in front. It is a modern study of the groves that have survived to be surveyed, in one part of China, so it records the pattern rather than a full premodern inventory, and it stands for a practice our maps also give to Japanese-flavored villages, where the same siting logic is assumed rather than separately attested.

## MISSING a limit, or INACCURATE

### `aburana-jawiki`

Kind: two encyclopedia articles (tertiary). Authors: Wikipedia contributors. Date: current. Place
and era described: Japan (アブラナ) and China/Taiwan (油菜), present day. Scale: a crop, not a place.
Method: summary.

**We use it for**: the rape calendar - sown autumn, overwintered, cut March-April - and rape sown
into harvested paddy and plowed in as green manure (archetypes.html fn 1, 2, supporting "rice and
rape are the two halves of one rotation in the SAME plot").

**Verdict: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS.** Limits: (1) tertiary summaries; (2) the green-manure passage is
an explicitly present-day Taiwanese double-crop practice, not an attested premodern one; (3) - the
one neither the entry nor the draft states - **the calendar quoted in fn 1 is the calendar of
ナバナ (nabana), the flowering-greens vegetable, described as a modern horticultural crop**: the
quoted sentence has seedlings of 5-6 true leaves *transplanted* at 30-40 cm spacing before
overwintering. That is a market-garden regime, not the broadcast oilseed stand the map draws, and
the harvest date belongs to cutting flower stalks for the vegetable. The dates may well be right for
oilseed rape too, but the source we quote is not evidence of that.

`What it is:` **INACCURATE** - it calls the fn-1 passage "the crop's calendar" for oilseed rape; the
passage is the nabana vegetable calendar with transplanting and plant spacing.

Limits: **MISSING** the nabana / modern-horticulture point in (3).

### `adachi-kosatsu`

Kind: a municipal museum's public collection page (Adachi Ward Local History Museum, 足立区立郷土博物館).

**Verdict: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS** for the placement half. Limits: a short public-facing museum

### `afcd-ncsc-9-06`

Kind: a government advisory-committee paper (AFCD to the Nature Conservation Subcommittee, Advisory
Council on the Environment). Date: December 2006. Place and era described: Hong Kong, surveyed
2002-2004; the woods themselves possibly 300+ years old. Scale: 115 village woods, territory-wide.
Method: field survey of species, boundary drawn on a survey map, area computed by GIS.

**We use it for**: the one large measured area distribution of village fengshui groves - the
record's own arithmetic over the Annex (median 9,866 m², mean 11,026 m², 58 under 1 ha, 45 at 1-2
ha, 12 at 2 ha or more, range 606-53,170 m²), vegetation.html fn 69.

**Verdict: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS.** Verified on the paper: "have surveyed 115 FSWs of various sizes
including the most representative sites in Hong Kong"; "A boundary of the FSW was drawn on survey
map and the area of the FSW was subsequently computed using the GIS system."; "The largest site is
Shing Mun with a total area of 5.3 ha."

`What it is:` ACCURATE on kind, body, date and the annex, with one nit: the paper describes these
woods as native forest that "villagers ... **preserved**", with fruit trees and economic plants
planted at the **edges** - so the draft's "since a village first planted them" mis-states the
origin.

Limits: **MISSING**, three of them, and the first two bear directly on the number we take:

1. **The sample is purposive and admittedly incomplete.** "Though the study aimed to be as
   comprehensive as possible, the surveyed sites were not meant to be exhaustive, given the large
   number and wide geographical coverage of FSWs in Hong Kong", and the 115 were chosen as "the most
   representative sites". A median and mean over those rows is a median over a selected sample, not
   over the population of village groves - and selection toward "representative" sites plausibly
   drops the smallest and most degraded. The write-up presents the annex as a measured distribution
   with no sampling caveat at all.
2. **The source scopes the feature to southern China**, calling the fung shui wood "a unique
   landscape and ecological feature in southern China". The draft says Hong Kong "stands in here for
   the wider East Asian practice"; the paper does not assert a wider East Asian practice, so the
   stand-in is broader than the source supports and should be named as ours rather than its.
3. Method: for large sites only "representative parts of the sites were covered" for species, and
   boundaries were drawn by judgment where the wood merged into secondary forest (stated in the
   companion `afcd-hkbio-8`) - so the areas carry a boundary convention, which the write-up mentions
   for the newsletter but not here.

### `artic-pigsty-latrine`

Kind: a museum catalog entry. Author: Art Institute of Chicago. Date: object Han dynasty (206 BCE -
220 CE), catalog current. Place and era described: China, Eastern Han. Scale: one 40.6 x 21.6 x 27.9
cm tomb model. Method: curatorial description.

**We use it for**: the Han pigsty-privy as one customary structure - the muck clusters with the
privy (homesteads.html fn 60).

**Verdict: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS.** Confirmed through `api.artic.edu`: title "Model of a Pigsty and
Latrines", 100 BCE-100 CE, gray earthenware, and the description does carry "latrines—or toilets—were
customarily built above a pigsty and connected by pipes to a cesspool", with the form compared to
models from tombs at Huixian. Limits: a catalog note, not an excavation report; a tomb model, that
is an idealized miniature; Han China, far earlier than the setting's Japan-leaning period.

`What it is:` **INACCURATE** in one particular: "The museum's own object page can be slow to open,
though its catalog text is public." The record itself says the page 403s; it is blocked to a fetcher,
not slow, and the catalog text is public through `api.artic.edu` specifically. A reader following
the footnote's link may get nothing, and the write-up should say where the text can actually be read.

Limits: **MISSING** (mild). Farm-scale pig husbandry is a Chinese practice rather than an Edo
Japanese one, so what transfers to a Japan-leaning map is the privy-and-muck adjacency, not the sty
itself. The draft comes close ("we use it for one placement rule") but never says the sty does not
travel.

Kind: an encyclopedia article (en.wikipedia "Rice broker") plus unnamed district histories. Date:
current. Place and era described: Edo, Tokugawa period. Scale: a city quarter. Method: summary.

2. **The "general histories of the Asakusa and Kuramae districts of Edo" are named nowhere, linked

### `aze-standard`

Kind: a modern public-works standard drawing set. Author: Aomori Prefecture (ほ場整備 standard
drawings, 2017 revision), plus a 大和川流域水田貯留技術基準 named in the entry but not linked. Place
and era described: present-day Japan, consolidated farmland. Scale: an engineered bund cross-section.
Method: a design standard.

**We use it for**: the standard outer bund as a trapezoid of 30 cm top width, 30 cm high, 1:1 side
slopes (~90 cm at the base), "enlarged to ~50 cm x 40 cm in cold regions for deep-water irrigation
and frost heave" (fields.html fn 73; vegetation.html fn 11; water.html fn 46, 50).

**Verdict: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS.** Verified on the sheet (`pdftotext -layout`): 畦畔工 注意事項
「1.畦畔の高さは、高位部田面高より30cm とする。」 and 「2.外法勾配は標準値であり、法面の土質等から
法面の安定を考慮して緩くすることを検討すること。」, with drawn dimensions 300 (crest, mm) and 1:1.0
/ 1:1.2, three types Ⅰ/Ⅱ/Ⅲ by field-level difference H from 0 to 4.0 m, and 400 / 600 mm berms
(小段) where H exceeds 1.0 m.

`What it is:` **INACCURATE** in one particular, and it is the one the entry's `Used for:` line leans
on. **I could not find any cold-region enlargement to ~50 cm x 40 cm on this sheet.** I searched the
extracted text for 寒冷, 凍上, 深水, 400 and 500: the 400 and 600 on the 畦畔工 sheet are berm widths
for tall bunds, not a bigger bund, and the only frost-heave text in the document is about replacing
subgrade with 難凍上性粗粒材料 under a flume, not about enlarging a bund. So the draft's explanation -
"Aomori is a cold northern region whose standards allow for frost heave and deeper water, which is
why the enlarged cold-region figure is kept separate" - attributes to the Aomori sheet something it
does not carry. No footnote quotes the enlarged figure either. If it comes from the Yamato-basin
standard, that document is neither linked nor quoted, and the Yamato river basin is in Nara, which is
not a cold region.

Limits: **MISSING**. The draft limits the standard's *regularity* ("a hand-piled premodern bund would
have been less regular") but not its *size*, and size is the entire use - these lines set how wide
the most repeated line on a paddy map is drawn. This is a post-war land-consolidation (ほ場整備)
standard for machine-formed embankments separating fields whose surfaces differ by up to 4 m, which
is a different object from a hand-piled aze between two level plots; the record's own fields.html
calls the 圃場整理 artifact anachronistic in the same breath. The honest limit is that the number is a
modern engineered minimum used as a calibration against the 1-2 ft the other sources give, not a
measurement of a premodern bund.

Kind: web species pages. Authors: site operators, unattributed. Date: current. Place and era

tokushima-yashikigami

What it is: A short field report, 「On the yashikigami of Misato Village」 (美郷村の屋敷神について) by Yuasa Yasuo, published in 2004 in issue 50 of the Bulletin of the Awa Academic Society (阿波学会紀要, pp. 131-133) by that society's history section, the Tokushima Historical Society, and posted online by the Tokushima Prefectural Library. It walks house by house through one village in Tokushima Prefecture on Shikoku, recording where each family's household guardian deity is enshrined and what its little shrine is made of.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a direct local record of exactly the thing we use it for - whether every house keeps a household shrine or only the old families do, the southwest corner as the usual seat, the roughly 40 cm stone hokora with a round stone inside, and one shrine standing at the foot of a persimmon twenty meters east of a house - so those details are counted from real homesteads rather than generalized from a handbook. Its limits are era and place: it is a modern survey of a custom that had survived into the twentieth century rather than an observation of a premodern village, and household deity practice varied by region, so we treat the southwest corner as a well-attested pattern rather than a national rule.

tontine-monastery-lending

What it is: A post, "Buddhist Monastery Lending," written by Daniel DeMatos in February 2024 for The Tontine Coffee-House, a financial-history blog running since 2018 that covers the history of financial institutions and innovations. It traces how Buddhist monasteries in China served as lenders and pawnbrokers from the arrival of Buddhism down to the nineteenth century, and closes with a short reading list that includes Jacques Gernet's Buddhism in Chinese Society.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the institutional facts behind a temple that lends - the monastery as the great pawnbroker, and pledged goods held in an associated warehouse or granary for the life of the loan - which is why a temple compound on our maps can reasonably carry a strongroom rather than only a hall. It is a secondary blog summary rather than a scholarly work, so we take from it only what its own cited literature supports, and it is about China; we apply it to a Japanese-flavored setting on the strength of the monastic economy the two shared, not as a statement about any particular Japanese temple.

tonya-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on ton'ya, the trade brokers of early modern Japan who acted as wholesalers, warehouse managers and shipment managers, and who became central to the economy of the Edo period (1603-1867).

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it only for what a ton'ya was and what work it did, which is enough to justify drawing a merchant's warehouse-and-office block in a town's commercial quarter and to name it correctly. It is a tertiary summary, so we take its figures and dates only where its own references support them, and it describes an institution rather than a building - nothing about the size, plan or placement of a ton'ya on our maps comes from it.

toribeno-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Toribeno (鳥辺野), the great burial ground on the eastern hills of Kyoto, one of the three famous funerary fields of the old capital along with Adashino to the west and Rendaino to the north, attested in literature from the Heian period onward in works such as the Tale of Genji and Essays in Idleness.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one point about form rather than any number: that the extent of such a field had no clear definition, which is our warrant for drawing a burial ground as an unbounded stretch of hillside rather than a walled or fenced plot. It is a tertiary summary, so we take from it only what its own references support; it also describes the capital's own enormous burial fields, so it tells us the shape of the thing and never the scale a village graveyard should have.

toyoko-kaki

What it is: A blog post of December 2012, 「Why are persimmon trees planted in the front yards of farmhouses?」 (農家の庭先にはなぜ柿の木が植えられているのか？), on the Ameba blog of Toyoko Housing, a rental-property company. It is a conversational piece about why the persimmon is the dooryard tree of the Japanese farmhouse, citing the Edo-period agronomist Miyazaki Yasusada's encouragement to plant them around the house and listing the tree's practical virtues.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the persimmon standing in every dooryard, the Edo-period agricultural recommendation behind that habit, and the summer shade it throws over the house - the reasons our homesteads get a fruit tree by the door rather than an ornamental one. It is a company blog written for general readers, not a scholarly source: the Miyazaki attribution is reported at second hand, and the "every dooryard" is a modern writer's impression of the countryside, so we use it for the practice and its rationale and never as a measured prevalence.

tricycle-temple-wives

What it is: "Temple Wives of Japan," an interview by Karen Jensen with the scholar Jessica Starling, published in the Spring 2022 issue of Tricycle: The Buddhist Review, a long-running nonprofit Buddhist magazine. It explains the bomori - literally the guardian or protector of the temple, in practice the wife of a Jodo Shinshu resident priest - and the household that a temple in that tradition actually is.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives us what a rural temple contains as a domestic institution: a married clergy exempted by the Tokugawa government so a temple head could be married and still hold priestly status, a wife who runs the temple, and succession from father to eldest son - which is why our temple compounds carry a priest's family dwelling rather than a celibate dormitory. It is a magazine interview rather than a study, and it describes one tradition, Jodo Shinshu, whose married clergy was the exception in the Edo period rather than the rule, so we use it for the shape of a temple household and not as a claim about every sect.

tsuijimatsu

What it is: The preservation website for the tsuijimatsu, the tall clipped pine windbreak hedges of the Izumo Plain, run by the city of Izumo in Shimane Prefecture through its architecture and housing division. Besides documenting the hedges and the dispersed-settlement landscape they belong to, the site runs pruning workshops and tree-health programs, and carries a page comparing Izumo's hedges with the homestead groves of other regions.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use its regional-comparison page for what actually grows in a homestead grove - a stand centered on cedar with zelkova, the kashi oaks, bamboo, persimmon and chestnut alongside it - and for what the grove was harvested for, fallen leaves and dead branches as fuel and bamboo as everyday material, which is what lets us plant a homestead's belt of trees as a working resource rather than decoration. It is a municipal preservation page describing a living landscape, so its stands are twentieth and twenty-first century ones, kept up under a modern conservation program; the species mix and the uses are the durable part, and the health of any particular hedge today is not something we take forward.

uehara-2009-agris

What it is: The bibliographic record, in the FAO's international agricultural database AGRIS, for Uehara, Shigematsu, Fujii and Iwamoto, "Succession of shrub-layer vegetation and situation of wild Rhododendron in the abandoned Satoyama coppice forest," Landscape Research Japan 72(5), 2009, pp. 511-516, with the paper's abstract. The study compares a coppice woodland in Hyogo Prefecture cut twenty-five years earlier with one left alone for fifty, counting 42 plant species and 13 floor herbs in the managed stand against 23 species and 3 floor herbs in the neglected one.

Why it applies, and its limits: This is our evidence that a managed coppice has an open, flowering, species-rich floor under a cut canopy while an abandoned one goes dark and bare, which is the difference between a village woodlot we draw as worked ground and a thicket - and it supplies the fifty-year figure for how long neglect takes to show. What we read is the database record and its abstract rather than the full Japanese article, and it is a single paired comparison in one prefecture measured in the 2000s, so we use its direction and rough magnitude, not its species counts, as a general rule about coppice woodland.

uekipedia-kaki

What it is: The entry for kaki (persimmon) in Uekipedia (植木ペディア), a Japanese online tree encyclopedia maintained by a person working in the gardening trade, which catalogs ornamental and useful trees by flower, fruit, leaf, growing conditions and landscape use for gardeners and landscapers choosing what to plant.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one measurement, the persimmon's mature height of 3 to 20 m, which sets how large a dooryard fruit tree may be drawn. It is a horticultural reference site rather than a peer-reviewed one, and it is describing the tree as planted in Japan today; height is a species trait that changes little between then and now, but the entry gives no crown width, so the spread of the tree on our maps rests on other grounds.

usu-windbreak

What it is: "Windbreak Benefits and Design," a Utah Forest Facts extension bulletin published by Utah State University Extension, which explains what a planted windbreak does and how far its shelter reaches, expressed as multiples of the windbreak's own height.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use its rule of thumb - shelter extending downwind up to thirty times the height of the trees, with full protection of a large area needing a windbreak every ten to twenty heights - to decide how far apart sheltering tree belts stand and how much ground one belt can be said to protect. The limits are place and era: this is a modern American agricultural extension document about Utah, written for tractors and center-pivot country, so what we take from it is the physics of air flowing over a barrier, which does not change with century or continent, and never its planting recommendations or species.

visit-toyama-sankyoson

What it is: The English page on the Tonami Plain dispersed settlement (散居村, sankyoson) from Visit Toyama, the tourism site for Toyama Prefecture. It describes an alluvial fan on which more than 7,000 farmhouses, each ringed by its own kainyo homestead grove, are scattered across roughly 220 square kilometers, a landscape it dates to more than five hundred years of formation.

Why it applies, and its limits: This is our anchor for the dispersed farmstead pattern and its density - farmers building in the middle of their own paddies so they could manage their own water, houses standing naturally apart, and about thirty-two farmsteads per square kilometer - and for what the surrounding grove was for, shelter from winter wind and snow, summer shade, and cedar, zelkova and bamboo as building and tool material. It is a tourist board's page, written to describe the place to visitors rather than to report a survey, so we lean on its two round figures as the scale of a still-visible landscape rather than as a historical census; the settlement is a living modern one, and it is one plain in one prefecture, chosen because it is the clearest surviving example of a pattern we wanted to draw.

wagner-fining-puddling

What it is: "Traditional Chinese fining and puddling," a page by Donald B. Wagner, the historian of Chinese iron and steel technology, on his own site. It describes how Chinese ironworkers turned cast iron into wrought iron: wood, charcoal and broken cast iron charged into a hearth and lit, the half-melted mass stirred with an iron rod under a blast of air, a family of methods known collectively as chao, "stir frying."

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for what actually happens inside a finery, which is what tells us the building needs a hearth, a bellows blast and room for a worker to stand and stir - the difference between drawing a smithy and drawing an ironworks. It is a specialist's web page rather than a peer-reviewed article, though written by the leading scholar of the subject and drawn from the Chinese technical literature; it is about China, and about a process rather than a workshop, so the arrangement of the buildings we draw around it comes from elsewhere.

wagner-ming-iron

What it is: "Iron production in three Ming texts," a page by Donald B. Wagner presenting translations and commentary on Ming-dynasty Chinese accounts of the iron industry, among them Song Yingxing's description of the chao fining hearth and a passage numbering the workforce of one ironworks.

Why it applies, and its limits: These are near-contemporary descriptions of a working premodern ironworks, which is exactly the era and technology our setting is modeled on: they give us the fining hearth built a few paces from the furnace and a step lower, men on the wall stirring with willow poles, and a labor establishment of some 200 charcoal burners, 200 furnace tenders, 300 miners and their oxen and boats - the numbers behind how much settlement an ironworks drags along with it. The limits are place and scale: this is Ming China, not Japan, and the figures come from one large enterprise, so they set the shape of an industry rather than the staffing of any works we draw; the page is a scholar's personal site rather than a journal, and what it offers is translated primary text.

waldrand-dewiki

What it is: The German Wikipedia article on the Waldrand, the forest edge, which sets out the structure of a fully grown one: from the open field inward, a herb fringe, then a belt of shrubs, then the forest mantle of trees whose crowns sweep down low on the field side.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for that three-layer profile, which is how we draw the boundary between woodland and cultivated ground as a graded edge rather than a hard line. It is a tertiary summary, so we take from it only what its own references support; it is also describing central European woodland, and it was consulted because the English-language article on woodland edges did not carry the layer terms - the layering is a general property of a sunlit forest margin, but the species that would fill each layer in East Asia are not taken from here.

wang-ochiai-2022

What it is: Wang Jingying and Ochiai Chiho, "Spatial composition and building techniques of farmhouses prone to windstorms: a case study in Arakawa Village, Shiga Prefecture, Japan," a peer-reviewed open-access article in the Journal of Asian Architecture and Building Engineering 21:6 (2022). It surveys the house lots of a village exposed to the Hira windstorms and records where each building on the lot stands - main house, storehouse, retirement house, toilet - and how the buildings are made.

Why it applies, and its limits: This is a measured, building-by-building survey of the very thing we place on a homestead, and it gives us the figure we use literally: 72.7% of toilets sited southeast to south, because the warmth sped the fermentation of night soil headed for the paddies. It is equally the source that settled where privies do not go - its wind-siting findings concern storehouses and retirement houses, and it contains no language about seating a privy downwind for odor, which is why we do not do that. Its limits are place and era: one village in Shiga Prefecture surveyed in the modern period, so the percentage is a strong local pattern in surviving houses rather than a national premodern rate, and the practice it explains - night soil as fertilizer - is the older one that the siting outlived.

wanli-fishpond-summary

What it is: Not one work but a set of readable Chinese-language pages about the dike-pond country of the Pearl River Delta, chiefly Shunde (顺德) county: a Guangzhou Daily feature and the Shunde archives timeline, which give the land resurvey figures of 40,084 mu of fishpond in 1581 and 58,094 mu in 1642; a Guangzhou municipal page citing the Agricultural Gazetteer of the Pearl River Delta for roughly 160,000 mu of taxable fishpond across three counties in 1581; and a late-1980s ecological survey of the same region reporting 86,632 hectares of dike-pond land, 35% of it fishpond.

Why it applies, and its limits: Together they give us the one thing we need, the scale of the sixteenth-century dike-pond zone: enough pond to make it a landscape and not a curiosity, but a small share of the cultivated land at that date - a few percent of the county's fields, with the famous "more pond than field" descriptions belonging to the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, not to 1581. Two honest caveats travel with it: the percentage shares are our own arithmetic over separately reported pond and farmland totals rather than a figure any page states, and one widely repeated claim that a particular township was already more than half pond in 1581 turned out to be traceable to an uncited blog and is contradicted by the archives' own 18%, so we use the surveyed acreages and treat the vivid summaries with caution. These are newspaper, government and archive pages rather than scholarship, and the modern survey figure is a twentieth-century measurement of a landscape that had gone on growing.
