shiniuba-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 死牛馬取得権 ("the right to take fallen cattle and horses"), on the hereditary privilege by which the kawata - the outcaste leatherworking communities of Tokugawa Japan - claimed the carcasses of dead livestock across a defined stretch of countryside, a right abolished in 1871.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives us the shape of the thing we need for a map - that the hide trade was territorial, each community drawing its raw material from a named collecting ground (a kusaba or dannaba) rather than from a market - which is what puts a tannery quarter where it stands in relation to the settlement it serves. It is a tertiary summary rather than a study, so we take its terms and the outline of the arrangement and rely on its own references for anything finer; it also describes Japan under the Tokugawa specifically, which is the era our setting leans on hardest but not the only one it draws from.

shitsuden-kotobank

What it is: The Kotobank entry for 湿田 (shitsuden, "wet paddy"). Kotobank is a Japanese reference site that reprints entries from established published encyclopedias and dictionaries rather than writing its own, so the entry is a dictionary definition of the badly drained rice field that stays waterlogged the year round, with a note on the long conversion of such fields to the drained kind.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it to establish that "paddy" is not one thing - that a poorly drained field that never dries is a distinct and much older class of paddy, and that the shift toward drained fields began in western Japan in the late Yayoi period - which is why some of our maps tint their fields differently. It is a short reference definition, a tertiary source condensing a large literature, so it supports the distinction and the rough direction of change and not a date or a proportion we would want to lean any weight on.

shizen-teibo-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 自然堤防 ("natural levee"), on the low ridge of coarser sediment a river builds along its own banks when it floods, and on the wetter backswamp (後背湿地) that lies behind it on an alluvial plain.

Why it applies, and its limits: This is the single most useful fact for laying out a lowland village: houses and dry fields go up on the levee, which is the only naturally drained ground for miles, and the paddy goes into the backswamp behind - a rule the article states directly for long-established Japanese settlements. It is an encyclopedia summary of settled physical geography rather than a survey, so we take the siting principle from it and not any measurement; and it describes Japanese alluvial lowland, so it applies to our river-plain settlements and says nothing about hill or fan country.

shoinzukuri-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 書院造 (shoin-zukuri), on the formal residential style that shaped warrior and priestly houses from the Muromachi period onward - the tatami-floored reception rooms, the built-in alcove and shelving, and the garden they were arranged to face.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one orientation rule that a plan cannot do without: the formal rooms of a house of standing look out south across the garden, past the outer aisle inside the eaves, which fixes which side of a compound is the show face and which is the working one. The article says nothing about the service side behind those rooms, so the north half of any plan we draw rests on other sources; and as a tertiary summary of an idealized style it describes the type rather than any particular house, which for a generated map is what we want but is worth knowing.

sinyoken-madori

What it is: An unsigned essay on a Japanese traditional-architecture site (sinyoken.sakura.ne.jp), 「間取りからみたトイレの位置の変遷」 ("Changes in the position of the toilet seen from the floor plan"), which walks through house plans from the warrior residence to the merchant house and the farmhouse and shows where the privy sat in each and why it moved.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the source that answers a question almost nothing else does - where on a farmstead the privy actually stood, out by the work shed and the back door where the night-soil cart could reach it - and it explains the separate upper and lower privies of a household of rank, which is a real distinction we draw. It is a website essay with no named author and no citations, not a survey or a peer-reviewed study, so we use it where it describes plan arrangements that other sources corroborate and never as the sole authority for a number or a date.

song-architecture-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article "Architecture of the Song dynasty", a survey of Chinese building and city form in the tenth to thirteenth centuries, including the collapse of the walled-ward city plan that the Tang had inherited from earlier dynasties.

Why it applies, and its limits: It carries the one change that decides how a town map looks: a Tang city sorted its residents and its markets into separate walled wards, while a Song city let shops line the street in front of ordinary houses - so a settlement in our setting is drawn as one or the other, and the difference is visible at a glance. It is a tertiary summary, so we take this well-established structural contrast from it and check its own references before using any figure; and it is about China, which our setting draws on alongside Japan, so where the two diverge the Japanese sources govern.

sotobori-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 外濠 (東京都), on the outer moat of Edo castle in what is now Tokyo - how it was dug, which watercourses were pressed into it, and what has since become of it.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for a point about how a fortified city treats its water: the Sotobori was not a ditch dug beside a river but the river itself relocated, the Hirakawa's course moved into the excavation, which is the pattern our walled maps follow when a stream meets a defensive line. It is an encyclopedia article on one specific and unusually large city work - a shogunal capital, not a provincial town - so the principle scales down to our maps only as a principle, and the dimensions of Edo's moat are not numbers we carry across.

sphere-unicef

What it is: A chapter of the Sphere humanitarian minimum standards - the water supply, sanitation and hygiene section, circulated here as a PDF on the European Commission's humanitarian aid site - setting out how many users a tap, a handpump or an open well can serve and how far anyone should have to walk to reach one.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is used for one deliberately blunt purpose: to show that a single open well can supply roughly four hundred users, and therefore that the number of wells in a village was never set by how much water a well could yield but by what one cost to dig and how long the morning queue was. This is a modern relief-agency standard, not a historical measurement, and the flow rate it assumes belongs to today's engineering; we use it only as an upper bound that rules a constraint out, and every positive claim about how many wells a village actually had comes from the historical sources beside it.

stcroix-boom-nps

What it is: "The St. Croix Boom", an article published by the United States National Park Service on the nineteenth-century log boom works on the St. Croix River between Minnesota and Wisconsin - the piers, pilings and floating log fences that sorted and held the timber floated down from the watershed.

Why it applies, and its limits: A boom is a piece of riverside furniture our timber towns need, and this describes exactly how one is arranged: the river divided lengthwise into log channels and holding pens with a navigation channel kept open alongside, a hinged sheer boom at the head that swings shut to let boats past, and the lawsuits that followed when logs spilled into the fairway - which is why our booms run along a bank rather than across the water. The obvious limit is place and period: this is industrial-era North America, not premodern East Asia, and we use it for the physical logic of the arrangement, which the Japanese timber-yard sources corroborate at a much smaller scale, never for the size of anything.

sugiura-1973-fuzoku

What it is: A peer-reviewed geography article by Sugiura Tadashi, 「農村集落における農家の付属建物について - 宮城県宮崎町の例」 ("On the outbuildings of farmhouses in rural settlements: the case of Miyazaki town, Miyagi prefecture"), published in Tōhoku Chiri 25(3), 1973, pages 145-152. It counts, household by household, which outbuildings each farmstead in the surveyed town actually had, and what stood inside the older main houses.

Why it applies, and its limits: This is the backbone of how our farmsteads are populated: it is a real count rather than an impression, so a privy appears on most homesteads, a firewood shed on three quarters, a storehouse on only about a quarter, and the map's variation from farm to farm reproduces measured frequencies instead of taste. Its honest limits are era and place - it is a survey of one town in the Tōhoku region taken in the early 1970s, so it records twentieth-century farmsteads whose buildings largely predate them, and the region is the cold northeast rather than the whole country; we state that scope wherever we quote it, and treat the pattern of which buildings are common as more transferable than the exact proportions.

suirokyo-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 水路橋 ("aqueduct bridge"), on the structures that carry a watercourse over a river or a valley, with Japanese examples such as the Tsujun bridge, the Meisho irrigation works and the Suirokaku arcade in Kyoto.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it to establish the form itself - that when a canal has to cross a valley the answer is a bridge carrying the water, and what such a bridge looks like - which is a piece of furniture our irrigated landscapes need and which readers rarely expect. It is a tertiary summary and does not date its examples, so it tells us the type exists and how it is built and nothing about when any given one was; the named examples are also nineteenth-century or later works, so we draw the form and not their engineering.

sumida-gawa-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 隅田川, on the river through eastern Tokyo, including the several older names by which different stretches of it were known - Ōkawa, Asakusagawa, Miyatogawa.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is cited for a small point of naming that matters on a map: one river can carry different names along different reaches and in different mouths, so a watercourse crossing a city need not be labeled the same at both ends. It is an encyclopedia article about one specific river in one city; we use it as an example of the naming habit rather than as evidence about any other river, and where it does not confirm a name we have seen elsewhere we do not claim it.

susquehanna-boom

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the Susquehanna Boom, the log-holding works at Williamsport, Pennsylvania, that ran some seven miles of river through the second half of the nineteenth century; the entry also gathers material from the Pennsylvania Conservation Heritage and Lumber Heritage Region pages on the same works.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is our upper anchor for how large a boom can get and how it is anchored - a diagonal line of three hundred and fifty odd stone-filled timber cribs standing twenty-two feet high, enclosing a pen that could hold three hundred million board feet of logs at once - which tells us that a boom is moored to fixed ground and how much water a working one occupies. Two limits, both plain: this is industrial North America rather than premodern East Asia, so it gives the physics of the arrangement and not its scale for our maps, and it is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where the article's own references support them - the lifetime log count sometimes attached to this boom is not on the page, so we do not assert it.

suzaku-oji-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 朱雀大路 (Suzaku Ōji), on the great central avenue that ran from the palace gate to the southern gate of Heian-kyō and of the earlier Japanese capitals, with the corresponding avenue of Chang'an in Tang China for comparison.

Why it applies, and its limits: Our capital maps need a number for the ceremonial spine, and this gives two: about 82 meters for Heian-kyō, the figure recorded in the tenth-century Engishiki code, and about 147 meters for its Chinese model - which sets both the width we draw and the honest gap between the Japanese city and the Chinese one it copied. It is a tertiary summary, but the Japanese figure it reports comes from a primary legal code and the width of these avenues is confirmed by excavation; the limit is scale rather than reliability - this is the grandest street of an imperial capital, and nothing about it transfers to a provincial town's main road.

suzugamori-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 鈴ヶ森刑場, on the Suzugamori execution ground that stood on the Tōkaidō at the southern approach to Edo from the seventeenth century until its abolition in the early Meiji years, and on its northern counterpart Kozukappara on the Nikkō highway.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supplies the placement rule our city maps use for a thing that has to go somewhere unpleasant: execution grounds sat at the entrances to the city, on the great highways, just outside where the built-up area ended, deliberately in the sight of everyone arriving - and that they came in pairs, one at each approach, is the article's own statement. It is a tertiary summary describing one shogunal capital in the Tokugawa period, so we take the siting logic and the pairing and not any measurement; how a much smaller provincial settlement handled the same need is inferred from the principle rather than found here.

tabayashi-1986

What it is: A peer-reviewed article by Akira Tabayashi, "Irrigation Systems in Japan", in the Geographical Review of Japan, Series B volume 60 number 1 (1987), pages 41-65. It classifies Japan's irrigation systems by their water source - river, pond, lake, groundwater, torrent - maps where each kind predominates, and traces when each was built, from the Kofun and Nara period works of the west to the Sengoku and Edo works of the east.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the scholarly backbone of how water is drawn across our field systems: that a storage pond must sit higher than the paddy it feeds and is tapped by a single outlet, that a main canal narrows step by step as branches take from it, that the smallest ditches belong to the handful of farmers they serve, and that supply and drainage were separated only where fields were reorganized. It is a modern academic study of systems that are mostly premodern in origin, which is the right relationship for our purposes, but part of its story runs into the industrial era - the field consolidation it describes follows an 1899 law - so we take the older gravity-fed logic from it and treat the surveyed rectangular grid of separated supply and drain canals as the modern arrangement it is. It covers irrigation and not the fields themselves; it says nothing about how deep a paddy is flooded, and we do not cite it for that.

kichinyado-kotobank

What it is: A page on kotobank, a Japanese reference site that reprints the entries several published dictionaries and encyclopedias give for a single word, gathering here the entries for 木賃宿 (kichinyado), the cheapest class of travelers' lodging in Edo-period Japan, where a guest paid a small charge for firewood and cooked their own food. The works reprinted on it include Shogakukan's Nipponica and Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten, Yamakawa's concise dictionary of Japanese history, and Heibonsha's revised Sekai Dai-hyakka Jiten.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for what the cheapest bed in a post town cost, and dated ordinance figures are exactly what these reference works carry, each attached to a year and a ruling; they also say who slept in such places, which is what a lodging on a town map is for. The limits are that these are tertiary summaries, compilers' condensations rather than the ordinances themselves, so we take only the figures they state and date, and that the three prices are two centuries and several places apart, marking the range of a cheap bed rather than one price.

kikoba-kenchi

What it is: A 1974 research paper in the Transactions of the Architectural Institute of Japan (number 222), the second part of a study called 「近世村方文書よりみた相模国三浦郡木古庭村の屋敷と家屋」 ("The homesteads and houses of Kikoba village, Miura district, Sagami province, seen through early-modern village documents"). It works through that one village's own paperwork, including a 1594 land survey and a homestead-area register submitted to the magistrate in 1691, to reconstruct how large peasant house plots and houses were and who held them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a study of primary village documents about the very thing we use it for - the spread of homestead-lot sizes in a real Japanese village, with a clear mode near the small end and the great holders roughly twice the ordinary size, and the fact that by the end of the seventeenth century every peasant household there held a plot, so the small lots on our maps are occupied rather than empty. Its limits are that it is one village in one province, so we carry the shape of the distribution across rather than its exact numbers, and that a survey register records a plot's assessed area, not the yard as it was actually used.

kiso-unzaihou

What it is: A page published by the Chubu Regional Forest Office of Japan's Forestry Agency, part of a public-history series on the Kiso forests, describing the Kiso-style felling and timber transport method - axe felling, the sledge and chute haul down to the water, loose-log drives, and rafting - as it was practiced from the late sixteenth century until 1924. The page notes that its illustrated guide is a Meiji-era copy made from Edo-period originals, and gives no author.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for how timber reached a town, and it describes that chain in order: the loose-log drive handed off to rafts at the tying station, three men riding each raft, and the run down to the timber storage yard at Nagoya and the bay port beyond, which is what puts a log yard where we put it. It is a government agency's explanatory page rather than a study, and it describes one valley's system, so the crew size and the yard locations are a worked example of how such a trade ran and not a national standard.

kitamoto-mushiro-niwa

What it is: A page of 北本市史 民俗編, the folklore volume of the published city history of Kitamoto in Saitama prefecture, read in that city's own digital archive. The passage records local farming custom, among it how big a farmhouse's work yard was, counted in the straw mats that could be laid out on it, with the conversion of two mats to one tsubo.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the one source we could read that states a farm work yard's size directly rather than leaving it to be inferred from a house plan, and it adds the reason the size varies - the yard tracked how much grain the household had to thresh and dry - which is why our yards scale with the holding. Its limits are era and place: a twentieth-century folklore volume recording remembered practice in one district of the Kanto plain, whose crop was barley, and a remembered "usually forty to sixty mats" is the range of a custom rather than a survey measurement.

kochi-seiri-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on 耕地整理 (kochi seiri, arable-land consolidation), the rearrangement of farm plots into regular rectangles squared to the compass, covering the Shizuoka method first carried out in 1872 and the national consolidation law of 1899.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for a date rather than a measurement: it places the neat rectangular grid of Japanese paddy in the Meiji era and after, which is why the fields on our maps keep the irregular shapes the ground gave them. It is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, and here what we take is an institution and its statute, which is the kind of thing such an article states plainly.

kohai-shicchi-jawiki

What it is: Japanese Wikipedia's article on 後背湿地 (kohai shicchi, the backswamp) read together with its companion article on 自然堤防 (the natural levee), explaining how a river builds raised banks along its own channel and leaves poorly drained, fine-grained lowland behind them, and how that lowland was farmed.

Why it applies, and its limits: The landform does not change with the century, so a modern description of it serves a premodern map directly, and we use it for what lies behind a river's bank - wet ground, traditionally worked as paddy, extended over time by draining marsh - which decides where our fields and our houses go on a floodplain. It is a tertiary summary, so we take the description of the landform and its traditional use and no number from it.

kojodan-dobei

What it is: A 2020 post by the writer Takamaru in "Takamaru's Castle Basics course", a long-running explainer series on Kojodan, a Japanese castle enthusiasts' site. It sets out the kinds of earthen wall used at castles - the framed and plastered wall, the rammed-earth tsuijibei built up in layers inside wooden forms, and the frameless neribei of old tile and stone bedded in clay - with how each was built and how thick it came out.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it to decide how thick to draw a compound wall, and it gives the two figures side by side, about a meter for the rammed-earth wall against roughly 30 cm for the frameless kind, which is the comparison a map needs. It is an enthusiast site's explainer rather than an archaeological report, and it hedges its own numbers as approximate, so we lean on the difference between the two wall types more than on either figure as a precise measurement.

kokudaka-en

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on kokudaka, the rice-denominated assessment by which Japanese domains, fiefs and stipends were rated.

Why it applies, and its limits: This one is cited for a caution rather than a fact: the article's own account of the assessment converting other crops and produce into their rice equivalent is what stops us from reading a domain's rice rating as evidence that its land was mostly wet paddy, which would put paddy on maps that should carry dry field. It is a tertiary summary, used here only for the definition of a fiscal convention, which is the kind of thing an encyclopedia states plainly, and for no measurement at all.

kokudaka-jawiki

What it is: Japanese Wikipedia's article on 石高 (kokudaka), the rice-volume measure used to rate land and to pay retainers, including what one koku was taken to represent and what a retainer was actually issued.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use its rule of thumb - one koku as an adult's rice for a year - to turn a settlement's assessed yield into a number of mouths it could feed, and the article supplies its own hedge, that a standard stipend ran nearer 1.8 koku of brown rice, which keeps the round figure from being treated as exact. It is a tertiary summary whose figures we take where it states them with that qualification, and the koku equivalence is in any case a convention of assessment rather than a measured diet.

kosatsu-jawiki

What it is: Japanese Wikipedia's article on 高札 (kosatsu), the boards on which laws, price schedules and prohibitions were written up and posted publicly, and on the kosatsuba where those boards stood.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives both the institution and the thing a map actually needs, which is where a board was put - the crossroads at a town's center, its entrances and exits, the foot of a bridge, a barrier station - and it names the principal boards of Edo. It is a tertiary summary; the placement rule is descriptive and the article's own examples match it, and the only counts it offers are a capital's, which we do not carry down to a village.

kotobank-benjo

What it is: The entry for 便所 (benjo, the privy) from Shogakukan's encyclopedia Nipponica, reprinted on the reference site kotobank. It describes how privies were arranged in different kinds of Japanese household - paired and attached to the main buildings in samurai and court-noble residences, gathered into one small separate building for a compound's rowhouses, set behind the guest parlor in townhouses and farmhouses, and provided in farm households as a single building standing clear of the main house.

Why it applies, and its limits: It answers the placement question a map has to answer - whether the privy is inside the house or a separate outbuilding - and it says the detached farm privy holding both the urinal and the privy was the usual arrangement, which is what we draw. Being an encyclopedia entry it is a tertiary summary and it describes a custom rather than counting it: "usual" is not a percentage, so how often our farmsteads show one is our own choice resting on the form the entry gives.

kotobank-fukada

What it is: Two Shogakukan dictionaries, the Digital Daijisen and the Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten, shown together on kotobank for the word 深田 (fukada), which both define as a paddy with deep mud, a swamp paddy, the opposite of a shallow one.

Why it applies, and its limits: A dictionary is the right authority for what a word means, and this word settles a distinction our paddy classes depend on: fukada names how deep the mud underfoot is, not where in the landscape the field sits. Nothing in these entries ties the word to a valley bottom, and none of them attaches a depth to it, so we use it for the sense of the term and take our depths from elsewhere.

kotobank-idoyakata

What it is: The Digital Daijisen and Nihon Kokugo Daijiten entries for 井戸屋形 (idoyakata, the well house), gathered on kotobank, each defining it as a simple structure of posts set beside a well with a roof on top of them and nothing more.

Why it applies, and its limits: Our well glyph puts a small roof over the well head, and these entries confirm that the roofed well of Japanese practice really was that plain - posts and a roof, not a shed. A dictionary gives the form of a thing and not how common it was, so how many of a settlement's wells are drawn roofed is not decided by this source.

kotobank-kanden

What it is: The Digital Daijisen and Heibonsha's revised Sekai Dai-hyakka Jiten entries for 乾田 (kanden, the dry paddy), shown together on kotobank: a paddy that drains well and dries out to the condition of a dry field when the water is let off, together with the national program that converted waterlogged paddy into it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the contrast term for the wet paddy our maps mostly show, and it carries the era point we need - that draining paddy into well-drained fields was a state undertaking from the Meiji period onward, which is why the setting's fields are the wet kind rather than the tidy dry ones a modern photograph shows. These are tertiary summaries, and the entry reports its "more than two thirds of the country's paddy" as what is commonly said, so we use it as an indication of how large that modern change was and not as a statistic.

kotobank-shitsuden

What it is: Three reference works shown together on kotobank for 湿田 (shitsuden, the wet paddy) - Shogakukan's Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten and Nipponica, and Heibonsha's revised Sekai Dai-hyakka Jiten. They define it as a badly drained paddy that stays waterlogged even when rice is not growing in it, and set out what that costs: no winter crop, heavy going for the farm work, soil that is colder and starved of air, and unstable, generally low yields.

Why it applies, and its limits: This is the class our blue plots belong to, and these entries are what let a reader clicking one of them learn why a wet field is a poorer field rather than simply a wetter one. They are tertiary summaries that characterize a type rather than measure any particular field, so which of a settlement's plots are wet is our own placement, made from the ground the map puts them on.

kotobank-yatsuda

What it is: The encyclopedia entry for 谷津田 / 谷地田 (yatsuda, the valley-bottom paddy) on kotobank, from Heibonsha's Sekai Dai-hyakka Jiten, describing paddy lying in the low ground of valleys cut into a plateau: wetland, opened up long ago, and in many cases dependent on rainfall because such valleys are not well supplied with water sources.

Why it applies, and its limits: Where our maps run fields up a valley floor, this is the field type they are, and the entry gives both the setting and its character - old, wet, and often rain-fed rather than fed by a channel, which bears on whether we draw a supply ditch to it. It is a tertiary summary describing a landform-and-field type rather than measuring one, so we take the character of the ground from it and no dimension.

santome-shinden-allotment

What it is: A 1992 peer-reviewed paper by Yoshiro Yamamori in the Journal of the Architectural Institute of Japan, Planning Series, no. 436, on the row settlements of the Musashino plateau west of Tokyo. It reconstructs how Santome Shinden (三富新田), a planned reclamation colony finished in 1696, was surveyed and handed out: every settler got a long strip running back from the road, with a thatched house set at the road end of it.

Why it applies, and its limits: Our homesteads normally vary in size, and this paper is the attested counter-case for the setting where they do not, because a planned colony issued every household an identical house lot even though the finished strips themselves came out uneven. Its limits are that it is a modern architectural study reading the survey record rather than an Edo document, and that it describes one deliberately planned colony on one plateau, so it is evidence for what a laid-out settlement looked like and never for an ordinary village that grew on its own.

satologue-yashikigami

What it is: A page on satologue.com, a present-day Japanese site that writes about country living and rural custom, describing the yashikigami, the deity of a farm household's own ground, and the small hokora shrine that stands in a corner of the plot to house it.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for two plain facts of a custom that is still visible on farms today and that we draw on every homestead: the shrine is tiny, and it sits at a corner of the grounds rather than at the center. It is a lifestyle site and not a survey or a historical document, so it is good for what the thing looks like and not for how common it was or how old the practice is, and because the page names no compass direction, which corner we put it in is our own choice.

satoyama-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on satoyama, the managed border zone between the wooded hills and the farmed flat in Japan, covering its mosaic of woodland, paddy, dry field, grassland and ponds and the ways villagers worked it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives us the shape of the ground between a settlement's fields and the hills behind it, together with two practices we render directly: Edo-era gathering of leaf litter from that belt to fertilize the paddy, and coppice cutting on a rotation of roughly 15 to 20 years. An encyclopedia article is a tertiary summary, so we take its figures only where its own references support them, and "satoyama" is itself a largely twentieth-century name for a much older way of working the land, so the term is modern even where the practice is not.

sdlib-shunde-jitang

What it is: An article from the Shunde Library's local-history series 发现顺德 (Discovering Shunde), economy volume, on the mulberry-dike fish pond (桑基鱼塘) of the Pearl River delta: the pond dug out, its own spoil heaped around the four sides to make the dike, mulberry planted on the dike along with hemp, soybeans, peanuts and melon trellises.

Why it applies, and its limits: This is a public library writing about the landscape on its own doorstep, and it gives us both the physical form we draw when a settlement's water is a pond-and-dike system and the sequence of its spread, from the Song-era 桑园围 embankment through the Jiajing-era expansion to the Xianfeng and Tongzhi peak. It is popular local history rather than a scholarly study, and it is written to celebrate a local heritage, so we take the form and the rough chronology from it and not precise figures; the place is subtropical southern China, which our setting admits because it is modeled on imperial China as well as on Japan, but it is not a Japanese form.

seijoue-kotobank

What it is: The entry for 正条植 (seijoue, straight-row rice planting) on Kotobank, a Japanese reference site that reprints entries from published dictionaries and encyclopedias, describing the practice and the national campaign that spread it.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it to date the practice, because it tells us straight-row planting was rare before Meiji and was promoted nationally through the 1890s and 1900s together with the hand-pushed inter-row weeder (田打車), planting ropes and rulers, which is why our paddies are not drawn as tidy grids of aligned seedlings. It is a tertiary reference aggregating dictionary entries, so we take the dating from it rather than fine detail, and because it is written about a Meiji reform, what it tells us about earlier practice comes by contrast rather than by direct description.

seijoue-seika

What it is: An essay on せいか舎, the local-history site of the town of Seika in Kyoto prefecture, about 正条植え, straight-row rice planting, and how it spread through the countryside.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a second and independent local voice agreeing with the same dating we take from the dictionary entry, that row planting spread in the Meiji period and brought weeder-based weeding and mid-season cultivation with it. It is a municipal essay written for residents rather than a scholarly study, and it speaks for one district, so we use it as corroboration of the general chronology and not as a measurement of anything.

sendai-igune-list

What it is: The city of Sendai's conservation page for igune, the farm windbreak groves of the Sendai plain, which links the city's own PDF list of tree species suited to one, sorted by height: tall trees of 15 m and over (sugi, black pine, the hinoki group, keyaki), sub-canopy and middle trees around 10 m, and shrubs around 3 m.

Why it applies, and its limits: A local government's own guidance about a living local form is exactly the right thing for what a homestead windbreak belt is made of and how tall its layers stand, which is what sets the belt's drawn height and its mix of species. Its limit is era: this is a present-day conservation document about groves that survive now, so the list records what is planted and kept today, and we treat it as a good guide to an older composition rather than as proof of what stood in a grove three centuries ago.

senjochi-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on 扇状地 (alluvial fan), including the land-classification terms used by Japan's infrastructure ministry for the three parts of a fan: the apex (扇頂), the middle (扇央) and the toe (扇端).

Why it applies, and its limits: Our settlements sit on fans, and this gives us the vocabulary and the physical rule we place them by, in particular the spring line at the fan toe where water sinking into the coarse middle comes back to the surface and the wet ground begins. It is a tertiary encyclopedia summary, taken for standard and well-established terminology rather than for any number, and what it describes is landform physics that does not change with the century, so its modernity costs us little here.

senmaida

What it is: A group of public pages about Shiroyone Senmaida, the terraced paddy that falls to the sea at Wajima in Ishikawa: the Japanese government's Highlighting Japan feature of June 2025, the Wajima cultural-property listing, and the national tourism organization's page, read alongside the listings for the similar terraces at Obasute and Maruyama.

Why it applies, and its limits: These fix the small end of a genuinely worked paddy, about a thousand basins on some four hectares, averaging under 20 square meters, many of them near a meter square and the smallest around half of that, which is why our minimum plot size is a ratio to the field's own layout instead of an absolute floor. They are government and tourism pages describing a preserved and celebrated site, so they are written to promote it, and the terrace is an extreme case whose basins are small because the slope is steep, so we use it as the low bound of what a real paddy can be and never as a typical size.

sento-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the 銭湯, the public bathhouse, covering the institution and how many of them a city carried, including more than 600 in Edo during the Bunka era of 1804 to 1818, when its population stood at roughly one to 1.2 million.

Why it applies, and its limits: A bathhouse count against a known population is what lets us decide how many bathhouses belong on a city map instead of guessing. It is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, and the number is for the largest city in Japan at its height, so scaling it down to a provincial city or a town is a step we take ourselves and not something the source says.

shanghai-xiancheng-zhwiki

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on 上海县城, the old walled county town of Shanghai, describing among other things the wall first thrown up around the town in 1553 against pirates coming up the river, and its roughly circular rather than square outline.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for two things about a walled town: that a Chinese county seat could go unwalled for a long time and then be walled in a hurry under a specific threat, and that such a wall could take a round outline rather than the textbook square. It is a tertiary summary taken where its references support it, about one town in the Yangtze delta, and while the record likes the idea of a wall raised very fast, the article does not put a season on it, so the speed we imply is ours rather than the source's.

shangxinhe-gazetteer

What it is: The encyclopedia article on 上新河镇 (Shangxinhe), the Nanjing river town that grew up around a timber market on a man-made side channel, together with Jiangsu provincial gazetteer material on the same place; it describes rafts moored in numbers along the banks at the channel mouth, a market that swelled into a town, and a Qing-era peak famous under the phrase "sufficient in all four seasons".

Why it applies, and its limits: This is what a timber city's water actually looked like, and it is what our log pen, moorings and lumber yard are drawn from: rafts held against the bank in a side channel rather than sticks scattered in the fairway. It is a tertiary summary standing on a local gazetteer tradition and it describes one Chinese river port, so we take the arrangement of rafts and yards from it and not measurements, and the channel it describes is roughly 9 km long, which is a city-scale figure we scale down rather than copy.

shaoxing-towpath

What it is: News features from CGTN and the Shanghai Daily on the ancient qiandao (纤道) towpath at Shaoxing on the Eastern Zhejiang Canal, read alongside general Grand Canal survey material; they date the path to 815 CE, put its length at over 40 km, and describe its two forms, one running along the bank and one carried out over the water on slab stones laid across countless stone piers about half a meter above the surface.

Why it applies, and its limits: A settlement on a navigated river needs to know what a riverside way really was, and the answer here is a narrow haulage path for pulling boats upstream rather than a road paralleling the water, in two built forms we can draw. These are broadcaster and newspaper features for a general audience rather than archaeological reports, so we use them for form and for widely repeated dates and not for precise dimensions, and the towpath is a Chinese institution being applied to a setting whose surface is often Japanese, which we do because Japan has no close equivalent to it.

shibata-ashigaru-nagaya

What it is: The Japanese Agency for Cultural Affairs' heritage listing for the former Shibata domain's ashigaru nagaya in Niigata, a thatched, hipped-roof terrace of 1842 housing eight foot-soldier families under one roof, 43.6 m along the ridge by 7.3 m deep, designated an Important Cultural Property in 1969; the listing describes one household's share as an entrance, two six-mat rooms, a three-mat room and a kitchen.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a surviving, officially documented building of exactly the type we draw for low-retainer housing, so it fixes the default terraced form and supplies real numbers for it: eight households in one range, about 18 ft of frontage each, roughly nine tsubo of floor apiece. Its limits are that it is one late-Edo building from one domain and that practice varied, since Kaga and Hikone housed their foot soldiers in detached houses with gardens, so the terrace is our default rather than a universal rule, and the listing is a modern conservation record of the building as it survives today.

shimogoe-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on 下肥 (shimogoe), human night soil used as fertilizer, which explains that fresh night soil harms crops and so is stored for a set period to rot down and mature, in a pit called the 肥溜め.

Why it applies, and its limits: It answers why a farmstead has a manure pit at all and why the stuff sits there instead of going straight onto the fields, which is what justifies drawing a separate pit on the plot rather than treating it as part of the privy. It is a tertiary summary whose statements we take where its own references support them, and it gives no storage times or pit dimensions, so the size we draw the pit at is our own decision.

shinano-gawa-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Shinano River, the longest river in Japan, which notes that the same river is the Shinano within Niigata prefecture and becomes the Chikuma once it passes up into Nagano.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supports a small point of naming that our maps follow, that one river can legitimately carry different names along its course, so a river labeled one thing at a settlement need not be labeled the same thing upstream. It is a tertiary summary about a single modern river, used only for a naming convention it states plainly, and nothing on any map depends on a number from it.

# source-applicability - batch 18 (16 keys)

Every source was opened. Two hosts served redirects that were followed (`doi.org` -> J-Stage;
`tobunken.repo.nii.ac.jp` -> Oracle object storage). No host refused. The tobunken PDF came back as
undecoded binary through the fetcher and was read with `pdftotext` from the downloaded file.
Two ja.wikipedia articles were additionally read as raw wikitext (`action=raw`) to settle whether a
sentence the write-up attributes to them is on the page.

---

## NOT-APPLICABLE

None. Every source in this batch bears on the use it is put to.

## INACCURATE write-ups (a statement about the source that the source does not bear out)

### `takayama-jinya-jawiki`

- **Kind / author / date**: ja.wikipedia article 高山陣屋, tertiary, short (about 6.3 KB of wikitext),
  two references - Uejima Zenji, "史跡高山陣屋跡", *Gifu Prefectural Cultural Properties Protection
  Center Survey Report 1* (1992), and the national cultural-property database.
- **Place / era described**: the Hida shogunal intendancy office, Takayama, from 1692 (Hida taken as
  直轄領) to the Meiji Restoration, plus Meiji-onward reuse, the 1929 historic-site designation and the
  1996 reconstruction.
- **Scale / method**: one compound; an encyclopedia summary of the survey report and the designation.
- **What we use it for**: the 1816 rebuild of the office block as one range (玄関・吟味所・御役所・大広間,
  buildings.html fn 10, 36, 51); the numbered storehouse rows (fn 33, 51); the 1996 restoration from
  an 1830 drawing (fn 10, 70); the sole-survivor status (fn 2). The registry `Used for` line adds
  "25 daikan/gundai over 177 years".
- **Verdict**: **APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS** for the rebuild, the storehouse rows and the survivor
  status. Limits: (1) tertiary; (2) one atypically preserved compound in a mountain province under
  direct shogunal rule; (3) the "surviving buildings" list describes the post-1996 state, in which the
  storehouse-keepers' rowhouse, the gundai's residence and the inner rooms are a reconstruction from a
  drawing, not standing Edo fabric.
- **`What it is:` INACCURATE.** It says the article covers "the succession of intendants who held the
  post". It does not. The raw wikitext contains no succession list and neither "25" nor "177"; the
  article names only 伊奈忠篤 in passing. The sentence with those numbers - 「それ以来、明治維新にいたる
  までの177年間に、25代の代官、郡代が江戸から派遣され」 - is on the **city** page
  (`takayama-jinya-city`), which is where that claim and the registry's `Used for` line belong.
- Limits otherwise honest; the write-up does say "we use its shape and not its exact dimensions",
  which is right.

### `tedai-jawiki`

- **Kind / author / date**: ja.wikipedia article 手代, tertiary, thin; its only inline citation is a
  2013 accounting-firm web page about modern commercial-law usage, so the Edo material is uncited.
- **Place / era described**: Japan, Edo period from the mid-period on; the junior official serving
  under a gundai or daikan, with the merchant-house sense as a secondary meaning.
- **Scale / method**: one office role; an encyclopedia summary.
- **What we use it for**: who the clerks were - mostly children of village and town officials, hired
  from peasants and townsmen versed in jikata (buildings.html fn 24, 26).
- **Verdict**: **APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS**. Limits: tertiary and effectively unsourced for the Edo
  material; a recruitment pattern rather than a measurement.
- **`What it is:` ACCURATE.** Limits **INACCURATE**: the write-up says the article "says nothing about
  how many clerks an office held". It does. 「例として、福山藩では手代は「御代官手代」という名称で、
  定員は12人であった…代官の定員は3人であったので、代官1人に4人の手代が配下としてついていたことになる」
  - a fixed establishment of 12 tedai under 3 daikan, four per daikan, with their stipends (15-18 hyo
  plus a two-person fuchi; and 20 ryo with a five-person fuchi for shogunal tedai from 1725). That is
  directly relevant to the stated use ("a magistracy compound has to house its staff"), and the
  write-up forecloses it. If the number is ever used, the limit to state is that it is a **domain**
  (Fukuyama-han) establishment, not a shogunal daikansho. "Nothing about birth order" is correct.

### `tobunken-mushiro`

- **Kind / author / date**: 今石みぎわ, 「莚と莚織りの技術 ――山口県下松市西谷を中心に――」, in
  『無形文化遺産研究報告』, National Research Institute for Cultural Properties, Tokyo, 2012.
  Institutional research report, freely downloadable.
- **Place / era described**: two halves. (a) Nishidani, Yonekawa district, Kudamatsu City, Yamaguchi -
  a hamlet of three households (現戸数３戸) where the craft was 消滅寸前, recorded from 2010; (b) a
  documentary survey of mushiro looms in period sources - 『東北院職人歌合絵巻』 (1789 copy),
  『耕稼春秋』 (Kaga, 1707), 『和漢三才図会』 (1713), 『民家検労図』 (c. 1830), Ryukyu goza looms, then
  the Meiji-onward semi-automatic machines.
- **Scale / method**: one village's technique, set against national documentary evidence; fieldwork
  plus source criticism.
- **What we use it for**: the mat's measured size, 幅およそ3尺 x 長さ6尺 (90 x 180 cm), which converts a
  mat count into an area (homesteads.html fn 15).
- **Verdict**: **APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS**. The measurement is of a present-day weaving of a craft that
  was once universal, so it is a modern measurement of a premodern form - but the same paper carries
  the premodern corroboration.
- **`What it is:` INACCURATE** in scope. It describes the work as a fieldwork report on one hamlet and
  nothing else; roughly half the paper is a comparative study of Edo-period loom illustrations and
  agricultural treatises.
- **Limits OVERSTATED.** "Made in a single village of a single prefecture ... we treat this
  measurement as a representative standard rather than as a fixed national one" understates what the
  paper shows: the 1707 Kaga agricultural treatise 『耕稼春秋』 quoted in it gives 「幅三尺の間に合莚」 -
  the same three-shaku width, in a period source, 500 km from Nishidani - and the paper's point is
  that the loom's structure was essentially unchanged from at least the early 1700s. The honest
  framing is stronger than the one written, not weaker. The one genuine size variation the paper
  reports is the Ryukyu goza at 3 shaku 2 sun.

### `tfd-hongou-fire-history` (minor)

- **Kind / author / date**: Tokyo Fire Department, Hongo fire station, 防火対策の歴史 - an official
  public-education history page; no author, no bibliography.
- **Place / era described**: Edo, from Keicho 6 (1601) through the Edo period, mostly 17th-18th
  century.
- **Scale / method**: a city; popular history written by a modern fire service about its own city.
- **What we use it for**: commoners keeping fire-water at the doorway and on the roof (buildings.html
  fn 67); tile, dozo and nuriya construction being permitted for townhouses (fn 45).
- **Verdict**: **APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS**. Limits: not a scholarly study and cites nothing; describes
  Edo, the densest wooden city in the country under a shogunal fire regime, so the habit travels
  further than the regulation does.
- **`What it is:` ACCURATE.** Limits **INACCURATE in one detail**: "it gives the practice with no
  dates, quantities or regional detail" is true of the passage we quote but false of the page, which
  carries dates (享保5年/1720, 享保15年/1730) and measurements (a bank 3 ken high and 9 cho long). The
  sentence should be scoped to the passage. The slip makes the write-up more cautious, not less.

fao-ac180e-rice-fish

What it is: A chapter of Fish Culture in Rice Fields, a technical manual published by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization on raising fish in flooded rice paddies. The "Culture Operations" chapter covers how such a field is prepared and managed, including the earth bund that holds the water in, which it says should stand at least 25 cm high and better still 60 cm.

Why it applies, and its limits: A paddy bund is a wall of piled mud whose height is set by how deep the water must stand, which has nothing to do with modern machinery, so the figure carries back to a premodern field. The honest limits are that this is a present-day extension manual rather than a historical record, and that a bund built to keep fish in is taller than one built only to keep water in, so we treat its 60 cm as the upper end of the range a paddy bund occupies rather than as a measured premodern height.

fao-ac241e

What it is: The Integration of Mulberry Cultivation, Sericulture and Fish Farming, a report published by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization with the Network of Aquaculture Centres in Asia-Pacific, describing the dike-and-pond farming of the Pearl River delta in southern China: mulberry grown on raised dikes, silkworms fed on the leaves, and the worm waste fed to fish in the ponds between.

Why it applies, and its limits: This is the same mulberry-dike-fishpond system our maps draw, and the proportions it reports - roughly one unit of dike to one of water, the pond depths, the slope up to the dike top - follow from the feed cycle itself rather than from any modern input, so they describe the shape of a landscape that had been worked that way for centuries. The limits are that it is a twentieth-century development report on then-current Chinese practice, and that its ratios are regional averages, so they tell us what a dike-pond block looks like in general and not what any one village held.

fao-ac264e

What it is: Integrated Fish Farming in China, a report from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization and the Network of Aquaculture Centres in Asia-Pacific; the chapter we cite introduces the major Chinese models of combining fish ponds with other livestock, including pig sheds built on the pond dike or out over the water and duck ponds with a fenced dry run on the bank.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives us the physical arrangement of a pond that also carries animals - where the shed stands, how the duck run meets the water - which is what a map has to draw. It describes practice as observed in the 1980s, so we use it for the form of the thing and never as evidence of how common such a pond was in a premodern village.

fao-charcoal-safety

What it is: The safety chapter of Simple technologies for charcoal making, a technical handbook from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization on small-scale charcoal production. It explains that freshly made charcoal heats itself and can catch fire on its own, that the fine dust is the worst offender, and that a fresh burn should be left in the open air before it is bagged or stored.

Why it applies, and its limits: The chemistry of fresh charcoal is a property of the material and not of the century, so it explains why a charcoal burner's stack and store sit apart from thatched roofs - which is all we take from it. The limit is that this is a modern handbook: the specific waiting times it recommends are today's handling guidance, an anchor for the practice rather than a rule anyone in a premodern village would have stated in hours and days.

fao-paddy-duty

What it is: Two irrigation training manuals from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization - "Scheme Irrigation Water Need and Supply" and "Determination of the Irrigation Schedule for Paddy Rice" - which teach how to work out how much water a rice scheme must be fed: the large one-off soaking that turns dry ground into workable mud, the water that soaks away through the floor each day, the standing layer kept on the field, and the resulting flow per hectare.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it to size a channel against the fields it actually serves, and that sum is arithmetic of soil, sun and standing water, none of which a premodern valley did differently. The limits are that these are modern teaching documents whose numbers are planning generalizations across many countries, so they give a defensible band rather than the true duty of any particular valley, and that a premodern channel was cut by eye and by custom rather than calculated to a figure.

fao-pond-water

What it is: The surface-reservoir chapter of Water for animals, a UN Food and Agriculture Organization manual on watering livestock. It describes what a dug pond loses - evaporation from the surface, which it puts as high as 2 m a year, and seepage through the floor - and why such a pond needs a spillway to carry storm runoff past the dam.

Why it applies, and its limits: Our maps need to know that a standing pond is not a sealed tank and that it must have somewhere for a flood to go, both of which this states plainly. The limits are that it is a modern development manual written for hot, dry grazing country, so its evaporation figure is an outer bound rather than a number for a temperate rice valley, and that it gives these losses in prose rather than as a worked water balance.

fao-rice-water

What it is: "Water Management in Rice in Asia: Some Issues for the Future", a paper by Thierry Facon published by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization, surveying how rice irrigation in Asia is run and where it is heading. Along the way it describes the ordinary mechanics of a paddy landscape: water passing from plot to plot so that irrigation and drainage cannot be told apart, and runoff being taken up again further down.

Why it applies, and its limits: That plot-to-plot cascade is the behavior our field layouts depend on, and it is a consequence of flat, bunded, gravity-fed paddies rather than of any modern works. The limits are that the paper is written about contemporary irrigation systems and their reform, and that what we draw from the cascade - which plot ends up wettest - is our own inference, labeled as such where we use it, not something the paper says.

fao-x6708e

What it is: The "Pond outlet structures" chapter of Simple methods for aquaculture: Pond construction, part of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization's training series for small-scale fish farmers. It describes how a pond is emptied and its level controlled, principally the sluice - a protected opening in the dike closed with wooden boards and screened so the fish cannot leave - and the older monk-style outlet.

Why it applies, and its limits: A board-and-slot sluice through an earth dike is a carpentry-and-mud structure with nothing modern in it, and the chapter tells us its form and rough size, which is what a map has to place. The limit is that this is a present-day training manual, so its recommended dimensions describe today's small ponds; we take the shape of the structure from it, not a historical measurement.

fei-1939

What it is: Peasant Life in China: A Field Study of Country Life in the Yangtze Valley by Fei Hsiao-tung (Routledge, 1939), the classic village ethnography of Kaixiangong, a silk-and-rice village on the lower Yangtze delta near Lake Tai. It records the place household by household: how the houses stand along the streams, what land a family held, boats, manure pits, and silkworms reared indoors on stacked trays.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a first-hand, room-by-room account of exactly the kind of settlement these maps draw, and almost everything we take from it - where the manure pit sits, that nearly every household kept a boat, that the village grew along its water, where rice was threshed - is arrangement rather than technology, and so belongs to the older village as much as to the one Fei walked through. The limits are real: it is the 1930s, and Fei himself notes practices that were recent innovations and a silk economy already disrupted by mechanized filatures; it is one village in one delta rather than a survey; and it is Chinese, standing beside the Japanese material for a setting built on both.

fei-xiaotong

What it is: The same 1939 village study by Fei Xiaotong, cited from a second full-text scan for its plan of the farm layout in the Xichang polder - the map and passages showing houses standing on the raised polder margin along the interior streams, with mulberry on the same high strip.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is our worked example of how a settlement sits inside deep-water, diked ground: not on a hill but on the only raised line there is, the dike itself. The limits are the same as for the book at large - one delta village observed in the 1930s, in China - and this key covers only the polder-layout case rather than the wider ethnography.

fengshui-woodland-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article "Fengshui woodland", a short encyclopedia entry on the patches of woodland kept behind and around villages in southern China and Hong Kong for geomantic reasons, giving the Chinese term 風水林 and some regional totals.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one thing only - that the village grove is a recognized, named class of woodland rather than a decoration we invented. It is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, and it carries no count of groves per village and no grove area at all, so the sizes and numbers on our maps come from the survey papers and, where those run out, are marked as guesses.

fires-in-edo-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article "Fires in Edo", an encyclopedia summary of the repeated great fires of the Tokugawa capital - how often they came, what set them off, when in the year they fell, and how the city fought them.

Why it applies, and its limits: We take from it the seasonal pattern, that the serious fires clustered in the dry, windy winter, which is a matter of climate and so applies to a town as much as to the capital. It is a tertiary summary, used only where its own references support the point, and it is about the largest city in Japan: the season transfers to a smaller settlement, the scale and frequency of its conflagrations do not.

forests-2020

What it is: "Village Fengshui Forests as Forms of Cultural and Ecological Heritage: Interpretations and Conservation Policy Implications from Southern China" by Chen, Lin, Zhang and colleagues, a peer-reviewed open-access paper in the journal Forests (2020). It surveys the fengshui groves of villages in southern China, what they contain, why they survived, and what protecting them would take.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is peer-reviewed work about the exact feature we draw, and it is where the figure of roughly two fengshui forests per village comes from, reported there from an earlier county survey in Fujian. It does not give us grove sizes: its own table records whole-village forest areas only, and it counts no trees or canopies, so the per-grove areas on our maps are labeled guesses. It is also a modern study of the groves that survived, in one province of China, so it describes a remnant landscape rather than the ordinary one of several centuries ago.

fortune-1843

What it is: Three Years' Wanderings in the Northern Provinces of China by Robert Fortune, the Scottish botanist and plant collector sent to China in 1843; it is his own travel narrative of the tea, silk and cotton districts, with an account of Chinese agriculture and horticulture. We quote his description of where tea was planted: always on the lower and most fertile sides of the hills, never on the low lands, in small gardens of one to five acres, every cottager having his own.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is an eyewitness account of tea growing before mechanization, before state terracing programs, and before the twentieth century rearranged the hillsides, which makes it about as close to a premodern observation of a tea slope as a readable source gets. The limits are that it is one traveler's narrative written for a Victorian British readership rather than a survey, that it covers the coastal and northern provinces he happened to pass through, and that it is Chinese practice standing beside our Japanese material.

fukada-kotobank

What it is: The Kotobank entry for 深田 (fukada, "deep paddy"), a Japanese online reference that reprints entries from published dictionaries and encyclopedias; here it defines the word as a paddy whose mud is deep, a swamp paddy (沼田, numata). It is cited together with the Japanese Wikipedia article on ヨシ (yoshi, the common reed), which covers reed beds and their cutting.

Why it applies, and its limits: Japanese dictionaries are good evidence that the deep-mud wet paddy we draw was a distinct and familiar kind of field, common enough to have its own everyday word. The limits are that a dictionary defines a word rather than measures a field, so there is no depth, no extent and no date here, and that the encyclopedia and Wikipedia entries beside it are tertiary summaries; anything more than the term and its sense comes from other entries in the record.

fukagawa-kiba-summary

What it is: The history page of a Japanese timber wholesalers' trade body, recounting the origin of Kiba, the lumber quarter of Fukagawa in Edo: after the great fire of 1641 the spread of the flames was blamed on the high timber stacks of merchants scattered through the city, the merchants were gathered onto Eitai-jima, another great fire followed in 1657, and Kiba Fukagawa-cho was laid out in 1703 over some 90,000 tsubo of made ground.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives us the thing we want to draw - a lumber yard as a large works on the water, deliberately pushed out of the built-up core because stacked timber carries fire through a wooden town - and it is a Japanese account of a Japanese quarter. The limits are that it is an industry body's own promotional history rather than a scholarly one, with no references a reader can follow, and that it gives an area for the whole quarter and none for a single yard, so the size of the yard on our maps is our own estimate.
