nougyoudoboku-matsutan

What it is: A page from のうぎょうとぼく ("Nougyou to Boku"), a Japanese agricultural civil engineering site written by a working agricultural engineer and farmer who publishes design notes and study material for others in the field. The page explains how the terminal irrigation channel, the smallest canal that carries water from a branch canal to an individual plot, is sized and placed, and how its counterpart the terminal drain is set below the field.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states, in one place, the order in which water reaches a paddy - trunk canal, branch canal, terminal channel, and the same chain reversed for drainage - along with the spacings and the bed heights relative to the field surface that decide where a ditch can sit, which is exactly what our paddy maps have to draw. Its limit is era and standardization: these are present-day Japanese engineering standards for consolidated, machine-worked paddy, so the branch spacings and the centimeter-precise bed levels describe a modern laid-out field rather than a village's hand-dug ditches, and we use the arrangement and the gravity logic, which wet rice has not changed, more than we use the exact numbers.

nougyoudoboku-suikou

What it is: A second page from the same Japanese agricultural civil engineering site, のうぎょうとぼく, covering the design of the two openings in a paddy plot's bund: the mizuguchi intake that admits water from the terminal channel and the mizujiri outlet that lets it go.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the plot-scale detail our maps draw at every bund - one intake per plot (two when the intakes would stand more than 50 m apart), an intake no wider than about half a meter, its sill just above the field surface and the outlet a little below it - so that water enters at one corner and leaves at another. The same limits apply as to its companion page: it is modern design guidance for engineered plots and concrete or pipe fittings, while a premodern plot's intake was a notch cut in an earth bund, so we take the arrangement and the relative heights and not the materials or the tolerances.

ogose-kosatsuba

What it is: A cultural property explanation page published by the board of education of Ogose town in Saitama prefecture, describing the site of the town's Edo period kosatsuba, the roofed board on which the shogunate's edicts and regulations were posted. It cites an 1830 provincial gazetteer for where the board stood and records that each of the seventeen villages that make up the modern town had one at a key point, with a surviving place name marking another at the foot of a pass on the Chichibu highway.

Why it applies, and its limits: It answers the question our town and village maps actually ask - where in a settlement the noticeboard stood - and it answers it with an Edo era source behind it, giving us the board at the village's center, its shrine precinct or its assembly place, ahead of the village officials' houses. Its limits are place and kind: this is one town in old Musashi province described by its own heritage office rather than a comparative study, and the board itself is long gone, so we take from it a pattern of siting rather than a rule that held everywhere.

ohmi-yoshi

What it is: A public information page, ヨシとは ("What the reed is"), from the Ohmi Environmental Conservation Foundation (公益財団法人淡海環境保全財団), a public interest foundation in Shiga prefecture whose work is the environment of Lake Biwa. It describes the common reed and the long standing practice of cutting the winter-withered stems for use.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is our evidence that a reed bed is a harvested resource rather than scenery - cut in winter for yoshizu blinds, thatch, summer shoji and standing screens, and left to deteriorate when nobody cuts it - which is what a reader is told when they click the reeds on a map. Two honest limits: it is a conservation foundation writing for the public, not scholarship, and everything it describes is a lake or river reed bed on Lake Biwa, so we cite it for lake and river reeds only; nothing we could read puts that harvest economy on the margins of a farm pond, and our record says so rather than stretching this page to cover it.

okayama-castle

What it is: The English history page of the official Okayama Castle site, the castle's own visitor documentation, recounting how Ukita Naoie and his son Hideie built the castle on the hill of Okayama in the late sixteenth century, how the branching channels of the Asahi River were arranged to protect its north and east sides and used to form its moats, and how the castle town was laid out long and narrow between them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is an attested Japanese case of a castle taking a river branch as the moat on two of its flanks, which is the thing our river city and edge castle maps need a real example for. It is a site's own account written to introduce the castle to visitors rather than an archaeological or documentary study, so we use it for the fact and the shape of the river diversion and would not press it for dimensions, dates or anything finer than it plainly states.

osaka-castle-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Osaka Castle (大坂城), a tertiary encyclopedia summary of the castle's site, its successive constructions and its history, including the plateau it stands on and the rivers running below it.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use a single geographic statement from it - that the Yodo and its tributaries below the northern plateau both served as a natural moat and were the water drawn into the moats inside the castle - because that double duty, defense and supply from the same river, is the relationship our capital maps draw. An encyclopedia is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them; here the claim is a matter of well known geography rather than a measurement, which is why we are content to rest one sentence on it.

osaka-kurayashiki

What it is: The English page on the Dojima Rice Exchange published by the exchange itself (the Osaka Dojima Exchange, through Japan Exchange Group), which recounts how the domains sold their tax rice through kurayashiki, the combined warehouses and residences clustered around Nakanoshima in Osaka, and how the rice bills issued to successful bidders were then traded; the entry also gathers a Japanese Wiki Corpus article on daimyogashi and surveys of the rice brokers.

Why it applies, and its limits: It settles what a kurayashiki was and, more usefully for us, where it stood - at the market in Osaka, at the selling end of the rice trade, and not in the domain's own capital - which is what keeps warehouse-residences off our provincial city maps. The limits are kind and scale: an exchange's history of itself is an institutional account rather than scholarship, and it describes late Edo Osaka at the peak of the trade, so a figure such as more than a hundred kurayashiki belongs to one exceptional city at one moment and is never scaled down to an ordinary town.

packer-2017-phragmites

What it is: A peer-reviewed review article by Jasmin G. Packer, Laura A. Meyerson, Hana Skálová, Petr Pyšek and Christoph Kueffer in the Journal of Ecology (2017), part of the long running "Biological Flora of the British Isles" series, which gathers what is known about the biology, ecology and habitats of the common reed, Phragmites australis.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use its account of the hydrosere, the succession of vegetation running from open water through the littoral zone to reed, marsh and alluvial forest, to decide which bands of plants a map paints around still water and in what order. The limit is place: it is a flora of the British Isles, so while the reed itself is the same plant that grows across Eurasia, the communities it names are European, and what we take from it is the depth-driven ordering of the zones rather than a species list for an East Asian pond.

paddy-field-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the paddy field, a tertiary summary of flooded rice cultivation, its history across Asia and the physical form of the fields themselves.

Why it applies, and its limits: One sentence in it, describing prehistoric Korean paddies laid out as squares and rectangles separated by bunds about 10 cm high, is where the height of the low earth walls our maps draw between plots comes from. Its limits are kind and place: an encyclopedia is a tertiary summary whose figures we accept only where its own references support them, and the example is Korean and very early rather than Japanese, cited because it is a readable public statement of a bund height and because a bund's height is set by how deep a flooded plot is held, which varies little across the rice-growing world.

pan-gate-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on Pan Gate (盘门), the surviving gate at the southwest corner of Suzhou's old city wall, which describes it as two separate gates in one structure, a land gate for road traffic and a water gate for boats, connecting the city's inner canals and its moat to the Grand Canal.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is our attested example of a walled Chinese city admitting a canal through its wall beside the road gate, which is what a river or canal city map needs before it draws water crossing a defensive line. It is a tertiary summary, used for what the structure is rather than for measurements, and it is one gate of one city; the sluice or portcullis we would have liked to draw in the water arch appears on no page we were able to read, so our maps do not claim one.

park-2013-maeulsup

What it is: A peer-reviewed Korean study by Park Mee Jeong, Kim Sang Bum, Jang Choul Soon, Shin Min Ji and Kim Eun Ja in the Journal of the Korean Society of Rural Planning (2013), which assembles a mapped database of 462 traditional village groves and field-surveys 100 of them, reporting each grove's area, its distance from the village and the kind of place it stands in.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the only publicly readable survey we found that actually measures the planted grove at a village's mouth, and its numbers are what our maps size that belt of trees by - most groves under a hectare, and the village-entrance grove, the sugumagi that blocks the water mouth, averaging around seven tenths of a hectare and accounting for 42 of the 100 surveyed. Two limits stated plainly: it is Korean rather than Japanese or Chinese, cited because no comparable public survey of Japanese village groves could be read, and Korea is offered as a fair analogue because it shares the region's geomantic siting tradition and its village scale; and the groves measured are the ones that survive today, so a present-day area is only an approximation of the original planting.

pawnbroking-history

What it is: The English Wikipedia article "History of pawnbroking", a tertiary summary of lending against pledged goods from antiquity to the present, with a short section on China that runs from the earliest monastic pawnshops through the Song.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use its statement that the earliest Chinese pawnbrokers were established and run by Buddhist monasteries, and its note that Southern Song laypeople formed partnerships with monasteries to open pawnshops, when deciding where a lending house belongs on a map - inside or beside a temple precinct rather than in a market row. It is a tertiary summary whose claims we accept only where its own references support them, and China occupies a few sentences of a global survey, so we take the institutional association it describes and not a chronology or a count.

phyllostachys-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on Phyllostachys bambusoides, the Japanese timber bamboo known as madake, covering the plant itself and the things traditionally made from its culms and sheaths.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is where the answer comes from when a reader clicks the bamboo stand behind a farmhouse and asks what it was for: baskets and fans from the long fibers, sheaths for wrapping food and for the coverings of geta, and shakuhachi flutes. It is a tertiary summary taken where its own references support it, and it describes the species and its craft uses without dating them or saying how much of it a household kept, so it tells us the purpose of a bamboo grove and not its size.

pingjiang-tu

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the Pingjiang tu (平江图), the plan of Suzhou carved into stone in 1229, together with the scholarship written about it; it describes what the carving shows - a rectangular walled city longer north to south than east to west, five gates each drawn with both a land gate and a water gate, and a broad moat outside the wall.

Why it applies, and its limits: The carved plan is about as close as we can get to a surveyed map of a city of the period our setting is modeled on, and we use what it shows for two things our own city maps decide: that by this date the old walled wards had become named districts marked by plaques rather than enclosures, and that in an elite quarter it is the depth of a plot that marks its owner's standing. The article is a tertiary encyclopedia summary of the object rather than the object or a study of it, so its statements are used where its own references support them, and it records one southern Chinese prefectural city at one date, which we treat as a well documented example of the form and not a template every city followed.

pingyao-chenghuangmiao

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the City God Temple of Pingyao, the Chenghuang temple in the walled county town of Pingyao in Shanxi, which describes the site as three separate temples standing together on one complex of more than 7,300 square meters and lists them individually.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the shape of a county seat's civic temple - not a single hall but a compound holding several cults side by side, the City God's own temple among them - which is how our town maps compose a precinct rather than dropping one building. It is a tertiary summary used for what stands on the site rather than for a measurement, the surviving buildings are later rebuildings of a much older foundation, and Pingyao was a wealthy town whose temple is a generous example rather than an average county one.

pingyao-shilou-zhwiki

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the Pingyao Shilou (平遥市楼), the market tower that straddles the middle of South Street at the center of the walled county town of Pingyao in Shanxi, giving its plan, its footprint, its height and the date of the rebuilding that produced the present structure.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supplies a measured size for an attested market tower - a ground story three bays across and three bays deep on about 133 square meters, standing 18.5 meters high - which is what our town maps scale the tower over a main street by. It is a tertiary summary whose figures we accept where its own references support them; the building measured is a late seventeenth century rebuild on an older site, and it is one unusually well preserved tower in a rich town, so we use it as a single attested size rather than a standard every market tower met.

## MISSING a limit

### `hudson-big-boom`
Popular history / Glenn Pearsall (verified on the page) / published 18 October 2016 in
*New York Almanack*, an online New York State history magazine, drawing on Hochschild's
*Township 34* / describes the Hudson "Big Boom" above Glens Falls, 19th-century
industrial North America / one operation / a narrative account, not a measurement.
**We use it for**: boom construction and anchoring, quoted into `urban-features.html`
fn 24 to support "Anchoring was always to fixed ground: bank abutments, stone-filled
cribs, driven piles - the Hudson's Big Boom rode on hewn timbers bolted four-together
raftwise, chained end to end over friction rollers to abutments on the banks."

**Verdict: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS.** Limits: a popular secondary account, with the
scholarly source (Hochschild) one step further out; industrial-era North America, not
East Asia; an operation far larger than any settlement we draw; and the specific
fittings it describes are industrial ironwork.

`What it is:` **ACCURATE** (author, date, publication kind and both quoted facts all
confirmed on the page).
Limits: **MISSING** - the ironwork. Bolted timber groups, end-to-end chains and
manufactured friction rollers are 19th-century hardware; a premodern river works would
lash and rope its floats and could not run chain over rollers at that scale. The
write-up says "we take the arrangement from it and not the dimensions," but the
arrangement is exactly where the industrial fittings sit, and the citing sentence in
`urban-features.html` carries the bolts, chains and rollers into our own text. The limit
to state is that what survives the transfer is the principle (a floating fence anchored
to fixed ground at both banks), not the fastenings.

### `ido-jawiki`
Tertiary / ja.wikipedia contributors / undated, continuously edited / Japan, no period
scope / national / an encyclopedia summary.
**We use it for**: the lined shaft (idogawa) that the well glyph stands for, and - the
assertion the footnote actually carries in `homesteads.html` fn 48 - that shared wells
outnumbered private ones because digging was costly.

**Verdict: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS.** Limits: tertiary; not period-scoped; Japanese,
quoted in our own translation; silent on where in a yard a well stands.

`What it is:` **ACCURATE**.
Limits: **MISSING** - the era. The article describes Japanese wells in general,
modern ones included, and dates none of what it says, so nothing in it establishes that

general Japanese one. The write-up names the tertiary limit and the placement silence
but lets the reader take the description as period evidence.

### `ifc-307-bonfire`
A modern model code / International Code Council, read in the 2010 New York State Fire
Code adoption at UpCodes (confirmed on the page: the header reads "New York State Fire
Code 2010"; the ICC's own site returned 403 to the record's reader) / present-day United
States / a jurisdiction-wide regulation / a prescribed minimum, not a measurement.
**We use it for**: the 50 ft clearance the pyre-ground setback in `cities/capitals.html`
is derived from.

**Verdict: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS, and only as an openly labeled modern bound.** Limits:
present-day American regulation, no East Asian or premodern provenance; it governs a
recreational bonfire, not a funeral pyre; a regulatory minimum carries a safety margin
chosen by a regulator, so it is not a measurement of anything. Used as evidence about
how a premodern town actually placed its pyres it would be NOT-APPLICABLE, and the
entry has to keep saying so.

`What it is:` **ACCURATE** (the code, the adoption we read, the host substitution and
the clause are all right).
Limits: **MISSING** - the record's own answer to this exact question. `cities/capitals.html`
finds that Edo's crematoria were never moved for fire, that the 1873 relocation was
argued on stench rather than sparks, and that the real practice was CONTAINMENT (a stone
hearth inside a walled kasoba, with Varanasi as the parallel). So this is not a modern
number filling a silence in the record; it is a distance rule standing in for a
containment practice the record documents. The write-up's "a defensible floor where no
premodern rule states a distance" reads as though the record were silent. Second, smaller:
"the hazard being regulated ... is a physical constant" overstates - 50 ft is a
regulator's margin keyed to a code-defined fire size, not an invariant, and the
write-up's own closing sentence ("a reasoned choice on our part and not evidence") is
the honest version of that claim.

### `irri-drying-floor`
A modern extension page / International Rice Research Institute, Rice Knowledge Bank /
present-day, tropical Asia (IRRI is based in the Philippines) / farm scale / how-to
advice.
**We use it for**: the spread depth and the one area statement ("500 square meters of
drying floor can handle 6 tons of paddy"), which `homesteads.html` fn 18 turns into the
drying yard's size.
Host note: knowledgebank.irri.org refused the connection today and the fetch tool
declines web.archive.org, so this is judged from the entry and the quoted footnote.

**Verdict: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS.** Limits: modern practice, modern varieties and a
modern milling-moisture target; a ratio for a solid drying pavement, not a description
of any historical yard.

`What it is:` **ACCURATE**.
Limits: **MISSING** - the drying regime the ratio assumes. The figure is floor area for
a whole 6-tonne lot spread at once on a hard drying floor. Our households field-dry on
hazakake racks first and then thresh and spread in batches, which is why
`homesteads.html` itself divides the derived area down. The write-up's "which is what
lets us turn a household's harvest into the size of the drying yard" hides that
correction; the honest form is that the source gives a depth-to-area ratio and nothing

## INACCURATE

### `ide-japanese-experience`
A research monograph in a series / Akira Tamaki, "Development of local culture and the
irrigation system of the Azusa Basin", Japanese Experience of the UNU Human and Social
Development Programme series no. 4, 1979, in the Institute of Developing Economies
archive (title, author, series and date all confirmed on the page) / the Azusa river
alluvium in the Matsumoto basin, Nagano, from the Tokugawa period into 20th-century
modernization / one river basin / a documentary and customary-law case study.
**We use it for**: `urban-features.html` fn 70 (hatake on the terrace uplands as against
suiden paddy) and fn 71 (the late-Tokugawa Hata irrigation schemes defeated by
downstream water rights).

**Verdict: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS.** Limits: one basin in one province, so its customs
are local before they are national; it runs forward into the modern period, so only its
older material bears on us; and the terrace-versus-paddy contrast is a fact about that
valley's landform, not a general rule.

`What it is:` **ACCURATE**.
Limits / uses: **INACCURATE**. The write-up lists among the things we take from it
"small holders depending on rainfall or natural underground sources," and the registry's
own `Used for:` line carries the same phrase as a quotation. It is not on the page. My
read of the page found no sentence contrasting rainfall with underground sources, and
the record already knows this: `urban-features.html` annotates that very phrase and the
crop list beside it as "(unsourced: this quoted phrase and crop list are not on the IDE
page fetched)". The write-up should be cut to the two uses the page does support (fn 70
and fn 71), and the registry's `Used for:` line with it - otherwise the entry tells a
reader the source says something our own page has already flagged that it does not.

### `isis-dykepond`
A secondary web article / Mae-Wan Ho, Institute of Science in Society, 9 October 2006
(all confirmed on the page) / the Pearl River Delta dike-and-pond system, southern
China, measured in the late 1980s / a district-wide survey it reports rather than
performs / a summary of Ruddle and Zhong 1988, Zhong et al. 1997 and Deng 1987/1993.
**We use it for**: nine assertions in `archetypes.html` - pond size and shape, dike
width, dredging and dike repair, livestock on the dikes, the late-1980s land-use shares,
and the sugar-cane loop.

**Verdict: APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS.** Limits: a secondary carrier, and the primaries it
carries have no publicly readable copy (the record says so at fn 84), so the numbers
rest entirely on work we cannot check; the publisher is a campaigning body rather than a
journal; the survey is late-20th-century with a modern market crop mix; southern China,
not Japan.

`What it is:` **ACCURATE**.
Limits: **INACCURATE on one point.** The write-up credits the page with "the system's
fourteenth-century origins." The page dates nothing of the kind: it says "The dyke-pond
system evolved over the past two thousand years, perfected by generations of Chinese
farmers," and separately "During the mid-fourteenth century, water control measures were
started in the lower-lying areas." The mid-14th century is when the water-control works
in the low ground began, not when the system originated, and the page's own origin claim
is two millennia. The registry line ("dike construction from the mid-fourteenth
century") has this right; the write-up drifted off it. Everything else in the paragraph
matches the page, including the 0.4-0.6 ha / 2-3 m ponds, the 6-10 m dikes, the
livestock, the draining and dredging, and the "late 1980s ... Guangzhou Institute"
dating of the land-use shares, which the write-up correctly presents as a modern
measurement of an old form.

### `nishikori-tsunaba`
- **Kind / authors / date**: a Kotobank reprint of the entry from 平凡社『日本歴史地名大系』(Heibonsha,
  *Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei*) - a scholarly historical-place-name gazetteer; undated on the page, the
  gazetteer is 1979-2005. The citation line also names "Yaotsu town history pages (yaotsu-mall.com)",
  for which the registry carries **no URL** and which was not read.
- **Place and era described**: the tsunaba site on the Kiso river at Nishikori, Mino/Owari; medieval and
  early-modern timber floating.
- **Scale / method**: one site; a gazetteer entry compiled from local records.
- **What we use it for**: registry - "the full-river rope catch at the gorge mouth; ~300,000 logs/yr; the
  autumn-to-spring season; the 138-official timber magistracy; 1340s origin". Citing footnote:
  `urban-features.html` fn 18, which quotes only the SITE and its position.
- **Verdict**: **APPLICABLE-WITH-LIMITS** for the catch's existence and its siting at the gorge mouth
  (era, place and method all bear; limit: a tertiary gazetteer reprint, one river standing in for the
  practice). **NOT-APPLICABLE for the four figures.** The readable extract carries none of
  ~300,000 logs/yr, the autumn-to-spring season, the 138-official magistracy or a 1340s origin - and on
  origin it says the opposite: 「いつ頃から行われたのかは不明」(when it began is unknown). Its only 1340s
  date (貞和元年 = 1345) belongs to an Ise Shrine timber levy, not to the boom.
- **`What it is:` INACCURATE.** It states that the Yaotsu pages "give the working detail: the autumn to
  spring season, roughly 300,000 logs a year, the timber magistracy of 138 officials, and an origin in
  the 1340s". Those pages are not linked, were not read, and `urban-features.html` itself already labels
  the same four figures "(unsourced: the source page displays only a partial extract ... not these
  figures)". The write-up converts a recorded absence into a cited local account.
- **Limits: INACCURATE / MISSING.** "the numbers and the staffing come from a town's own local history
  rather than from a scholarly count, so we treat them as a local account" claims a provenance the record
  denies. The honest limits are: the gazetteer extract supports the site and its position only; the
  figures rest on no readable page; and the entry states the origin date is unknown, so "in use from the
  1340s" has nothing behind it. (Also: `yaotsu-mall.com` is a town commerce/mall domain, not a municipal
  or scholarly publisher - "local history pages published by the town of Yaotsu" overstates it.)

jawiki-koedame

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia articles on 肥溜め (koedame, the night soil pit) and 下肥 (shimogoe, night soil used as manure). They describe the pit or buried jar in which a household's human waste was collected and left to ferment before it went onto the fields, giving the two forms it took and the rough size of the jar kind.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the size and form of the fermenting pit that stands on a farmstead, and it is one of the few plain descriptions of an everyday fixture that no survey bothered to record; it is a tertiary encyclopedia summary, so we take its figures only where its own references support them. It describes a practice that continued in Japan well into the twentieth century, which is what makes it readable at all, and it says nothing about where on a plot the pit stood, so the placement on our maps comes from elsewhere.

jawiki-yashikigami

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on 屋敷神 (yashikigami, the guardian deity of a household's own plot), together with matching pages on the same subject from two Japanese folk-culture sites, minka-en.com and satologue.com. They cover the two patterns of household worship and the form the shrine takes, which is almost always a small stone or wooden hokora rather than a building.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for whether a farmstead carries a household shrine at all, what it looks like at map scale, and where it sits on the plot, usually a corner and often the northeast one that folk belief treats as the demon gate. It is a tertiary summary of a folk custom that varied by region and by household, so it gives us a common pattern and a prevailing corner rather than a rule every homestead in a single district would have followed.

jinya-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on 陣屋 (jin'ya), the walled administrative seat of a lord too small to hold a castle, or of a shogunal deputy. It sets out what such a seat contained: the lord's residence, the offices, official houses for retainers, earth-walled storehouses and a drill ground.

Why it applies, and its limits: The list of buildings is exactly what we need to lay out a small domain's seat on a map, and it is the compact statement of a program that longer works assume rather than list. It is a tertiary summary, so it gives the program and not any one seat's measured plan, and the passage we lean on describes a small domain's own seat rather than a shogunal deputy's office, which was a different institution with a different program.

jokamachi-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on 城下町 (jokamachi, the castle town). It describes how such a town was zoned around its castle, with samurai quarters ranked by their distance from it, merchant and artisan quarters beyond them and a temple district on the outer edge, and how streets were deliberately bent into right-angle dog-legs and stopped with dead ends to lengthen an attacker's approach.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the source of the zoning and the street tricks that give our towns and cities their shape, and it states in one place what scattered town histories show one town at a time. It is a tertiary summary describing the castle town as a general type, so it gives us the pattern rather than any single town's plan, and Japanese castle towns were an Edo-period form, which is later than parts of the setting our maps also draw on.

jokamachi-wiki

What it is: The English rendering of the Japanese Wikipedia castle-town article published in the Japanese Wiki Corpus, a collection of translated Japanese encyclopedia articles on history and culture. The passage we use covers the temple district placed at the town's outer rim, whose walled precincts were counted as part of the town's defenses.

Why it applies, and its limits: It tells us why temples cluster on a town's edge rather than at its heart, which decides where the religious quarter goes on a city map and what it is doing there. It is an encyclopedia article at one further remove, a translation of a tertiary summary, so we use it for the arrangement and its reason and take numbers only where its own references support them.

jokamachi-wiki-corpus

What it is: The same translated castle-town article in the Japanese Wiki Corpus, read through for the whole of its account of how a castle town was arranged: the castle at the center, rings of samurai and foot soldier quarters graded by rank, streets named for the trade that worked them, the temple district on the rim, main roads led past the castle's front to show off the lord's standing, and the total outer enclosure that a few great towns built.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supplies most of the vocabulary our capital maps are built from, including the ward names that let a quarter be labeled for what actually lived or worked in it. It remains a translated encyclopedia summary rather than a study, so it is good for the pattern and the names and not for measurements, and its examples are the largest Japanese towns, which is a scale we have to reduce carefully before it reaches a provincial seat.

jokamachi-zoning

What it is: The "Castle Towns" essay in the Nakasendo Way series that Walk Japan, a company running guided walks along the old Nakasendo road, publishes alongside its tours. It explains how a castle town separated samurai from townspeople, and notes that the townspeople's wards typically formed narrow strips between different bodies of samurai, laid along the main thoroughfares.

Why it applies, and its limits: That detail is what we use to interleave commoner streets with samurai ground instead of stacking the two in solid blocks, and to keep the separation inside the samurai quarter at the level of each compound's own wall and gate rather than a district palisade. It is a tour operator's history page, written for travelers, with no named author and no references, so we use it for the shape of the arrangement and not for any number, and the same zoning claims are also carried by the Japanese Wikipedia article on castle towns.

jsidre-minumadai

What it is: An article in the "history of regional development" series published by the Japanese Society of Irrigation, Drainage and Rural Engineering, on the Minuma-dai canal completed in 1728 on the Kanto plain, a shogunal reclamation carried out by Izawa Yasobei of the Kishu school of engineering. It describes the works and the reclamation layout that drained the old reservoir and watered the land in its place.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives us the comb layout our field blocks use, with the supply channels running along the higher rim and the drain down the lowest line through the middle, and it comes from the engineering profession that still maintains these systems. It is a society's popular history article rather than a peer-reviewed study and no author is named, and it describes one very large project, so we take the principle of the layout from it and not the dimensions, which belong to a scheme of thousands of hectares rather than to one hamlet's fields.

jstage-admin-natural-village

What it is: Tadashi Kondo, "The Relation between Administrative Village and Natural Village in the Edo Era", a research article in the Japanese Journal of Human Geography, volume 19 issue 2, 1967. It examines how the villages the Edo tax system recognized related to the settlements that actually existed on the ground, and finds that a taxed village on a plain was usually a single settlement while one in the mountains gathered several, more of them the deeper into the hills it lay.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is peer-reviewed work on exactly the question our maps face, whether a named village is one cluster of houses or several, and it is the closest thing we could find to a statement about how common each form was; we cite it as evidence that the record describes terrain rather than ranking one settlement form above another. Only the English abstract can be read on a public page, so we quote the abstract rather than the study's own data, and its evidence is drawn from one district, which makes it a pattern we can lean on and not a rate we can count with.

jta-ashigaru-kaga

What it is: Two entries from the Japan Tourism Agency's multilingual commentary database, the English texts written to explain historic sites to foreign visitors, covering the foot soldier districts and the ranking of samurai in the Kaga domain around Kanazawa. They give the rows of hedged plots the foot soldiers lived on, each about 165 or 230 square meters and divided between house and garden.

Why it applies, and its limits: Very few sources put a measured plot size on the humblest warrior housing, and these give us both a size and the way enclosure rose with rank from hedge to fence to wall, which is what sets the fringe of our castle towns. The commentary is interpretive writing for visitors rather than a survey, and it says plainly that Kaga's detached foot soldier houses were unusual for the period, most domains housing them in row tenements, so we treat these plots as one domain's practice that our maps may follow rather than a national norm.

jta-nagayamon

What it is: An entry from the same Japan Tourism Agency multilingual commentary database, on the nagaya-mon, the long low range of building with a gate passage cut through it that fronted a samurai residence in the Kaga domain. It describes what the range held, including the gatekeeper's and servants' rooms, a stable and storage, and who was allowed one.

Why it applies, and its limits: It tells us that the wall around a warrior compound is often a building rather than a fence, which changes both the outline we draw and what we put inside it, and it explains the lookout windows that face the street. It is visitor commentary rather than a survey, and the rank rule it quotes, that the form was permitted from middle rank upward, is Kaga's own regulation, so we use it as an example of how rank was shown at a gate rather than as a rule in force everywhere.

kagawa-tameike

What it is: The Kagawa prefectural government's pages on the structure of a tameike, the earth-banked irrigation reservoir, from the prefecture that has more of them than any other because it gets the least rain in Japan. They set out the parts: the inclined intake pipe laid up the inner face of the dam with holes at several heights, the conduit through the base that carries the water away, the spillway that keeps a storm from washing the bank out, and the way a larger pond can feed a smaller one below it.

Why it applies, and its limits: These are the parts we have to draw and place when a pond appears above a field block, and the arrangement is the traditional one that the prefecture still maintains rather than a new design. It is a modern engineering and repair page, so the materials it names belong to the present day, and we use it for where each part of a pond sits and what it does rather than for what a premodern one was built of.

kagawa-tameike-structure

What it is: The same Kagawa prefecture page on reservoir structure, read for two further points: that the intake is one facility, an inclined or vertical pipe drawing off stored water into a conduit through the dam base, with a sediment gate at the very bottom for clearing and for the last of the water, and that the water-facing slope of the bank is armored against wave erosion with riprap, stone pitching or concrete facing.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is why our reservoirs get a single intake works rather than scattered openings, and why one stretch of a pond's shore is deliberately bare stone while the rest can be planted, which makes the rule about a pond's margin a matter of position instead of one answer for the whole edge. Again it is a modern maintenance page: the concrete facing is of our time, the stone pitching and riprap are old, and we take the engineering reason for the armoring rather than the modern material.

kaifeng-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on Kaifeng, the Chinese city on the Yellow River that served as an imperial capital and has been repeatedly buried and rebuilt by floods. The passage we use counts the disasters: five major floods between 1375 and 1416, and more than three hundred flood events from the Southern Song to the late Qing.

Why it applies, and its limits: Our river cities need a sense of how often a great river actually broke over a city that lived beside it, and this gives a count across centuries for the clearest case there is. It is a tertiary summary, so we take the figures only as far as its own references support them, and Kaifeng sits below a notoriously silt-choked river whose bed rose above the surrounding plain, which makes it the extreme of the danger rather than the average one.

kaifeng-flood-1642-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the 1642 Yellow River flood, in which the dikes above Kaifeng were cut during a siege and the city was destroyed. It gives the traditional casualty figure, some three hundred thousand of the city's three hundred and seventy eight thousand inhabitants lost to the flood and to the famine and disease that followed.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for what a river city stands to lose and for the fact that its worst floods can be deliberate acts of war rather than weather, which is a thing a map of a walled river city should make legible. It is a tertiary summary and the death toll is a traditional figure carried down from the chronicles, so it is best read as an order of magnitude, and it records one catastrophic year rather than the ordinary risk of living on that bank.

kaifeng-pmc7048742

What it is: Storozum and colleagues, "Geoarchaeological evidence of the AD 1642 Yellow River flood that destroyed Kaifeng", a peer-reviewed open access paper in Scientific Reports, 2020. The authors read the flood deposits under the modern city and set the 1642 disaster in the river's long record, which brought roughly forty floods to Kaifeng over the past three thousand years.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the strongest evidence we have for how often a great river city floods and for the layered rebuilding that follows, measured from the ground rather than counted out of chronicles, which is why we prefer its frequency to the looser numbers in circulation. Its subject is a single Chinese city on the most flood-prone river in the region, so we treat its rate as the upper bound on what a river settlement faces, and it speaks to the imperial Chinese half of the setting more directly than to the Japanese half.

maff-water-history

What it is: A twelve-page briefing deck of May 2012 from the Water Resources Division of the Rural Development Bureau of Japan's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, titled 「On the history of agricultural water and water rights」 (original: 「農業用水の歴史と水利権について」). It sets out how the right to take irrigation water came to be settled in Japan, the other uses a village canal served besides watering the crop, and worked historical cases, among them the long quarrel over the Takina river in Iwate.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the ministry that administers irrigation water writing about how that water was historically shared, which is what we want it for as background to Japanese irrigation, and its count of recorded disputes on a single river is the kind of documented quarrel that supports our rule that the settlement upstream on a canal holds leverage over the one below it. Its limits are that it is a modern government presentation arguing about present-day water rights rather than a historical study, that its historical cases are compressed summaries whose own sources are not reproduced, and that the case it treats in detail is one valley in northern Japan rather than a national pattern.

magariya-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the magariya (曲屋), the L-shaped farmhouse of northern Japan in which the stable is built onto the dwelling as a wing of the same roof.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one point of form - the stable projecting from the lower end of the house on the south side, where the kitchen hearth warms it - which is a house-and-yard arrangement our homestead maps draw. It is a tertiary summary rather than a survey, so we take its statements only where its own references support them; it describes a regional house type rather than the ordinary farmhouse of the whole country; and it says nothing at all about the well, so nothing about where a well stands is taken from it.

matsue-bukeyashiki

What it is: The building documentation published by the museum that operates the Matsue Buke Yashiki, a preserved middle-rank samurai residence standing on the Shiomi Nawate street in the castle town of Matsue, describing the house room by room and the gate on its street front.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a surviving building described by the people who keep it, which is why we use it for the nagayamon standing on the street and doubling as the quarters of the gatekeeper and the household servants, and for a room program that includes the servants' service rooms - both things our residence plans have to place. It is one house in one castle town, presented for visitors rather than as a study, and a restored and interpreted one, so it tells us what a middle-rank residence in Matsue is like and not what a typical residence anywhere was.

matsumoto-goten

What it is: The pages of the official Matsumoto Castle site describing the Honmaru and Ninomaru palaces that stood inside the castle's enclosures.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one concrete case of an administration outgrowing its castle: the ninomaru palace was about two thirds the size of the honmaru's, and the county office and the town office were moved out of it into Rokku town and the conference hall for the lord and the village headmen into Agetsuchi town - which is our warrant for putting some of a castle town's official buildings outside the walls. Its limits are that it is a castle's own visitor-facing page, a summary with no citations behind it; that it is a single case; and that the offices named are those of the administration that occupied the palace after the domains ended, so it evidences that an inner enclosure could not hold a whole administration rather than describing Edo-period practice directly.

mdpi-kunisaki

What it is: A peer-reviewed open-access article by Jansing, Mahlknecht and colleagues in the journal Sustainability (2020), comparing how paddy irrigation is managed in Karangasem in Indonesia and on the Kunisaki peninsula in Japan, the Japanese half of it resting on the peninsula's small tameike irrigation ponds.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives us a real, counted case of how much land a cluster of small farm ponds waters and how many households share it - one ward's systems serving about fifty hectares for eleven farmers - which is the scale at which we draw a pond against the fields below it. It describes irrigation as it is managed today, in one peninsula, with modern equipment and a modern number of farmers; its own counts of the ward's ponds differ between passages; and it states no typical or maximum command area at all, so the upper bound our maps work to is our guess rather than its finding.

mdpi-sho-fan-groundwater

What it is: A peer-reviewed open-access paper in Geosciences (2021) tracing, through a year of oxygen-isotope and chemical measurements, where the shallow groundwater of the Sho River alluvial fan in Toyama comes from.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the ground under the scattered farmsteads of the Tonami plain: the plain is that river's alluvial fan, and the shallow water beneath it is a mixture of river water and rainfall, which is the setting for a farmstead that draws its own water. The paper is a modern geochemical study concerned with where the water comes from rather than how deep it lies, and it does not discuss paddies at all, so the idea that a farmstead there could reach water with a shallow well is an inference of ours and is labeled as a guess where it is used.

meiji-jingu-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Meiji Jingu, the large Shinto shrine in Tokyo, covering its grounds, its approach and its buildings.

Why it applies, and its limits: It was consulted to check a claim about how many torii stand along a shrine approach, and the point of the citation is that it does not bear the claim out - the article counts eight, not three, and gives no distances between them, so no spacing figure on our maps comes from it. Beyond being a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, it describes a modern shrine of exceptional scale, which makes it a poor model for the small country shrines our settlements mostly carry.

minami-2022-igune

What it is: A 2022 research article by Minami, Yonezawa and Okaze, published on J-STAGE, measuring the wind flow around igune - the belts of tall trees planted around the dispersed farmsteads of the Osaki plain in Miyagi.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a direct study of the thing we draw, and it supports the two parts of our rule that matter most: the belt is a windbreak of roughly ten meters and it stands on the side the prevailing wind comes from. Only its abstract is on a page a reader can open, the full text being closed, and the abstract names no compass side, so which side of the yard our belts sit on is not carried by anything readable; and it measures surviving belts today with modern instruments rather than describing a historical planting.

mineta-2007-tameike

What it is: An article by Mineta Takuya in the Journal of the Japanese Society of Irrigation, Drainage and Rural Engineering (原文: 農業農村工学会誌) 75(8), 2007, part of a series on the ecological basics of farmland, dealing with the plants of paddy fields and of irrigation ponds.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the one source with numbers behind our rule that a farm pond's shallow shore is reeded, giving the zoning of reed and cattail by water depth and bank slope, and it corrected an assumption we had held: a Kagawa study it reports found more emergent and floating-leaved species where ponds are dredged and their algae cut, and it is the ponds that have fallen out of use that lose their variety, so a working reservoir does not have a bare margin. It is a professional-society review reporting recent surveys of ponds still in use rather than primary evidence of its own or evidence about any earlier century, and the correlation it reports comes from a single prefecture, so we take a pattern of where plants stand from it and not a figure about how a premodern pond looked.

mingguanci-zhwiki

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the mingguanci (名宦祠), the shrine in which a locality offered sacrifice to former officials of the place who had governed it well.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for what the building is and where it belongs - a state institution from the early Ming onward, standing in the Confucian temple precinct east of the Dacheng gate rather than inside the magistrate's own compound - which is how we place and label it on a town plan. It is a tertiary summary whose statements we take only where its own references support them, and it describes the Chinese institution, which our setting adapts rather than copies.

minka-en-yashikigami

What it is: A page on minka-en.com, a site about Japanese folk houses and their fittings, describing the yashikigami (屋敷神) - the household deity whose small shrine stands in the yard of a farmstead.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives us both halves of what we draw: the shrine's form, a little hokora of stone or wood or with a straw-thatched roof, and its customary place, a corner of the yard and especially the northeast kimon corner. It is a general-interest explanatory page rather than a survey, with no author or date given and no count of how many farmsteads kept one, so the form and the corner come from it and no figure for how often the shrine appears does.

miragenews-polders

What it is: A news item on Mirage News reporting research from Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University on the history of China's polders, the embanked field islands of the lower Yangtze, quoting the researcher directly.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is our warrant for the shape of a polder landscape - by the early twentieth century the large enclosures had been subdivided into small islet-like "fish-scale" polders, and it was only after 1949 that their organic outlines were replaced by standardized rectangles for industrialized farming - which is why our maps draw irregular polder blocks instead of a grid. It is a press release republished as news rather than the study itself, so it is a summary in the researcher's own words that a reader cannot check against data; and its dates run later than our setting, so we read it as the end point of a long development rather than as a picture of any one earlier century.

mizumaki-goemonburo

What it is: A page from the historical museum of the town of Mizumaki on the goemonburo (五右衛門風呂), the iron-bottomed bath tub heated by a fire lit directly underneath it.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one sentence that decides where we may put a bath: this kind of tub was used widely in self-sufficient farm villages, which lets an ordinary farmstead have one rather than reserving the bath for a wealthy house. It is a short municipal museum page written for visitors around an object in its own collection, with no date and no count behind it, so "widely" stays a word and never becomes a proportion in our generator, and it speaks for the practice of one region rather than of the country.

mlit-senjochi-kurashi

What it is: A teaching document from the land-classification survey material of Japan's Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, 「Alluvial fans and the lives of the inhabitants」 (original: 「扇状地と人々の暮らし」), explaining how an alluvial fan is built and how settlement and cultivation arrange themselves across it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It carries the point our fan maps are built on - that the water sinking into the coarse upper fan re-emerges as springs at the fan's toe, and that villages and their paddies have sat on that spring line since ancient times. The document itself would not open as readable text for us, so the claim rests on summaries of it and of related ministry pages rather than on a passage a reader can go and read; and it is modern educational material describing a landform pattern in general terms rather than a study of any particular historical village.

mlit-vegetation-classes

What it is: The vegetation-class reference list of the national river-environment survey run by the National Institute for Land and Infrastructure Management, part of Japan's Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, which defines each plant community the survey records and the ground it grows on.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it to decide what to draw at a wet margin, and it names the communities and their habitats plainly: reed in the lower reaches, the tachiyanagi willow association on the sand and mud deposits of lower rivers, and the alder community on waterlogged ground. It is a modern survey's classification key, so it records what grows along Japanese rivers now, after centuries of embanking and channel work; it gives habitats and not densities or sizes; and it says nothing about how inhabitants cut or used any of these plants.

nabunken-azemame

What it is: A short explanatory article of June 2023 from the Asuka Historical Museum of the Nara National Research Institute for Cultural Properties on azemame (畦豆), the soybeans sown along the bund of a paddy field.

Why it applies, and its limits: It describes the practice exactly as our maps need to draw it - beans put in along the bund after the rice is transplanted, grown in a row on the bund itself, and harvested when the rice is - and it tells us the custom was once found throughout the country, which is why we treat a planted bund as ordinary rather than exotic. It is a museum's short piece for a general audience rather than an agricultural study: it gives no figure for how much of a bund was sown or how many households did it, and its statement that the practice is now rare is about the present, so how common to make it in our own period is our decision and not its finding.

weinei-he-summary

What it is: A November 2020 feature article by Huang Tao in 中国国家地理 (Chinese National Geography), a popular geography magazine, on the polder fields (圩田) of southern China - farmland made by throwing up a dike around low-lying ground beside a river, a lake or the sea. It describes the constant of the form (a dike at the low place, fields enclosed within, water held without) and the way a polder reads from the air as a chessboard of dikes, channels and roads.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for that plain definition of a polder and for the chessboard look of one from above, which is exactly what a general-audience geography magazine reports well. It is written for readers rather than reviewed by scholars, and it describes polders as they survive today; the more particular claim once hung on it - that a polder's internal channels take crescent and bow shapes and are gated at their ends - is not on the page that can be read, so nothing on our maps rests on it.

wengcheng-zhwiki

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article 瓮城 (wengcheng, "barbican"), a tertiary encyclopedia entry on the walled outwork built in front of a Chinese city gate, the half-round and square shapes it takes, and named surviving examples such as the Zhonghua Gate at Nanjing, whose barbicans sit inside the gate rather than before it.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it only for what a barbican is and which forms it takes at a gate, which is the kind of settled definition an encyclopedia carries dependably. It is a tertiary summary written by volunteers, so we take its figures only where its own references support them, and it describes Chinese city gates - the setting's towns take the form from the imperial-Chinese side of their ancestry rather than from Japan.

wikipedia-soybean

What it is: The English Wikipedia article "Soybean", and in particular its Description section - a tertiary encyclopedia entry on the plant, its habit and its cultivation.

Why it applies, and its limits: We take two facts about the plant itself, that a mature soybean stands 50 to 125 cm and that the crop is an annual, and those decide how tall a bean plot is drawn and whether it is shown replanted each year. These are botanical constants rather than historical ones, so a present-day encyclopedia is a fair place to get them; it is still a tertiary summary, and we use its numbers only where its own references support them.

willow-palisade

What it is: The English rendering of the Baidu Baike encyclopedia entry on the Willow Palisade (柳条边), the Qing dynasty's willow-planted border embankment across Manchuria, including the statute that laid down how the willows along it were to be set.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use one planting measurement from it - three willow stakes about 13 cm thick and 2 m long at every 5 chi, roughly 1.67 m, along the bank - which fixes how densely a willow-planted embankment is drawn. Two honest limits: it is a collaborative online encyclopedia, a tertiary summary rather than the statute itself; and the Willow Palisade was a frontier barrier, not a field dike, so it stands here as an analog because no planting rule written for a polder dike could be found on any page open to the public.

woodland-edge-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article "Woodland edge", a short tertiary encyclopedia entry describing in general terms how the trees and plants at the margin of a wood differ from those growing inside it.

Why it applies, and its limits: This one is cited for an absence rather than for a figure. The layered vocabulary we use for the edge of a wood - herb fringe, shrub belt, mantle - comes from the German-language article on the same subject, and the English page is named so that a reader following the obvious English link is not left thinking those three layers were drawn from it.

woods-westbrook-2006

What it is: A peer-reviewed hydrology paper by Woods, Westbrook and colleagues, "Hydrologic interactions between an alluvial fan and a slope wetland in the central Rocky Mountains, USA", published in the journal Wetlands in 2006, which traces where the water in a wetland at the foot of an alluvial fan actually comes from.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the mechanism behind a marsh drawn at the edge of a fan - groundwater discharging out of the fan keeps the wetland wet, and seepage from the stream is what recharges that groundwater - so the chain from stream to fan to marsh holds together on the map instead of each piece being placed by eye. Its limits are place and era: it measures one site in the Rocky Mountains in the 2000s, not an East Asian one, so we cite it for the physics, which does not change by country, and never for a measurement of a particular place. Only the abstract and the summary sections are on a public page, the full paper being behind a subscription.

xian-moat-zhwiki

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article 西安城墙 (the city wall of Xi'an), in the section on its moat - a tertiary encyclopedia entry on the Ming dynasty wall that still rings the old city, and on the water ditch outside it.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one dimension every walled map has to settle, the size of the ditch outside a great city wall: about 20 m wide and 10 m deep, holding water all year and read as part of the defense rather than as a stream. Two limits are worth stating: it is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, and Xi'an is an imperial Chinese capital, so its ditch is the top of the range rather than anything a provincial town would dig.

xian-wall-zhwiki

What it is: The same Chinese Wikipedia article 西安城墙, here for its account of the rampart itself - 12 m high, 15 to 18 m thick at the base and 12 to 14 m across the top, with 98 projecting towers standing 12 m out from the outer face and rising level with the wall.

Why it applies, and its limits: These are our anchor numbers for how tall and how thick a great city wall is drawn, and for how far its towers jut out - a wall wide enough to walk formations along is a very different mark on a map from a garden wall, and the reader should be able to see which is meant. The same two limits apply: an encyclopedia article is a tertiary summary trusted only as far as its own references, and Xi'an's Ming wall is among the largest ever built, so it sets the ceiling for the setting's capitals rather than the norm for a walled town.

yashikirin-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 屋敷林 (yashikirin, "homestead grove"), a tertiary encyclopedia entry on the belts of trees Japanese farmhouses planted around themselves against wind and snow, covering the regional names for the same thing - the northeastern igune (居久根) and the Izumo tsuijimatsu among them - along with the species used and the sides of the house they stand on.

Why it applies, and its limits: This is the backbone of how we plant a farmstead: which sides carry the grove (north and west against the wind, the east left open for the entrance and its ornamental garden), which trees make it up (sugi, matsu, hinoki and keyaki), and the part that turns a fact into a choice - that the Izumo form once enclosed the whole circumference of a house and was later cut back to a hook covering only the north and west, which is why our maps treat a full ring and a two-sided belt as two correct answers rather than one. It is a tertiary summary rather than a survey, so it gives us forms and species names and not counts or measurements, and the practice is Japanese and regional, the north-and-west rule following a wind that a warmer corner of the setting need not share.

yato-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 谷戸 (yato, also read yatsu), a tertiary encyclopedia entry on the small spring-fed valleys that bite into the hill country of eastern Japan, how their floors were farmed and how the woods on the slopes above them were used in common.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for why a narrow valley floor makes easily worked paddy once it drains, and for the common rights villagers held over the neighboring woods, which is what puts a firewood wood on the slope beside a valley-bottom field on our maps. It is a tertiary summary, so we take the pattern from it and not a number; it speaks for eastern Japan in particular; and carrying those common rights on from firewood to a reed bed is a step our own record takes, not something the article says.

yonekura-mushiro

What it is: An exhibit page from the 米倉町内博物館, a small neighborhood museum of old farm, fishing and household tools kept by residents of the Yonekura district of Okayama City and published on the city's community web pages. The page describes the mushiro, the woven rice-straw mat - how it was made on a mat loom, its size, and what a farm did with it. No author or date is given.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for a single household number, that a farm kept about fifty straw mats, which matters because mats spread out to sun-dry grain need floor space and a work yard has to be drawn large enough to hold them. Its value is that it is an independent local account agreeing with a count recorded elsewhere; its limits are what kind of thing it is - a community museum's note written from local memory rather than a survey - and how narrow it is, speaking for one district of Okayama and for the last farming generations before machines took the work over.

yuan-liu-2009

What it is: A peer-reviewed article by Yuan Juanwen and Liu Jinlong, "Fengshui forest management by the Buyi ethnic minority in China", published in Forest Ecology and Management in 2009, on how Buyi villages in Guizhou province hold and manage the sacred groves kept for a settlement's fengshui.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for how many such groves a village keeps - two parcels apiece in the two villages studied - and for how large one can grow, the 133 hectare Letu lineage forest that marks the far end of the range against which an ordinary grove is drawn. It is a close study of two villages of one ethnic minority in one province rather than a national survey, so it gives us the shape of the practice and its extremes rather than an average, and it describes an inland southern Chinese custom that the setting's Japanese side keeps in its own forms. The full text is behind a subscription; what we quote comes from the abstract and the section snippets on the publisher's public page.

zennoh-mizukanri

What it is: A rice-growing leaflet, 水管理について ("On water management"), published by Zennoh, Japan's National Federation of Agricultural Cooperative Associations, as part of the advice it gives its member farmers on producing good rice.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for how deep the water in a paddy stands and when it is let out - about 2 to 3 cm held through the twenty days after the ear emerges, and the season-long sequence from deeper water through midseason drying and intermittent irrigation to the final drain a week or so before harvest - because that is what decides whether a given field on the map is drawn wet, drying or dry. The honest limit is era: this is present-day guidance written for cooperative farmers with modern varieties and modern control of the inlet, so we use it for the shape of the rice year, which the crop itself imposes and which is far older than the leaflet, rather than as a record of what a premodern farmer measured.

zhongshan-fsw-2016

What it is: A peer-reviewed survey by Sun Hongmei, Zhang Dongdong and Xiu Xiaojuan, 「The medicinal plant resources of the fengshui groves of Zhongshan City」 (中山市风水林的药用植物资源), published in 热带生物学报 (Journal of Tropical Biology) in 2016; the authors work for the state forest resource protection center of Zhongshan in Guangdong and for the forestry bureau of Fuxin in Liaoning, and the fieldwork behind it covers that one municipality's fengshui groves.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it not for its botany but for the count it had to make first: 66 groves in 66 natural villages totaling 269.85 hectares, which works out at about four hectares a village and gives us a typical grove to draw against the very large outliers other studies report. Its limits are place and era - the Pearl River Delta is subtropical southern China, warmer and wetter than the setting's Japanese model, and the groves were measured as they stand now, so the figure describes the survivors of a century of clearing around them rather than what a village once held.

zhwiki-liuchu

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article 六畜 (liuchu, "the six domestic animals"), a short tertiary encyclopedia entry on the classical Chinese grouping of livestock - horse, ox, sheep, pig, dog and chicken - that Chinese writing has treated as a set since antiquity.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one small thing, that the chicken belongs to that classical set, which is what puts a hen-house on a farmstead in a setting built on imperial China and Japan; the article is in Chinese because the category is a Chinese literary one. It is a tertiary summary of a term rather than evidence of how many birds any particular farm kept, so it settles that chickens belong on a farm and nothing at all about their numbers.
