takada-teramachi

What it is: An English-language local history article on Joetsu Stories, a bilingual site about the city of Joetsu in Niigata Prefecture, telling how the temple quarter (teramachi) of the castle town of Takada came into being after Matsudaira Tadateru moved his seat there in 1614. It describes the ground west of the castle that was set aside for temples, the first wave of temples that moved in, and what the domain expected of them.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one attested count - roughly twenty-five temples relocated in the 1614 wave - and for the reason a lord gathered temples in one quarter at all, which is why our castle towns put their precincts in a belt rather than scattering them. It is a heritage site written for residents and visitors rather than a peer-reviewed study, its own figure is an approximation ("probably about 25"), and it describes one town in one province, so it serves as one point in a range of attested temple counts rather than as a general rule.

takayama-jinya-city

What it is: The city of Takayama's official page for 高山陣屋跡 (the site of the Takayama Jin'ya), the one surviving Tokugawa provincial governor's office and compound in Japan, published by the municipality that manages the designated historic site. It lists the buildings and how they are built, notes which structures were moved in from the castle and when, and gives the extent of the protected ground.

Why it applies, and its limits: An intact government compound described by the body responsible for it is the best single anchor we have for what a magistracy actually contained - an examination hall and its gravel court laid with coarse cobble and roofed over, granaries brought down from the castle's third bailey in 1695, and an enclosure whose size we can measure against our own. Its limits: it is one office in one mountain province, its buildings carry centuries of rebuilding and modern restoration, and one figure on the page (the recorded area of the designated site) is labeled oddly enough that we treat it as approximate rather than exact.

takayama-jinya-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 高山陣屋 (Takayama Jin'ya), a tertiary encyclopedia summary of the same compound: its history under the shogunate, the 1816 rebuilding that put the entrance hall, examination hall, main offices and great hall into a single range, the rows of numbered storehouses, and the succession of intendants who held the post.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supplies the internal arrangement and the sequence of offices that the city's own page states more briefly, which is what tells us that a magistracy's public rooms sit in one connected range rather than as separate pavilions. It is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, and like the city page it describes a single unusually well preserved compound, so we use its shape and not its exact dimensions.

takayama-teramachi

What it is: "Takayama's historic 'Temple Town'", a visitor's guide article by Sandra Isaka on Japan Travel, a community travel site written by contributors, walking the reader through the temple quarter on the eastern edge of Takayama and noting who founded most of its temples.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives us the size-matched end of our temple range - a small castle town with "over 10 temples and shrines" in one quarter - which is the scale our own town maps work at, and it is a claim any visitor can check by walking the street. It is promotional travel writing rather than a survey, and "over 10" is a rough count, so we use it as the low anchor of a range whose other points come from much larger cities.

tamagawa-josui-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 玉川上水 (Tamagawa Josui), on the aqueduct built in the 1650s to carry drinking water from the Tama River across the Musashino plateau into Edo - its route and the ridge lines it follows, its total length and fall, the water-watch station at the city edge, and how the water was distributed once inside.

Why it applies, and its limits: Our capital-tier maps have to show how a very large premodern city was watered, and this gives the whole shape of the answer: an open cut of some forty-three kilometers dropping about ninety meters, run deliberately along the high ground so gravity does the work, then a control point at the city boundary and buried wooden and stone pipes beyond it. It is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, and it describes one exceptional work built for the shogun's own capital, so it marks the top of what a premodern state could manage rather than ordinary practice; the article also gives no total length for the buried pipe network, so we do not state one.

tameike-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article ため池 (tameike, "retention pond"), on the irrigation reservoirs that store water for rice fields across Japan - how they are built and managed, how the embankment is kept sound, and what grows on it as a result.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for a maintenance practice it states plainly and that prefectural and national agriculture sources corroborate: an embankment is kept strong by forbidding cultivation on it and by regular mowing and controlled burning, which is why dry grassland herbs, not reeds, are what one finds growing on a raised bank - the independent confirmation of how we plant our own pond banks. It is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, and the plants it names are recorded from ponds as they are managed today, so we take the practice and the vegetation it produces rather than any date.

tedai-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 手代 (tedai), on the clerks of that name - both the shop clerks of merchant houses and the junior staff who served under a Tokugawa intendant in a rural district office - covering where they came from and what they did.

Why it applies, and its limits: A magistracy compound has to house its staff, and we use this only for who that staff was: mostly the sons of village and town officials, hired from commoners who already knew the district, which tells us what kind of household the clerks' quarters on a compound plan represent. It is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, and it says nothing about how many clerks an office held or about birth order, so we take the recruitment pattern from it and nothing further.

tenmacho-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 伝馬町牢屋敷 (the Tenmacho jail), on Edo's main prison near Nihonbashi, in use until the 1870s - its extent, the plastered wall and outer moat that enclosed it, its internal divisions, and the categories of prisoner it held.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives a measured anchor for a jail compound - about 2,677 tsubo, roughly 8,850 square meters, behind a solid wall and a moat - and it settles what such a place was for: people awaiting judgment, with life imprisonment and imprisonment as a penalty being the exceptions rather than the rule, which is why our lockups are small holding buildings and not penitentiaries. It is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, and it describes the shogunal capital's central jail, so a provincial magistracy's lockup is scaled far down from it rather than copied.

terauke-seido-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 寺請制度 (terauke seido), on the Tokugawa requirement that every household register with a Buddhist temple, and on the growth in temple numbers that followed it.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for a single figure that tells us how recent a dense temple landscape actually is - six thousand Jodo-sect temples in existence in 1696, nine tenths of them founded from the sixteenth century onward - which is the check on how many precincts a settlement of a given age should carry. It is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, the count covers one sect rather than all of them, and the page carries no all-sect total, so we do not put one on a map.

tetsu-to-hagane-91

What it is: "History of Iron and Steel Making Technology in Japan", a review article by Mitsuru Tate published in 2005 in Tetsu-to-Hagane, the journal of the Iron and Steel Institute of Japan (volume 91, issue 1), tracing the tatara smelt and the refining that followed it across the long history of Japanese ironmaking.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is peer-reviewed metallurgy from the field's own journal, and we use it for one structural fact that decides what an ironworking premises on a town map is doing: the tatara produced pig iron, which then had to go through a second and separate refining stage to become the wrought iron a smith works, so smelting and refining are distinct operations in distinct places. It is written for metallurgists about process rather than about buildings, so it tells us that two premises exist and not how large either one is; the sizes come from elsewhere.

tfd-hongou-fire-history

What it is: A page on the history of fire precautions (防火対策の歴史) published by the Hongo station of the Tokyo Fire Department, a short public-education account of how the inhabitants and authorities of Edo guarded against fire, including the water kept ready in ordinary households.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one everyday habit that we draw on the street: commoners kept water standing by as a matter of course, in buckets and rainwater butts set at the doorway and up on the roof, under several different names - exactly the small permanent fixture that makes a townscape read as inhabited. It is a modern fire service writing popular history about its own city rather than a scholarly study, and it gives the practice with no dates, quantities or regional detail, so we take the habit from it and not a number.

thepaper-city-walls

What it is: 圆形、方形、卵形？ ("Round, square, oval? What shape were China's ancient cities"), a 2014 article by the historical geographer Cheng Yinong (成一农) in 澎湃新闻 (The Paper), a Shanghai-based news outlet, surveying the plan forms that Chinese walled cities actually took and why they took them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supplies the rule our walled outlines follow: capitals laid out in advance were essentially square, while cities in hill and mountain country had to bring the commanding high ground inside the wall for defense and so ended up markedly irregular, Beijing's 凸-shaped plan among the named examples. It is a popular article by a specialist rather than a peer-reviewed paper, and it generalizes over the whole span of imperial China at once, so we take the principle and its named examples from it rather than any measurement.

thepaper-taipinggang

What it is: 这口大缸能防火？！ ("This great vat can fight fire?!"), an article in 澎湃新闻 (The Paper) about the bronze and iron water vats standing in the courtyards of the Forbidden City - how many there were, the grades they came in, and the rule that governed where each grade stood.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the idea that firefighting water was fixed equipment rather than improvisation: Qing regulation set which kind of vat and how many stood in which courtyard, three hundred and eight in all by the statutes with two hundred and thirty-one surviving, placed wherever a timber hall stood far from a water source. It is popular journalism rather than a study, and it describes the imperial palace, the most heavily regulated and best funded compound in the empire, so we carry the principle down to a magistracy yard and leave the count where it belongs.

timber-rafting-wiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article "Timber rafting", a tertiary summary of how cut timber was moved on water before roads and railways, distinguishing rafting - logs bound together and navigated, sometimes with cabins and steering oars aboard - from log driving, and giving raft sizes from several regional traditions.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it to keep two different river systems straight on a map, since a raft needs a wide steady channel and a landing where it can be broken up, while driving loose logs does not, and to keep raft sizes within a plausible order of magnitude. It is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, and its detailed dimensions come from European rivers such as the Rhine, so we treat them as the outer bound of what a raft can be rather than as a measurement of an East Asian one.

tobunken-mushiro

What it is: 「莚と莚織りの技術」 ("Mushiro mats and the technique of weaving them"), a fieldwork report by Imaishi Migiwa (今石みぎわ) published in 2012 by the Tokyo National Research Institute for Cultural Properties, documenting straw-mat weaving as it survived at Nishidani, a mountain hamlet of three households in Kudamatsu City, Yamaguchi Prefecture, where the craft was on the point of dying out.

Why it applies, and its limits: The straw mat is the unit in which floor and yard space gets described in this period, and this report gives a measured one - about three shaku by six shaku, or 90 by 180 centimeters, a little over 1.6 square meters - which is what lets a count of mats become an area on a plan. It is a recent record of an old and once universal craft, made in a single village of a single prefecture, and mat sizes did vary from place to place, so we treat this measurement as a representative standard rather than as a fixed national one.

tokaido-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 東海道 (the Tokaido), on the highway between Edo and Kyoto - its post stations, its administration under the shogunate, and the orders that shaped its surface, its width and its markers.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the order of 1604 that directed officials to make the highway five ken wide (about nine meters, or thirty feet), plant hackberry trees along the verge and set a marker at every ri, which is what fixes how broad a great imperial road is drawn where it enters one of our towns. It is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them; the width is the decreed figure for the busiest highway in the country, which is the upper end of what a road could be, and a decree records what was ordered rather than what every stretch was built to.

hotes-wetland-diversity

What it is: A 2007 review article by the wetland ecologist Stefan Hotes, then in the conservation ecology laboratory of the University of Tokyo's Graduate School of Agricultural and Life Sciences, published in Japanese in 地球環境 (Global Environmental Research, volume 12) by the Association of International Research Initiatives for Environmental Studies. It surveys the ways wetlands are classified and what those classifications are worth for conserving and restoring them, and along the way sets out the Japanese wetland types and the plants that characterize each.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for what grows where along a wetland's edge - the large sedges, reed, cattail and alder stands of a nutrient-rich lowland mire - which is the plant zonation our marsh and pond margins are drawn from, and a scientific description of which plants take which ground holds as well for a premodern marsh as for a modern one. Its limits: it is a present-day scientific review, written about Japan's surviving wetlands and about the problem of classifying them rather than about any historical landscape or about how villagers cut and used those margins; it is in Japanese, and we quote it in our own English translation.

hu-2011-fengshui-patches

What it is: A peer-reviewed article by Hu, Li, Guo and colleagues, "Values of village fengshui forest patches in biodiversity conservation in the Pearl River Delta, China", in Biological Conservation volume 144 (2011). The authors surveyed thirty-two well-protected village fengshui forest patches, sampling one 1,200 square meter transect in each, and report the species richness, stem density and basal area they found.

Why it applies, and its limits: A fengshui forest is the protected wood a village keeps at its back, which is exactly the feature our homestead and village groves are modeled on, and this is a direct measurement of how thickly such a grove actually stands (about 3,400 stems and 49.1 square meters of basal area per hectare, which the authors themselves put on a level with well developed evergreen broadleaf forest). Its limits: only the abstract is on a public page, so we take nothing beyond the figures the abstract states; the survey is of patches that survive in one region of southern China in the twenty-first century, and choosing the well-protected ones means these are the healthiest examples rather than an average grove; and southern China is not Japan.

huangshan-daily-jiekou

What it is: A newspaper article from 黄山日报 (the Huangshan Daily), 「林长制的黄山探索」 ("Huangshan's exploration of the forest-chief system"), dated 1 January 2022 and mirrored on a Yangtze River Delta party news site. It reports on a modern forest-stewardship program in Anhui province, and in passing describes the water-mouth grove standing at the entrance to Jiekou village in Shexian.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one concrete measure of a water-mouth grove - over a hundred mu (roughly seven hectares), nearly a thousand old trees, and fifty-six yews more than five centuries old - and the record treats that as the extreme end of the range rather than the ordinary case; a stand that has been kept at a village mouth for that long is evidence about the form even though the article around it is current news. Its limits: it is journalism rather than scholarship and it is promotional about a government program; the numbers are the reporter's, unsourced; the article is in Chinese and we read it in machine translation, so the wording is not the newspaper's own English; and it describes the largest example anyone in the region can name, so nothing in it should be read as typical.

hudson-big-boom

What it is: An article by Glenn Pearsall, "The Big Boom: Old Hudson River Chain Recalls Logging History", published on 18 October 2016 in New York Almanack, an online magazine of New York State history and natural history. It describes the log boom that held floated timber on the Hudson above Glens Falls - hewn timbers bolted together raftwise, the groups joined end to end by chains running over friction rollers, each end anchored to a heavy bank abutment - and the 1859 break that scattered logs forty miles downriver.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for how a boom is built and held, which is what the log booms on our timber-town rivers are drawn from, and a working nineteenth-century boom demonstrates the mechanics any such device needs: floating timbers chained across a current, jointed so they ride the water, tied to solid ground at both banks. Its limits: it is popular history rather than a technical or scholarly account, and it is about industrial-era logging in North America rather than East Asia; the Hudson operation was far larger than anything at our settlements, so we take the arrangement from it and not the dimensions.

hutong-enwiki

What it is: The English Wikipedia article "Hutong", on the alleys of Beijing that are formed by lines of siheyuan, the walled courtyard houses of the traditional city, and on how such neighborhoods grew.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one structural point that shapes how our town blocks are laid out - the lane is the space left between rows of walled courtyard houses, and a quarter grows by joining one courtyard to the next and then one lane to the next, with smaller passages threading between. Its limits: an encyclopedia article is a tertiary summary, so we take only general description that its own references support and no figure of our own from it; and it is about Beijing, an imperial capital, so the pattern carries over to our towns while the scale and density do not.

hyojosho-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 評定所 (Hyojosho), on the Tokugawa shogunate's high council of judicature - the body made up of the town magistrate, the temple-and-shrine magistrate, the finance magistrate and one member of the shogun's senior council, which heard important matters of government and the suits that crossed several magistrates' jurisdictions.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for a single fact of placement: the Hyojosho stood at Tatsunokuchi outside Edo Castle, on ground that is now Marunouchi, and not within the castle walls - which is why a capital on our maps puts its high court outside the lord's enceinte. Its limits: it is a tertiary summary, taken only where it states a plain checkable fact of location and composition; it describes one specific Tokugawa institution in one city, which our fictional capitals resemble rather than copy; and it is in Japanese, quoted here in our own translation.

ide-japanese-experience

What it is: "Development of local culture and the irrigation system of the Azusa Basin" by Akira Tamaki, published in 1979 by the Institute of Developing Economies in the Japanese Experience series of the United Nations University's Human and Social Development Programme, and kept in the institute's online archive. It studies the Azusa River basin near Matsumoto in Nagano: the customary rules by which villages shared irrigation water, the difference between the dry fields on the river terraces and the wet paddy below them, and the repeated attempts to bring water up onto the terraces.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the distinction between dry field (hatake) and wet paddy (suiden) and for why a settlement sitting above the water is stuck with the former - small holders depending on rainfall or natural underground sources, and the late-Tokugawa schemes to irrigate the Hata fields that were defeated again and again by the downstream villages who would have lost the water. Its limits: it is a close study of one river basin in one province, so its customs are local before they are national, and it runs from the Tokugawa period through twentieth-century modernization, so only its account of the older arrangements bears on our settlements.

ido-jawiki

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article 井戸 (ido, "well"), covering how wells in Japan are dug, lined and owned.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the construction of the shaft that the well glyph in a yard stands for - firm ground will hold a bare dug shaft, while ground liable to collapse needs a lining (idogawa) - and for the related point that wells were often held jointly rather than by one household, because digging one was expensive. Its limits: a tertiary summary, taken only for plain description of the thing itself; it says nothing about where in a yard a well is placed, so that decision on our maps rests on other sources; and it is in Japanese, quoted here in our own translation.

ifc-307-bonfire

What it is: Section 307.4 of the International Fire Code, the model fire-safety code published by the International Code Council and adopted, with local amendments, across much of the United States. We read it in one such adoption - the 2010 New York State Fire Code, section 307.4.1 - reproduced on the code-hosting site UpCodes, the publisher's own site being closed to us; the clause forbids a bonfire within fifty feet of a structure or combustible material unless the fire is contained in a pit.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supplies one number, the working clearance around a large open fire, from which the cleared ground around a capital's pyre is derived; the hazard being regulated - radiant heat and drifting embers from an unenclosed fire - is a physical constant, so a modern regulator's minimum is a defensible floor where no premodern rule states a distance. Its limits: it is a present-day American code, not a historical or East Asian source, and it governs a recreational bonfire rather than a funeral pyre; a premodern town set its own distances by custom and by how much open ground it had, so this figure is a reasoned choice on our part and not evidence about any real settlement.

ijc-yamaguni

What it is: "External impacts on traditional commons and present-day changes: a case study of iriai forests in Yamaguni district, Kyoto, Japan" by Daisaku Shimada, a peer-reviewed article in the International Journal of the Commons, volume 8 issue 1 (2014). Working from interviews and archival documents, it traces how the eleven villages of the Yamaguni district hold and manage their customary common forest (iriai), and how those institutions have bent under depopulation and cheap imported timber.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the finding that each of eleven neighboring villages runs its common woodland under its own distinct institutions, with detailed local rules on the method, season and quantity of what each household may take - which is why the villages on our maps differ from one another in how their woodland is held rather than sharing a single scheme. Its limits: it is a modern study whose main subject is recent change, though the institutions it describes are inherited ones; it covers a single district near Kyoto rather than the country; and it describes no boundary marks on the ground, so where a common forest ends on our maps does not come from it.

inamino-tameike-museum

What it is: A page on aquatic plants from いなみ野ため池ミュージアム (the Inamino Tameike Museum), the public-education body that documents the dense cluster of irrigation reservoirs on the Inamino plateau in Hyogo prefecture. It describes the shallow embanked "dish ponds" of the lowland and the plants that ring them and cover their water.

Why it applies, and its limits: It corroborates the pond-margin planting on our maps at exactly the right scope - not wetlands in general but tameike, the built irrigation ponds themselves - with reed, Manchurian wild rice and lesser cattail forming colonies at the rim and floating-leaf plants over the open water, and it comes from an institution documenting a real, still-working pond cluster. Its limits: it is an outreach page written for visitors rather than a scientific survey, and it describes those ponds as they are now, including the eutrophication of the modern water; so it is a good guide to which plants belong at a pond's edge and a poor one to how much of them there would have been; it is in Japanese, quoted here in our own translation.

irri-drying-floor

What it is: A page from the Rice Knowledge Bank of the International Rice Research Institute, the agricultural research organization based in the Philippines, explaining how paddy is dried in the sun: how thin the grain is spread and how much floor a given tonnage of it needs.

Why it applies, and its limits: It carries the only plain statement of area we could find on a public page - grain spread a few centimeters deep, five hundred square meters of drying floor handling six tons of paddy - which is what lets us turn a household's harvest into the size of the drying yard in front of its house. Its limits: this is modern extension advice written for today's farmers, and we flag it as such wherever it is used; sun-drying grain on a hard floor is nonetheless an old technique whose arithmetic does not change with the century, so we take the ratio from it and nothing else.

isa-auf-fukugi-2011

What it is: A peer-reviewed article by Chen and Nakama on the Fukugi homestead windbreaks of Okinawa, in Arboriculture & Urban Forestry volume 37 issue 1 (2011). The authors surveyed the old Fukugi trees still standing around houses in several villages, recording their heights and which side of the house each one stands on.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the shape and orientation of a homestead windbreak - a line of trees set around the house, thickest on the sides the damaging wind comes from, most of the large trees to the north and then to the east - which is how the shelter belts around our farmsteads are drawn. Its limits: it measures trees that were planted long before the survey, so it records a surviving form rather than a documented historical practice; and Okinawa is subtropical and typhoon-swept, standing in here for the main islands of Japan, so the species and the exact wind sides are local while the principle we carry over is shelter on the weather side.

isis-dykepond

What it is: "The Circular Economy of the Dyke-Pond System" by Mae-Wan Ho, published on 9 October 2006 by the Institute of Science in Society. It is a summary account of the mulberry-dike and fish-pond farming of the Pearl River Delta in southern China, taking its figures from the research literature on that system (Ruddle and Zhong, Zhong and colleagues, and Deng).

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the dimensions and the working rhythm of the dike-and-pond landscape our delta maps are built from - ponds mostly rectangular, 0.4 to 0.6 hectares and 2 to 3 meters deep, dikes 6 to 10 meters wide, pigs and poultry kept on the dikes, the ponds drained two or three times a year and the bottom mud dredged up onto the dikes to raise and repair them - together with the system's fourteenth-century origins. Its limits: it is a secondary summary from an advocacy organization rather than the original field studies, so its numbers are only as reliable as the work it draws on; those studies measured the system in the late twentieth century, when its crop mix answered modern markets, even though the dike-and-pond form itself is far older; and it is southern China, not Japan.

jaanus-yashikimon

What it is: The entry for yashikimon 屋敷門 in JAANUS, the Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System, an online dictionary of Japanese art and architectural terms. It defines the word as the front gate of a warrior's manor house and illustrates it with the former Tojin yashiki gate of 1740, now at Kofukuji in Nagasaki.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for vocabulary - what the formal front gate of a walled residence is called and what one looks like - when naming and drawing the gates on our compound plans. Its limits: it is a specialist dictionary, which is to say a compact summary rather than a survey, and its illustrated example is a single eighteenth-century gate; and the term as JAANUS defines it belongs to a warrior's residence, so nothing about a farmstead's gate or about what such a gate meant for a farming household's standing can be sourced to it.

japanese-wiki-corpus

What it is: The English rendering of the Japanese Wikipedia article on jori-sei 条里制, the ancient grid system for subdividing farmland, hosted on the Japanese Wiki Corpus, a collection of Japanese Wikipedia articles translated into English by Japan's National Institute of Information and Communications Technology. The article sets out the geometry: a basic unit about 109 meters square, thirty-six of them making a ri, each unit divided into ten strips, the grid lines generally north-south and east-west but tilted in a fair number of regions, with land first recorded this way in 743.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for that grid module and its proportions, which is the frame our regular field patterns are laid out on and the reason a long-settled plain reads as ruled rather than as a patchwork. Its limits: it is an encyclopedia article, a tertiary summary, so we take the plain geometry and dates and not its interpretation; it is a translation rather than the Japanese original; and jori was an ancient state land system whose regularity survived only where the ground and the centuries allowed, so a grid this tidy suits a broad old plain and not every valley we draw.

- Limits: **HONEST** - the modern-formula, colonial-canal-calibration and small-ditch limits are all

geography-hub-satoyama

What it is: "Japan's Satoyama Landscapes", an article on The Geography Hub, a general-audience educational geography site that publishes explainers under headings like cultural, historical and biological geography. It carries no named author and no date. The piece surveys satoyama, the managed mosaic of coppiced woodland, paddy, grassland and water that sits between a Japanese village and the mountain behind it, how centuries of cutting and gathering produced it, and how it has fared since.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives, in plain terms, the three things we use for drawing a village's wood edge: that fallen leaves were gathered for fertilizer, that oak and chestnut were cut back on a cycle for firewood and charcoal, and that cutting to the stump let light onto the forest floor and kept an undergrowth alive there. It is a popular secondary overview rather than a field study or a piece of scholarship, and it is unsigned and undated, so we use it for the character of the practice and take nothing quantitative from it - no rotation length, no yield, no distance from the houses - and where our maps need a number it comes from elsewhere.

EOF cat > r2.html <<'EOF'

guernica-night-soil

What it is: "Raising a Stink", a November 2021 piece by Lina Zeldovich in Guernica, a nonprofit magazine of art and politics, adapted from her book on human waste and sanitation. It describes the night-soil economy of premodern and early modern Japan - human excrement treated as a valuable farm commodity rather than as refuse, with collection contracts, contested collection rights and disputes over price - and sets it against European practice of the same centuries.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is where we get the shape of the bargain that makes a privy a valued thing rather than a nuisance: annual contracts called tsuke-tsubo in which a farmer paid a town household in rice for a year's collection, and wealthier farmers supplying a lord's estate with firewood and seedlings for the privilege of emptying its toilets. It is a magazine adaptation of a popular book rather than a peer-reviewed study, though it quotes historians of Japan such as Susan B. Hanley, and the academic paper standing behind part of it could not be re-opened - so we use it for the existence and the form of these arrangements, who paid whom in what, and not for prices, volumes or rates.

What it is: A 2019 English-language article on IHCSA Cafe, the cultural information site of Japan's International Hospitality and Conference Service Association, written with the cooperation of the local Harie Shozu no Sato committee. It describes the Harie district in Shiga - "the village of living water" - where spring water rises into kabata, built basins inside and beside the houses, and explains how households use that water and how the community looks after it.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the character of a village water point rather than for any measurement: that one source served drinking, cooking and washing, and that the place where water was drawn was also where villagers stopped to talk - which is why a well on our maps is drawn as somewhere people gather and not as plumbing. It is a short institutional piece written with the village's own preservation committee to introduce the place to foreign readers, and it describes a surviving village as it is today, so it is evidence for a continuing practice rather than a documented historical one; Harie is also unusual in having spring water at every door, which most villages did not.

    n_water=0; buried=0; samples=[]

# Lessons from ch33 (three audit rounds, two full rewrites)

New molds that appeared AFTER the ch39/ch41 lists were already being avoided. Grep for these after every rewrite.

1. **Diminutive hedge.** "a little X / a bit Y / a small Z" hit ~35 in 16k words. It's the essay's politeness turned into a tic; it shrinks every reaction uniformly. Keep ≤8 where smallness is the point.
2. **"X is what Ys me" cleft.** "the 'too' is what kills me," "that's the part I can't put down," "here's what got me coldest." ~17 at peak. It ranks reactions instead of having them. Say the plain spoken form.
3. **"And then / Then" as the universal pivot.** 33 at peak. Every beat became thing-then-turn. Cut to single digits; let discoveries arrive unannounced or as a question.
4. **Time-boxed joy.** "for one second I'm thrilled," "for half a second I was glad." Every pleasure allotted a literal second before the shadow. Let some beats be warm the whole way.
5. **Quantified time tags + fact drift.** "an hour ago" ×5, "ninety seconds ago," "nine minutes ago" — invented intervals that contradicted each other. One continuous scene; say "still standing in the same scorch marks."
6. **Callback tokens re-quoted verbatim 3–6 times** ("melt the universe" ×5, "that fucking RULED" ×4, the ch3 FIX line ×3). A callback loses its jolt on the third firing; quote once, reference obliquely after.
7. **Quote-fragment beat openers** hit 29/75 even after "fixing" them; the fix pass converted openers to `"fragment," and I ___`, same grid. Real fix: reaction first, then the quote; or a question at a character; or paraphrase.
8. **Tag triads in the closing**: "X, and I'm glad. Y, and I'm cold. Z, and I don't know what to do with that." Bred by threading feeling into a summary chain. Vary syntax per item; let one run long.
9. **"Here's what / here's the part" essay setups** (×5). Drop the frame.
10. **Scheduled second feeling**: "The queasy comes second," "it also unnerves me, a beat later." The two-feelings mold reappearing as a timetable.

Because the healer on this team is the one who's "worse than useless against cancer," he says so at the hospital every Saturday, and the founding legend of Robot turns on a death that Hip's power specifically can't touch, and I got a shiver I can't justify. It's probably nothing. It's lodged in my head like a splinter anyway. And "we don't know who he collaborated with," oh, that's the one with the drop under it: Daedalus is a myth, Robot is a hundred million dollars a year of research, and somebody, somewhere, has the blueprints to the most trustworthy mind in that building. The one who can't lie. The one Hip deleted footage in front of. That last one stung going down.

> "We've always suspected the Architects of Tomorrow had a hand in your creation, my friend."  Each of Alien's eyestalks turn toward Robot.  "This does support that theory.

I was about to say it. I had the name in my mouth and I didn't want to be the one, and then Al says it, casually, "we've always suspected," every eyestalk on Rob, "my friend," and my jaw is on the floor. The ARCHITECTS OF TOMORROW built Robot? The mechanist collective with a near-monopoly on mad scientists, the org Rastrick ran to with Mediquest's research and a ninety-million-dollar bounty on his head, and I said "oh no" before I'd finished the sentence. Because think about what Rob IS to this team. He's the security. He's the surveillance, the comms, the R&D, the thoughtscan dampeners, the keeper of the deleted footage, the mind whose honesty is structurally guaranteed and therefore the thing every person in that building leans their whole weight on, and if the Architects made him, then the enemy has held a key to that building since before Luna arrived. Since before Sunbeam died, maybe. Hip pours a hundred million a year into a lab run by a machine whose maker might be on the other side, and I felt the floor of the whole story shift under that. And ALWAYS? "We've always suspected"? Excuse me? Years? The two non-human founders have been privately carrying this and nobody thought to tell the class, and either Hip has known and never told the team or two of his founders have a shared theory they never briefed him on, and both of those made me want to bang on the table. And Rob doesn't deny it. He's sitting right there and he doesn't deny it. Does ROB suspect? Has he suspected this whole time, alone, in a body he didn't choose?

> 'Where there's smoke, there's fire,' is it not?  Or as my people would say, 'a shed carapace means a larger form is near'."

And he does the idiom bit, "is it not?", and I laughed, honestly, because the timing is so alien: cracking the old joke while announcing the end of the world. But then the proverb, and the proverb is not a joke. "A shed carapace means a larger form is near." I said "oh no" under my breath and then read it again just to feel it, and every hair on my arms went up, and I've read it four times since. The chassis in the alley is the shed skin. The thing that made it is bigger, and close. And hold on, his people's version is about CARAPACES. They shed. Somewhere out there is a culture whose "where there's smoke, there's fire" is "something bigger left this skin behind," which means growing by abandoning a body is so normal to them it became a PROVERB, and he dropped that into a slideshow about Rob's wreckage like it was small talk, and I'm going to be thinking about Al's childhood all week. There's something tender under it too, and it got to me: he's consoling his friend. He reached past the human cliché into his own faraway culture's folk wisdom to tell Rob how to read the danger, an eight-foot exile offering the only comfort he has, which is a sentence from home. For a machine watching footage of his own ruined body, "this was a molt, not a corpse" is almost kind and absolutely terrifying, and it's the line I'm going to be repeating to people.

> "Well fuck, that just clinches it."  Luna rises slowly to her feet, shooting Tempest a grateful smile as the Latina lets her arm slide down to rest supportively around Luna's waist.  "This is all connected.  Trenchcoat is wrapped up with this Mediquest shitshow, no question."

SHE'S UP. Luna rises, "slowly," she's not all the way back, and the first thing out of her mouth is "well fuck," and I snorted into my hand, because Al just said something that belongs carved over a temple door and Luna's entire response is "well fuck." The tonal whiplash is SO her, and it's the sound of her coming back online. She returns to herself every time she's handed a case: the dumpster, the safe ripped out of Bloodhound's wall, the ring-tan on Bella's finger that nobody else saw, and remembering that last one made me proud of her all over again. And the grateful smile at Tempest, whose arm slides down to her waist and STAYS, "supportively," the scold and the hug fully merged now, and I'm so warm about those two. A month ago Luna thought "bicha" meant bitch and Tempest let her; today Tempest is the one holding her up while she talks, and that's a friendship I'd have bet against in chapter eight. "Mediquest shitshow." Her taxonomy, and I'm grinning, because everyone else in this room says "the Architects of Tomorrow" and "Heroic Reinforcement Assessments" in full and Luna will not give any of it a proper noun. "This is all connected," the vigilante's creed, the one that's been right every single time in this story, from the bank being a decoy to Bloodhound's Mediquest contract, and her track record is the reason I'd follow her nose over anyone's at that table.

> "For real?"  Phoenix slowly sits back down.  "Are you sure?"

Phoenix sits. "Slowly" too, the second slow motion in a row, one girl rising and one sinking, and the little "for real?" is so Phoenix it made me smile: she's been in a courthouse all morning and she's three plot beats behind everyone. "Are you sure?" isn't doubt. Awww, it's her asking Luna to hold the certainty for her so she knows where to aim. Phoenix, honey.

> "Positive.  I mean, there probably aren't a hundred supes in the country with a tier 9 rating, so the odds that one just coincidentally shows up in Delaware at the same time as this Mediquest fuckery?  That alone should make us assume it's all related.  But this next-level mechanist crap makes it a sure bet."

And this is the one spot in Luna's whole case where I have to admit I wobbled. "There probably aren't a hundred supes in the country with a tier 9 rating," okay, but this TABLE has two of them, Hip's a tier-9 healer, Al has "consistently demonstrated" tier-9 bruiser numbers, both parked in Delaware, so the lightning-strike framing sagged on me mid-sentence. The coincidence argument is fine as a hunch and shaky as math, and I think Luna knows it, because she shores it up immediately with "but this next-level mechanist crap makes it a sure bet," and THAT I buy completely. The jammer is the actual evidence. The tier-9 thing is just vibes, and I love that she can hear the difference inside her own rant. Also, "Mediquest fuckery." "Next-level mechanist crap." Three for three now, and the contempt is the method, and it's making me giggle: if you never let a thing sound official, you never get impressed by it, and getting impressed is how people get conned. She'd have refused to say "Heroic Reinforcement Assessments" on principle.

> Luna takes a steadying breath, her dark blue eyes flicking nervously around the room.  "We know Mediquest restarted their Nexase research, trying to resume Doctor Rastrick's work.  What if they partnered with the Architects of Tomorrow to do it?  They wouldn't be the first greedy corporation looking to make billions from patenting mad scientist tech.

"Nervously." Her eyes are flicking around the room the way they did at that first podium a month ago, when it bent under her grip, and she's still afraid of this table and she does it anyway, and that gets me every time. The theory itself, oh, it's GOOD: Mediquest brings the legitimacy, the Architects bring the mad science, and Rastrick, who walked out of one and into the other, is the hinge, and I sat up straighter when the joint clicked. That closes the loop the big Nexase briefing left dangling, why a dead 2009 trial has mercs kicking doors in RIGHT NOW, and I'd been waiting a month for someone to close it. "They wouldn't be the first greedy corporation looking to make billions from patenting mad scientist tech," and, wait, there's a PATTERN? There are precedents? This has happened before, it's a business model, and she waved at a whole industry in one clause, and that's a worldbuilding grenade I'm still picking shrapnel out of. In a story called Informed Consent, a company whose product is legitimacy, consent forms and trials and recalls, in bed with the people who build plasma cannons into coat sleeves. I don't like how well that fits.

> Mediquest provides the legitimacy and finds test subjects, with the Architects feeding them the secret sauce.  Rastrick could be personally involved, or handed the project to a flunky.  Either way, it explains Trenchcoat's expensive toys, AND how he'd know Robby's vulnerabilities."

"The secret sauce." I laughed and then felt gross about it, because that's MBA-speak, she's describing a mad scientist as a proprietary ingredient, and the awful part is that's exactly the register this thing operates in. But one phrase stopped me. "Finds test subjects." Luna says it as corporate logistics, Mediquest's half of the partnership, and I read it and thought: Bella. Bella Brown's kids. A man in a fortune of gear hanging around a women's shelter for a month, and a mother who's certain her children are safe and certain no one can help, and the longer I sit with those two facts the worse they fit together. What if Trenchcoat wasn't there for a custody grab at all? What if "finds test subjects" is literally what he was doing? I don't know. Luna didn't say it. But she said "test subjects" in the same sentence as "Architects," and the shelter is where she first met him, and I can't unthink it now. "Rastrick could be personally involved, or handed the project to a flunky," and I appreciated her leaving the door open on that, the vigilante not overclaiming. And "AND how he'd know Robby's vulnerabilities," the half of her theory that closes the Rob loop, delivered with the caps of someone who knows she's just tied the two scariest things in the room together, and I'd cheer if I weren't busy being scared.

> "The available data supports other conclusions."  Robot's head swivels to face Luna.  "However, if my creator was affiliated with the Architects of Tomorrow, it would explain the effectiveness of the countermeasures deployed against me."

"The available data supports other conclusions." STOP. That's verbatim. Word for word, that's what Rob said to Luna in the very first briefing, when she pointed at the Mediquest building and said the robbery was a cover, and he told her the data supported other conclusions and she stammered about a contact she couldn't name, and remembering that stammer next to this podium voice put a lump in my throat. Same sentence, same girl, same wall, a month later. Eli, I see you, and I'm delighted. Except, and this is the part I cheered, last time he STOPPED there. This time he keeps going, "however," and concedes the point, on the record, about his own maker, and the shape of it made me laugh too, the maximum pedantic brush-off followed instantly by the walk-back. No. However, yes. Rob agreeing with Luna's theory of Rob, head swiveled toward her, no emotion in the voice, and I supplied all of it. The most honest mind in that building just said out loud that the enemy might have BUILT him, and I'm not okay. I keep thinking about the self-destruct mechanisms he builds into every creation so nobody can seize them. Did somebody build one into him?

> Luna nods.  "There are two other things as well.  The main one is Bloodhound's kidnapping.  I keep replaying the other night in my head, and something doesn't sit right.  Robby, can you display a timeline of Tuesday evening, starting from when Phoenix called Bloodhound's cellphone?"

"I keep replaying the other night in my head." Of course she does. She's been replaying it since she kicked a dent into that dumpster, and picturing her lying awake running the tape while everyone else was busy with Trenchcoat and confessions and psychic ambushes made me ache for her. "Something doesn't sit right," and I trust that sentence from her more than I'd trust a signed affidavit from anyone else at that table. And watch her take the room: "Robby, can you display a timeline." That's the podium voice, the one that out-detected the whole team over a smudge on the pavement, and hearing it come out STEADIER made me absurdly proud. "Two other things," she says, and gives the main one first, such a Luna structure, saving the smaller thing for last, and I'm already suspicious of what "smaller" means.

> "Affirmative."  The screen instantly updates to a list of times and actions.

Instantly. He had it ready; Rob has probably had this timeline sitting in a buffer since Tuesday, waiting for someone to ask the right question, and I grinned like a kid watching the two best detectives on this team, the vigilante and the machine, just CLICK into gear together. Hell yeah. Favorite duo in the book. No fuss. Screen. Go.

> "Okay, look."  Luna walks to the screen, pointing.  "We call Bloodhound.  We text Bloodhound.  We figure out someone has his phone, and call the FBI.  They submit that emergency warrant to whatever federal judge.  During ALL that time, Bloodhound's phone STILL shows as being at his house.  But AFTER the phone company gets the order for the location trace, only THEN does the signal disappear, until the phone suddenly turns up in that dumpster by the docks, a few minutes later."

Okay, THIS is why I love her. She lays it out with her finger on the wall and I followed every step like it was happening again: the call, the text, and then "we figure out someone has his phone," which was the moment that night turned, and I remembered the lurch of it. The FBI, the judge, and through all of it the phone sits obediently at home, and "obediently" is my word, not hers, because that's how it reads, a phone behaving like a decoy, and it's creepy and it's a puzzle and I love a puzzle. Then the phone company gets the order. THEN it moves. The kidnappers didn't react to the Guardians being suspicious, Phoenix's texts didn't spook them. They reacted to the paperwork, and I got the good kind of chills, the puzzle kind, and then the bad kind right behind them. And "whatever federal judge," I barked. WHATEVER federal judge! Ma'am, your entire deduction rests on that judge's signature, the warrant is the tripwire, the paperwork is the CLUE, and you cannot make yourself care what his name was. The eye-roll survived contact with being helped by the system, and I love her for it and I'm worried about her for it too. "A few minutes later," too. Not hours. Whoever moved that phone was fast, and close, and waiting, and "waiting" is the word that put me on edge. And the part I really sat up for: Rob flagged the anomaly on Wednesday, "shortly after the FBI began tracking the phone, it disappeared," and Hip's theory was that the texts spooked them into ditching a liability. Hip was wrong. On the record, confidently wrong, and that's rare enough in this book that I blinked at it, and Luna has looked at the same data he had and found the real trigger, and watching her out-detect the man who reads people for a living gave me a real buzz. The warrant was the tripwire. Which means someone saw the warrant, and "someone saw the warrant" has only a few possible meanings and none of them are Scoundrels.

> She turns to face the room, her expression grim.  "There's no way these Scoundrels have compromised a major telecom provider.  But the Architects of Tomorrow?"  She shakes her head.  "This whole thing only makes sense if the Architects are pulling the strings, and some high-tier mechanist hired the Scoundrels - whoever Trenchcoat's mysterious 'employer' is, probably Doctor Rastrick himself."

And she says it. Rastrick. The ninety-million-dollar man, the one who wiped Mediquest's servers and vanished, and I got that satisfied click-of-the-lock feeling, because that name's been lying around since the big briefing and nobody had picked it up and walked it over to the guy in the alley until this second. And oh, the irony: Luna herself, a month ago, described him as keeping his nose "relatively clean," and now she's naming him as a kidnapper and a tier-9's paymaster, eating her own assessment in front of the room, and it delighted me, and then it scared me. I believe her. I don't think she's proven it; "only makes sense if" is doing a lot of lifting, and I can picture a mid-tier mechanist with a friend at the phone company. But the SHAPE is right, and that's the part that scares me: the Scoundrels are rent-a-muscle, the two from the bank don't even know the two from the hotel, and muscle doesn't tap a telecom. Somebody with a LAB does. And she's just standing there, grim, having told a room of superheroes they're hunting a legend with a bounty on his head. Nobody laughs at her. GOOD.

> Luna takes a deep breath, locking eyes with Psycheout.  "Headcase-whisperer is right about one thing; going back to the feds risks another leak.  I..."

"Headcase-whisperer." She's using the nickname to AGREE with her, and that's the tell with Luna, the insults are how she says "you're one of us," and getting one in the same sentence as a concession is so deeply her that I grinned. "Right about ONE thing," the most grudging concession in the English language, and I'm snorting. And "locking eyes with Psycheout," not with Hip; the person she chooses to look at while making her case is the psychic who covered Phoenix's hand and told Moonlight God would forgive her, and watching Luna pick her, without being able to say why, made me hopeful in a way I didn't expect this chapter to let me be.

> She casts her gaze around the room, her dark blue eyes pleading.  "I know I'm always... skeptical, about... collaboration.  And - and I'm sorry.  Um, about before.  It's my fault you all got hurt, and -"  Her voice catches.  "I'm sorry.  But please.  Don't go to SCUS with this.  Going federal again is just gonna spring another leak.  It'll blow up the investigation, and maybe get Bloodhound killed."

"I know I'm always... skeptical, about... collaboration." Luna naming her own defect out loud, with the ellipses, and I'd have hugged her for that alone. And "it's my fault you all got hurt." There it is. That's the thing Hip installed in her a few minutes ago coming back out of her mouth as her own belief, mid-argument, in front of everyone, exactly as instructed, and I felt it like a door closing. She remembered. Of course she remembered. Eli, I winced at "and - and I'm sorry. Um, about before," because that stammer is the one from the first briefing, the withdrawal-tremor voice, and she's not in withdrawal now. She's in something else he gave her. And the awful part is that the apology is stapled to the best argument in the room: don't go federal, it leaks, and a leak might get Bloodhound killed. She's pleading, "but please," her eyes going around the table, and she's RIGHT, and she's right while believing she's the reason Rob got torn apart, and I can't pull those two facts apart. The girl who stood in Moonlight's reading room a month ago insisting "we have to stop him" is now begging her teammates for the thing she wants and apologizing for existing on the way there, and I had to read that one with my jaw set. I'm so proud of her case. I'm sick about the shape she's making it in. I can't separate the two, and I don't think you want me to.

> "I agree."  I make sure to meet everyone's gaze, letting my confidence radiate, my voice steady and firm.  "That's a brilliant deduction, Luna.  YOU'RE brilliant.  And I think you're spot-on.  Does anyone disagree?"

"I make sure to meet everyone's gaze, letting my confidence radiate." He's narrating the stagecraft again, and every time I catch it fresh it bothers me more than the last time: not "I agree" and done, but I'm meeting every eye, radiating, steady and firm, the way he told me last night he was "glad for the hours I've spent ruminating" so he could "shepherd" the girls' reactions to Moonlight. The man REHEARSES sincerity, and I clock it every single time now. The swing comes next. "YOU'RE brilliant." From "you don't know" to "YOU'RE brilliant" inside one debrief, break her and then crown her, and I can feel from here how good that must feel to her, and that's the problem. That's the cycle I've been watching without a name for it: grumpy girl, proud of you, that's enough, proud of you. The praise is real, and it's also the reward for having taken the hit correctly, and I want to shake him for making both of those true. "Does anyone disagree?" is such a leader's sentence, too, because after "YOU'RE brilliant" from him, who on earth is going to? I'd have voted yes and I don't even like him right now.

> Moonlight gives a sharp nod of conviction.  Tempest cracks her knuckles, a predatory grin spreading across her face.  Phoenix pumps her fist as Psycheout inclines her head solemnly.  Alien's many eyestalks swivel to a single point of focus, while Robot's eye-lights flash a silent affirmative.

Roll call! One vote per body, and I am OBSESSED with how differently each of them says yes. Moonlight: "sharp nod of conviction," and oh, Moon, conviction is the only currency she has left to spend on belonging, and it hurts to see her spend it so fast. Tempest cracks her knuckles with a PREDATORY grin, and I barked a laugh, because Tempest promised to punch Bloodhound for Luna and has clearly upgraded that to whoever took him. Phoenix pumps her fist, and I felt a pang of affection and a pang of worry right behind it, because she doesn't need the argument, she needs a target, and she just got handed one after a morning of having nothing to hit. Psycheout "inclines her head solemnly," the smallest yes in the row, and I'd love to know what that solemnity is weighing. Alien next: "many eyestalks swivel to a single point of focus," and that made me sit up, because he usually points them everywhere, one per Guardian, and for this all of them converge, the most attention I've ever seen him give anything. And ROB. His eye-lights flash "a silent affirmative," the catchphrase in Morse, and I grinned right before it hurt, because that's the mind whose maker just got put on trial, voting to go after whoever made him, without hesitating and without being asked, and if the Architects built him then that's a machine choosing against its own origin in one flash of light. I'm in awe of him. Six yeses, six completely different ways of saying it. That's a FAMILY, Eli. Whatever else is going on in that room, that's a family.

> Luna lets out a shaky breath, leaning heavily on the table.  "Th-thanks, Hip.  Um, and I really am sorry, for -"

"Th-thanks, Hip." With the stammer. That's the exact line, letter for letter, from the end of her first briefing, "Th-thanks, Hip. I, uh...", when she was white-knuckling the podium and he'd just defended her to the team, and I remember grinning at it then, the tough girl going shy. Tonight the same syllables make me feel sick. Same bit, different organ. A month later she's leaning on the table because her legs are going, and the thanks is for the same thing, he stood up for her in a room, he always stands up for her in rooms, and he's also the one who put her on the floor first, and I can't hold those two facts side by side without something creaking. I don't think Luna can see both halves from where she's standing, and I'm not sure I could either if I were her. And she's STILL trying to apologize. "I really am sorry, for -" He's going to cut her off, I'd bet anything, and he's going to be gracious about it, and the grace is going to be his.

> "There'll be time for that later, gumshoe girl."  I beam with pride.  "But you said there were two things, and your Bloodhound deductions were the main one.  What's the other?"

"Gumshoe girl." Add it to the collection, grumpy girl, wild girl, worry girl, sassy girl, and now gumshoe girl, and the double-take I did was at realizing each one gets minted at the precise moment she does something he likes. I laughed, I did; it's a cute nickname and she's earned it and there's real pleasure in hearing him call her a detective right after she detected. And "there'll be time for that later," so he keeps her apology on account, not waived, deferred, and I noticed the interest accruing. He beams, and the beam is real, and I'd be lying if I said I didn't feel some of that warmth myself, and that's how the beam works. And the good-leader question, right on cue: what's the other thing. He heard "two things" and tracked it, and I liked him for tracking it, ugh. So did I. Here we go.

> "You."  Luna meets my eyes, her face serious.

"You." One word and the floor tilted under me. She meets his eyes. Not looking down, not away, not turned by anyone's fingers: Luna, on her own power, looking straight at the man who took her chin, and saying the other thing is him, and I felt myself lift with her, right there, goosebumps and all. The tsundere who calls him leads-from-behind and dealer-in-chief has been doing homework on her boss, and she's about to show it, and I'm gripping the edge of the desk.

> "Trenchcoat said you and his employer had 'common interests'.  Wikipedia says you became a superhero in 2012.  That's the right timeframe for you to have gotten your powers after taking Mediquest's recalled Nexase.  I think that's the 'common interest', and Doctor Rastrick..."  Luna takes a deep breath.

Wikipedia. She read his Wikipedia page, and I grinned, because of COURSE she did; she's the one who snapped at Phoenix, "it's on his fucking Wikipedia page," about the murdered girlfriends, the one who told Tempest and Phoenix they'd joined a team without doing the most basic research on the man leading it. Luna did the research. And she's put it together from the OUTSIDE, from public facts and one villain's phrase, and it's the thing I've been carrying since that night on his couch with Tempest: "I got my powers back in 2012. Which, as we learned today, might have been from taking recalled NeuroSpark." He told Tempest that in the dark. He has never told the team. And here's Luna, who wasn't on that couch, arriving at the same place by pure arithmetic, and I grinned, and the chill arrived a beat after. The recall was 2010, the bottles had been on shelves for a year, and Jackie got her powers from them, and I felt a pang at Jackie's name, a person I've been worrying about for weeks turning up as a data point. Slipstream too. And so, probably, did the man in the white and red uniform, and I said it slowly to myself to make sure I believed it. The title just turned over in my hands. "Common interests" isn't money and it isn't a merger. It's Nexase. It's in his BRAIN, and that thought made me put the phone down. And Doctor Rastrick, dot dot dot, and she takes a breath, and I'm holding mine.

> "I think he knows how your healing powers REALLY work."

REALLY. In caps. Eli. ELI. Okay, okay, in order, because this went off in four directions at once and I need to walk them.

Start with the obvious one, the one that made my hands go still: that's the biggest mystery in the book, and it's been HIS mystery, stated in his own voice from the very first chapter. Why does the energy flow farther than it heals? Why can Luna FEEL it in her chest when it's only fixing her ribs? Rob's scanners can't answer it and Al's alien quantum tech can't, and Hip once mused, half-joking, "maybe Robot's right, and I get my own subtle effect others don't," and waved it off for lack of evidence, and I remember filing that line as charming. Now somebody might have the evidence, and my whole spine tightened at the thought.

Then there's who the somebody is, and that's not even the worst part, though it's bad: a mad scientist with ninety million dollars on his head who apparently wants to MEET him, and the invitation is somehow scarier than an attack would have been. He sent a man in fifty million dollars of gear to deliver it, and the courier's price tag is the data point that made me swallow. And the courier's parting line, "you'll regret not having taken the opportunity," which I'd filed as villain bluster in the alley, now reads like a man who knows what's in the envelope, and I don't want to know what's in the envelope. I do. I don't.

And then the one that made me set the whole thing down. Every unexplained fact about that power lines up behind her sentence like iron filings, and I made myself go through them one at a time. Psycheout addicted in two days when Rob's own numbers say it takes a week, and nobody chased that number, and I didn't either, and I should have. Effortless with his own team, exhausting with strangers, which I'd accepted as a quirk of the power and now can't. Phoenix's fire climbing because she's stopped thinking of it as hers, and I read that as growth at the time, I cheered it, and now it sounds like something else and I feel foolish for cheering. Tempest, who swore on camera that she'd never share a man, and I watched that vow get quietly dissolved over twenty chapters and called it love, and re-reading it as a symptom is the single worst thing this chapter did to me. Luna's own "I can't stop thinking about it" in the reading room, and Luna is the person who just handed him this theory, standing inside her own evidence without seeing it, and I could see it, and I wanted to tap on the glass. If someone knows how it REALLY works, then, oh no. Moonlight's "it doesn't have any mind-altering effects, it just makes you feel good" was never a fact. It was a hope, and she's the team's scientist and she was guessing, and she's sitting at that table apologizing for other things. And that means every warning he's ever given about informed consent was a warning about the wrong thing, and I had to sit back from the screen, because the title of this book just flipped over in my hands for the second time in two paragraphs, and this time it took fifty-eight chapters of disclosures with it. He may be as uninformed as anyone he warned, and I don't know whether that makes it better or so much worse.

And the last one, which I don't know what to do with: he didn't take the meeting. He said "I'll pass" to the one person offering to tell him what he is. I can't decide whether that no was the healthiest thing he's done in fifty-nine chapters or the most frightened, and there's a third option I like even less, which is that he'd rather not find out on the record. The loudest thing on the page, though, is a silence. This narrator annotates EVERYTHING, he tells me when he's radiating confidence and when he's shepherding reactions and when he's pressing forward, and the chapter ends on Luna's line with no narration after it at all. No smile. No managed beat. No "I keep my pulse steady." The one moment he doesn't tell me what he's doing. Luna's face is serious; she's not accusing him. She's just the only person in the room who reads Wikipedia, and she's handed him a mirror, and then the chapter ENDS, Eli, before he looks in it, and I made a noise at my screen. Out loud, in a room, in front of six women who are all dosed, somebody just said "nobody knows what this does to you," and nobody reacts, because the page runs out first.

Okay but can we TALK about this chapter, because it's two thousand words of people sitting at a conference table and I feel like I got hit by a bus. Two buses, from opposite directions. The first is Hip and Luna, and the line I go back to is "I've never seen Luna shrink into herself before, but I press forward," because it's the first time the narration has shown me the lever with his hand on it. Not implied. Shown. And what wrecks me is how it's built out of things I LIKED. The "Deal?" from chapter one, which I thought was cute. "Remember this feeling" from the psychic exercise, which I cheered yesterday, and I'd cheer it again, and that's the trap. The shoulder squeeze. "I'm proud of you." He's not doing anything new, he's doing everything he's always done, at a girl who'd already flinched, and telling me he noticed, and every time I re-read that clause I like him less. Your blurb calls him the most reliable narrator I'll ever meet, Eli, and I hear it differently tonight. He IS reliable, that's the joke of it. He reports the chin-turn in FULL. He just doesn't think there's anything in it worth reporting, and that's the thing that's going to keep me up.

The second bus is that Psycheout was in the room for it, with the sense on, and that's what I can't stop turning over. She got a "strange look," and then she spent the rest of the debrief quietly running the opposite program, and the one that still gives me chills is "God WILL forgive you," because that's the sentence Hip cannot say. She never once contradicted him to his face and she contradicted him three times, and writing that out gave me a giddy thrill of dread. And he said "well said." I've spent two chapters wondering what she told Tempest that Tempest heard as "babosadas about papi," and I think this chapter is the answer she couldn't get out on Alien's couch: she's watched someone be magnanimous before. This week. In family court. She almost missed it. I don't know if she's right about him, and I'd give a lot to know, and until then I'm going to hold onto the fact that she's the only one in that building running the check.

Also: Rob. I did not have "the Architects of Tomorrow may have made Robot" on my card for this chapter and I'm still dizzy. It makes me re-see everything, the self-destructs he builds into every gadget, the hundred million a year, the note nobody ever authenticated, and, oh no, THAT pause. The one-second pause he took while Hip deleted footage in front of him, which I read as politeness at the time and now can't read at all. If the enemy knows his seams, then the most secure building in Delaware has a door somebody else holds a key to, and I do not like standing in it. And Al's carapace proverb is going to live in my head for a week.

Now Moonlight and Phoenix, because they were at that table the whole time and I've barely said their names in this wrap-up, and that's on me. Moonlight said the chapter's key number and couldn't get through it without apologizing, and Phoenix sat two chairs down from her and nobody, not the leader, not the psychic, not the narration, touched it, and I kept waiting for the moment someone would and it never came. One of them apologizing for nothing, one of them unable to sit beside her, both waiting on a forgiveness the leader has explicitly withheld and the psychic has explicitly granted, and I'm carrying both of them out of this chapter like two hot plates.

And Luna. Can I just, for a second, about Luna. She ran that debrief. She flinched, she folded, she got up, and then she ran it, and I was so proud of her by the end that I was grinning at a wall. The moment I'll keep is her turning the whole thing on her boss with a Wikipedia citation, calm, serious, looking him in the eye. And lining this up against her first briefing made me GIDDY, it's so exact: Robot's line, her stammer, "Th-thanks, Hip," a girl at a screen out-detecting a room, except back then she was hiding a secret for someone else and here she's uncovering one about him. She hasn't stopped being the person who told Moonlight, on day two, that they had to stop him. She's learned to do it with a projector, and I'm so stupidly proud of her I could cry.

That's also the thing I'd shake you by the shoulders about, Eli: this is the first chapter where the conspiracy actually gets ASSEMBLED, collectively, on a wall, six people each contributing the one piece only they could see. Psycheout the federal triage. Rob the jamming. Moonlight the price tag. Hip the battery weight. Al the Architects. Luna the warrant timeline and then the 2012 math. That's an ensemble-competence chapter, the whole team being excellent in sequence, and it's the exact inverse of the ch4 briefing where the same room dismissed her, and I loved that so much I almost forgot how sick the opening stretch made me.

Nothing got HEALED, though, and that's what's eating me. Phoenix is still two chairs down from Moonlight. Bella Brown just got handed proof that nobody can help her. Bloodhound's been gone four days and Luna is the only one who'll say the word "killed" out loud. And Hip said NO to the meeting; Trenchcoat said "you'll meet my employer eventually," and now the employer has a name and a reason and might know what Hip's power does to the women in that room, and I keep hearing "I'll pass" in his voice and not knowing what it cost him. What I'm actually scared of is Hip alone with his monitors tonight, hearing "REALLY work" on a loop and doing what he always does with something that hurts, which is take his own pulse and delete something. What I WANT, badly, is for Psycheout and Luna to already be having a conversation I haven't been allowed to hear. And hey, the comedy survived even THIS chapter, which is honestly wild: "not a primary determinant." "Affirmative" to an idiom check. "Whatever federal judge." Tempest's knuckles. Gumshoe girl. And the thing that still makes me laugh out loud is Hip beaming "well said" at the woman who had just, very gently, told the room he was wrong.
